Machine Learning in Social Science

“Computational social science is reshaping sociology, and this book highlights the critical role Chinese sociologists play in that transformation. Written by an exceptional team based in China, it offers bold and original chapters that push the boundaries of theory, method, and empirical inquiry. Essential reading for anyone interested in the frontiers of contemporary sociology.”
—Yu Xie, Bert G. Kerstetter ’66 University Professor of Sociology and Director of Center on Contemporary China, Princeton University

“This book provides an excellent introduction to how machine-learning methods can be used for addressing important social-science questions. The authors have accomplished the difficult task of writing clearly and accessibly about a highly technical subject. The book covers a broad range of topics and includes numerous examples illustrating how machine-learning techniques can be fruitfully applied in social-science research. Its non-technical exposition makes it highly accessible and well suited as an introductory textbook across several social-science disciplines.”
—Peter Hedström, Professor of Analytical Sociology, Linköping University. Senior Research Fellow at Nuffield College, Oxford University

Preface

The origin of this book can be traced back to 2020, when my team and I were conducting a series of studies that used unsupervised machine learning to analyze cultural texts and supervised machine learning to model social dynamics. We noticed a clear shift in the intellectual landscape. The rapid growth of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) was changing the foundations of social research. The wider availability of multisource information opened new possibilities for understanding collective behavior and social change, while progress in computational modeling made it possible to uncover patterns once hidden in the complexity of social life. For social science, this transformation has particular meaning. The field has long tried to understand the connections between individual experience and social structure, yet the growing complexity of modern life now calls for new ways of observation and analysis.

Building on this awareness, our research gradually evolved into a reflection on how computation reshapes the production of knowledge. Algorithms are no longer merely technical instruments; they have become part of the ways knowledge is created, interpreted, and sustained across the social sciences. In the changing context, this interdisciplinary field is entering a new period of integration and renewal. Computational methods now open wider perspectives and provide more refined tools for examining social life across multiple scales. From this realization emerged the idea for this book. Machine learning has entered many areas of the

PREFACE

social sciences, yet these endeavors remain scattered and without a shared foundation. We seek to weave a unified chain of them, to trace their common principles, and to offer a coherent account of how computation can deepen the study of society in the digital age.

Throughout the writing process, we found ourselves continually returning to a set of essential questions: as datafication becomes a defining condition of social life, and as algorithms become embedded in governance, culture, and everyday experience, how should social science reconceptualize prediction and explanation? How should it rethink the meanings of human action, structure, and significance within a new epistemic framework? These questions form the intellectual foundation of this book and guide its direction. Our purpose is to seek a renewed balance and dialogue between data and theory, between technology and the humanities.

Guided by this perspective, we focus on groups and communities that are often overlooked in grand narratives, as well as on cultural phenomena that traditional quantitative social science has struggled to capture in full. We seek to show how machine learning, especially supervised and unsupervised methods, can extend both the scope and depth of social research. Yet technology is not the ultimate concern of this book. It is, rather, a way of approaching a fuller understanding of society. Our hope is that this volume will serve as a practical guide for scholars, students, and readers interested in computational social science, helping to connect abstract algorithmic methods with the lived realities of human experience and to turn them into tools for interpreting people and their social worlds.

The completion of this book was made possible through the collaboration of my three co-authors, talented young scholars whom I have had the privilege to supervise. Their persistence, purpose, and passion have laid the foundation for this work. Together we have built one of the pioneering research teams in China dedicated to exploring the application of computational methods in interdisciplinary social science research, and we will continue to advance along this path.

With my co-authors, I would also like to express our sincere gratitude to the many colleagues whose generosity and expertise made this project possible. We owe special thanks to Xiaogang Wu, Anning Hu, Senhu Wang, Wansu Zhang, Wen Sun, Guangye He, and Ying Li, who assisted with data processing and offered thoughtful feedback that strengthened the manuscript. We are particularly grateful to Zhi Zhang,

CHAPTER 1
Introduction: The Rise of Machine Learning in Social Science

What is machine learning? Susan Athey of Stanford University, the first female economist to win the Clark Prize, defined machine learning in the context of social science, that is, to achieve tasks such as clustering, classification, and prediction by developing computer algorithms suitable for specific data (Athey 2018). To put it more precisely, machine learning tries to constantly optimize the performance standards of statistical calculation programs, enabling the program to achieve the task of “learning,” discovering data characteristics and making a statistical prediction, based on a large number of data features.<sup>1</sup>

In the early days of computer data processing technology, social scientists were skeptical of it as a tool to help study social problems. On the one hand, the complexity of human society is much greater than that of nature; on the other hand, the available data and computing tools in traditional social sciences are relatively limited. However, the rapid expansion of information and data in the network era has brought unprecedented opportunities to social science. As early as 2009, Lazer and his colleagues predicted in Science that the era of computing social science would dawn (Lazer et al. 2009; Lazer and Jason 2017). In the past ten years, the

1 Machine learning and data mining are often used as equivalent concepts in many disciplines and academic practice. Comparatively, whereas machine learning emphasizes that computer programs apply existing data information to new research objects, which is the so-called “learning,” data mining emphasizes the extraction and simplification of data features.

Y. CHEN ET AL.

network has developed and research has accumulated rapidly. In addition to Lazer’s original expectation, a new wave is surging. With the development of machine learning, the emergence of large-scale social survey data and big data, and the improvement of computer processing performance, the era of solving problems related to data, algorithms, and computing power, as well as realizing social understanding and prediction has dawned.

Another major impediment to the advancement of machine learning in social science has to do with the paradigm shift that is difficult to perform. Social scientists, whose main approach to the causal explanation of social processes is through description, explanation, and induction, are not accustomed to the social predictions that machine learning can achieve. Different from the generative modeling followed by classical statistical analysis, predictive modeling, as employed in machine learning, can account for model uncertainty and out-of-sample performance (Donoho 2017). Although social theory and data are rarely used to make predictions over a long period due to the complexity of social systems, the significance of prediction in the history of social science research cannot be ignored (Martin et al. 2016; Chen et a l. 2021). Machine learning techniques can help interpolate potential indicators, generate new theories, and improve causal inference, which brings social prediction, once one of the most far-reaching topics, back to social science. In this book, Parts II, III, and IV illustrate cases of social prediction using machine learning.

In addition to social prediction, machine learning can help classify and cluster data to produce findings that differ from traditional methods. The ever-changing Internet has constructed datasets of unprecedented size and scope, recording all the footprints of people wandering, connecting, and aggregating in the social world. For social scientists, such a society built on data is a fertile ground that can provide new research resources and theoretical opportunities, where machine learning technology is the most effective discovery tool (Lazer and Jason 2017; Chen et a l. 2021). It can reduce the dimensionality of data, thus helping social scientists process new kinds of data and theorize the relationships, structures, and topics within them. This technique of clustering can also be used to discover heterogeneity within populations, with insightful connections to the traditional inductive and deductive reasoning in social science (Bonikowski and DiMaggio 2016; Baumer et al. 2017). In this book,
1 INTRODUCTION: THE RISE OF MACHINE LEARNING …
Parts V and VI elaborate on the application of machine learning in text analysis.

Prediction and clustering tasks represent the two major categories of machine learning, supervised machine learning and unsupervised machine learning (Mitchell 1997; L i 2012). They are distinguished according to whether the target feature label is given in the dataset. This classification is based on the experience that the two tools are allowed to have in the learning process (Goodfellow et al. 2016). In supervised machine learning, the algorithm observes an output (Y) for each input (X). The output provides a target to predict. In unsupervised machine learning, the algorithm only observes the input and needs to make sense of the data without a prediction target or a correct answer (Molina and Garip 2019).

Supervised machine learning can provide the predicted label results by testing the fitting effect of the given training set model and applying the model to the test set in the data set with given features and labels. In the quantitative terminology of social science, when the covariate matrix (i.e., features X) and the explained variable (i.e., target Y) have been given, an appropriate algorithm would be adopted to fit the conditional expectation of the explained variable given the covariates, and the fitting effect would be evaluated against the real value of the explained variable. This process requires that the original label (Y) provided by the data set is objective and accurate, and the training set is consistent with the covariate standard of the test set, that is, the data set has to be independent identically distributed (IID).<sup>2</sup>

Take image recognition, a classic task in machine learning, as an example. To enable a computer to identify a “car” in an image, humans must first label a set of pictures manually. If there was a car in the picture, it would be marked as 1. Otherwise, it would be marked as 0 to generate a training set with a “standard answer.” “Whether there is a car in the picture” is the explained variable Y, and the covariates X can be obtained by quantifying the image pixel information. By training the algorithm and adjusting the parameters, the properties of the explained variables can be

2 The IID condition requires the training set and the test set to have the same probability distribution and to be independent of each other, so that the model obtained from the training set data can be applied to the whole dataset and the training effect can be guaranteed. To ensure the generalization capacity of the algorithm obtained from the training set, it is typical to use methods like random splits or cross-validation in practice.

predicted by using the covariate matrix information, and the prediction can be ideally accurate. Then, the algorithm obtained through training can be applied to the image library without manual marking, thereby realizing the real “automatic recognition.” As for specific methods, supervised machine learning methods include regularized regression, decision trees, random forest, support vector machines, neural networks, Naïve Bayes, ensemble learning, etc.

Unsupervised machine learning is suitable for data sets without labels. When the covariate matrix is available and the explained variable is not, the algorithm will calculate the distance between different samples based on the given covariate information, and cluster the samples. This method is essentially a process of dimensionality reduction, which can be applied to unstructured data such as texts, pictures, audio, and video, and can expand the scale of empirical data available in the social sciences. For example, in image recognition, the algorithm directly processes the unlabeled image data set, calculates the similarity or difference degree of different pictures through the image pixel matrix data, and then makes the classification according to the principle of “minimum intragroup distance and maximum intergroup distance.” The interpretation of category meaning is determined and defined manually. The common methods of unsupervised machine learning include cluster analysis, factor analysis, sequence analysis, principal components analysis, K-means clustering, topic modeling, community detection, etc. Among them, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic model and other topic modeling tools have been widely applied in cultural research within the social sciences (Blei et al. 2003). Poetics, a leading journal in the social sciences focusing on culture, communication, and the arts, published a series of studies based on topic modeling in a special issue in 2013 (Mohr and Bogdanov 2013).

The innovations in social prediction and clustering brought about by machine learning have undoubtedly opened the door to a new world of social science. These tools not only help improve existing methods such as counterfactual constructions in causal inference and supplementation of incomplete samples, but also provide new avenues for theory construction through data-driven discovery, as demonstrated in Part III. Furthermore, they enhance traditional approaches to causal inference via model optimization and high-dimensional data processing, as illustrated in Part IV. Together, these developments are reshaping the classical research paradigm, expanding the capacity of the social sciences to uncover the
1 INTRODUCTION: THE RISE OF MACHINE LEARNING

experiences of previously silent groups and their neglected cultural practices. They also extend social research across broader temporal and spatial horizons, allowing scholars to better understand the dynamics of diverse societies.

However, we must also be fully aware of the context in which machine learning techniques are applied. The exploratory results should be validated, especially in unsupervised machine learning, where the lack of explicit predictive targets makes robustness checks within the model or based on other external data necessary (Molina and Garip 2019). The ethical issues posed by machine learning also deserve special attention, as algorithms that define target variables based on specific category labels may reproduce existing social inequalities and discrimination (Barocas and Selbst 2016). Therefore, machine learning techniques can complement existing methods in social science, but they are not perfect, nor are they a substitute for traditional methods. It is exactly the vigilance rooted in the heart of social scientists that enables the leaders of disciplines, advocates of paradigms, reformers of thinking, and innovators of methods to consistently maintain the spirit of academic reflection, respect, and perseverance in the theoretical tradition at every critical historical juncture.

In this sense, excellent social science research must exemplify the rational use of advanced methods with humanistic feelings and theoretical concerns. Humanistic feelings, theoretical concerns, and methods of the times are indispensable to academic background, historical heritage, and the contemporary pulse of social science. Research without the above features, no matter how powerful its methods and data are, cannot obtain historical respect and academic depth. Meanwhile, research without scientific research methods, no matter how strong its theoretical consciousness and humanistic spirit are, cannot reach the real historical height.

Same as the introduction and emergence of every new thing and new field in the history of discipline development, the introduction and emergence of machine learning into the toolbox and thinking mode of social scientists will neither change the research merit of social science nor diminish the traditional social research paradigms and methods. Computational social science represented by machine learning is one of the frontier areas of quantitative social science research. Social scientists’ constant inquiry into causal mechanisms, continuous pursuit of the breadth and depth of social information, and unremitting exploration of social processes and the certainty of social phenomena together constitute the historical drive and discipline’s endogenous power in this frontier area.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

If we approach methods such as machine learning in the right way, with both enthusiasm and caution, then we can make it work for us to explore social reality, which is what this book truly aims to convey. This book provides an exhaustive view of the principles of machine learning, its development, and its application in social science. Through diverse and rigorous studies, both social scientists and readers interested in social computing methods will be able to deepen their understanding of this new approach while drawing their insights into how to maximize the data’s potential.

Part I of the book provides a literature review on the application of machine learning methods in social science. Chapter 2 focuses on supervised machine learning, which makes possible the paradigm of social prediction. Chapter 3 introduces unsupervised machine learning, highlighting its use in the field of cultural research.

Part II concerns vulnerable and minority groups, making predictions on immeasurable hidden data. Chapter 4 studies Chinese individuals who are victims of domestic violence and are reluctant to share their experiences in the questionnaire. Chapter 5 examines sexual minorities in China who are not comfortable being open about their sexual orientation. To understand the current situation of these groups, data supplementation using machine learning methods holds significant social value.

Part III reverses the traditional social research paradigm to develop novel theories. Based on the grounded theory, Chapter 6 demonstrates the computing grounded theory in producing theory from data through supervised machine learning algorithms, which can deepen the connection between causality and predictivity. Chapter 7 extends the work presented in Chapter 6 by conducting extensive testing on specific datasets to generate new theories of subjective well-being. It concludes with five major contributions of computing grounded theory.

Part IV focuses on causal inference and shows how machine learning can enhance the performance of traditional causal analysis methods. Chapter 8 examines the integration of supervised machine learning with classical causal tools such as Propensity Score Matching, Instrumental Variables, and quasi-experimental designs to improve covariate balancing, reduce bias, and optimize model fit. Chapter 9 introduces the framework of Double Machine Learning, which enables flexible causal estimation in high-dimensional settings and supports the identification of heterogeneous treatment effects, offering a robust solution for complex empirical questions.

Part V applies unsupervised machine learning methods to conduct large-scale text analysis, focusing on topic modeling to explore underlying themes and patterns in the data. Chapter 10 explores a contemporary, web-based niche literary form, Boys’ love fiction, uncovering the feminist values and gender dilemmas embodied in it. Chapter 11 reviews the classic works in history, surveying the panorama of Marx/Engels Collected Works and tracing the evolution of their ideas about society.

Part VI continues to apply unsupervised machine learning methods to analyze media texts, with a particular focus on sentiment analysis. Chapter 12 examines the image of China in films outside of China, especially in Hollywood, while Chapter 13 compares this national image in films fromChinese mainland, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), and Taiwan, Province of China. In addition to understanding the history and reality, as well as the change and development of this cultural image, causal analysis is also used to identify the socioeconomic factors behind these changes.

To help readers better understand the practical applications of machine learning methods in social science research, this book provides basic Python code examples in the appendix. These examples cover key analytical techniques such as regression, classification, topic modeling, word embeddings, and model interpretability, offering readers a hands-on reference for implementing and explaining machine learning models.

To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first attempt to exhaustively address the application of machine learning technology in social science. Using a series of typical research cases, it illuminates the way forward on unsupervised and supervised machine learning methods, as well as big data in social science research. This book furthers the field of social science in three aspects.

First, in terms of computational social science, this book introduces key machine learning algorithms and their application scenarios, highlighting their ability to uncover latent indicators and enhance causal inference. By optimizing matching, instrumental variables, and quasi-experiments, and by enabling flexible estimation in high-dimensional settings, machine learning reduces model constraints, captures heterogeneity, and stabilizes causal effects—especially by constructing accurate counterfactuals and integrating complex confounders.

Second, in the context of cultural research across the social sciences, computational methods offer new ideas for dealing with large-scale literary and media data, thus adding to the theoretical understanding

of the long-term interconnections between symbolic systems, communication media, and social reality. Machine learning methods enable researchers to capture the broader contexts and complex systemic dynamics of culture by drawing on extensive digital cultural resources that span wide spatial and temporal scales.

Third, for the social sciences more broadly, the rise of machine learning opens the door to new theoretical perspectives and research agendas. By extending the explanatory factors and dimensions of models, this approach revitalizes the sociological imagination and brings theoretical inquiry into dialogue with large-scale empirical analysis. It allows for the discovery of hidden social patterns, cultural trajectories, and emergent collective behaviors, deepening our understanding of issues such as inequality, power, and cultural change. In doing so, it helps the social sciences integrate macro structures with individual experiences across historical, contemporary, and future horizons.

1 Introduction

For Max Weber, sociology is a science that concerns itself with the interpretive understanding of social action as well as the causal explanation of its process and result (Weber 1968 [1921]: 4). His formulation exemplifies a broader orientation that has long shaped the social sciences: to describe and explain social processes and phenomena, to seek the meaning and interpretation of social actions, and to verify social hypotheses and theories. Consequently, description, interpretation, and statistical testing have become traditional and mainstream approaches within social scientific research.

In contrast, prediction seems to have had no role within the discipline for a long time. This phenomenon also widely exists in social sciences such as economics, political science, and social policy, which has not drawn concern or reflection. However, scholars have already emphasized that a causal interpretation must serve as the “basis for predicting social phenomena” (Hempel and Oppenheim 1948: 138). Hence, predictability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the causal mechanism, as although predictability does not equate with causality, a prediction could be formed if there were causality. Based on this rationale, prediction should be regarded as a proper pursuit of the social sciences, particularly in fields such as sociology and economics, where the establishment of causality has long been a central concern. For example, in 2014, Duncan

Watts argued that if sociology is a science, sociologists’ interpretations must be evaluated by scientific standards; that is, the science must be capable of making predictions.

Over the past century, social scientists have explored the meaning and explanation of society and social processes and devoted attention to providing theoretical guidance and evaluative examinations of social transformations. However, the social sciences pay significantly less attention to ex ante prediction than ex post facto evaluation and interpretation (Hofman et al. 2017). A series of papers on the topic of “prediction and its limits” has been published by Science (Jasny and Stone 2017). Although these articles came from different disciplines of social sciences such as economics, sociology, and political science, scholars’ consensus was that in contrast to natural science, theories and data of social science were rarely used to make predictions. Martin et al. (2016) highlighted that the significant complexity of the social system and the limited information (the lack of data and models) have made social science research unable to make predictions over a long period.<sup>1</sup>

In the history of social science research, scientific practices for predicting social phenomena or processes have remained absent. However, the concept of “social prediction” has always lingered in the minds of scholars. As early as the 1940s, Kaplan (1940) proposed the concept of “social prediction,” emphasizing that social science should predict social phenomena. In the 1980s, Chinese scholars also proposed this concept (Yan 1986). However, in both international and domestic academia, substantive prediction research in social science has not been fully developed, nor has it aroused academic resonance, due to limitations in data availability and econometric methods. The long-term absence of social prediction in empirical research impedes quantitative researchers as they seek to exert scientific power in influencing policy and promoting the discourse power of the media. Compared to scholars who emphasize theoretical criticism and interpretation, quantitative researchers are

2 The History of Social Prediction
2.1 The Rise and Fall of Prediction

The prediction has involved logical and sequential consideration of natural and social phenomena since ancient times (Goodman 1983). However, it is a modern development that prediction has become a scientific category. The prediction of social phenomena and human behavior has long been
Y. CHEN ET AL.

compared with the prediction of natural phenomena or animal behavior but has been regarded as a more difficult task. As early as the 1940s, scholars suggested strengthening the work of prediction in social science and proposed the concept of social prediction (Kaplan 1940). Although Kaplan (1940) recognized the difficulty of prediction, he believed that social behavior was even more predictable than natural phenomena at the micro level.

However, since the mid-twentieth century, the development of social science has failed to make a substantial breakthrough in prediction. When Kaplan put forward the concept of prediction in social science, he predicted that it would be very challenging. In particular, there were four obstacles to be overcome: first, many influencing factors would be neglected; second, the sequence in the prediction may not be taken into account; third, it is difficult to capture accurate information on known variables; fourth, the complex association among social variables would be neglected (Kaplan 1940). Generally, these problems correspond to missing variables, logical chains, measurement errors, and the complexity of social phenomena in quantitative research in contemporary social sciences. Another development is the path model, which was popular in the 1970s and 1980s. The path model attempts to expose the implications of data and the complex associations among variables by including dozens of factors in the model. The method of variable packing is similar to the data mining model of machine learning, but the purpose and implementation of the path model differ significantly from those of machine learning.

In the Chinese academia of the humanities and social sciences, some scholars have proposed the concept of social prediction and carried out exploration based on early warning indicators of social stability; some of this work dates back to the 1980s (Yan 1986, 2005). In the Sociology Dictionary edited by Deng Zhiwei (2009), “social prediction” is defined as “speculation or analysis of possible social phenomena in the future… its purpose is to reveal the most important factors that determine the future development and the most important relationships of social phenomena, for decision-making reference.” The dictionary even distinguishes “intuitive prediction” based on subjective experience and “quantitative prediction” based on data. Since the 1990s, scholars of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, namely, Xin Ru, Xueyi Lu, Peilin Li, Guangjin Chen, and Yi Zhang, have used the term “prediction” in a series of Blue Books on Social Analysis and Prediction. However, the
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

related research methods primarily involve data displays of time trends, intuitive trend prediction, and traditional regression. In this sense, empirical prediction with scientific standards based on data is almost blank, although the concept of social prediction has been in use for a long time. Indeed, elaborations of its significance and difficulties are available in both international and Chinese academic publications.

The reasons for the poor development of social prediction are not complicated. Even in the twenty-first century, social scientists still cannot solve the problems posed by Kaplan (1940). Due to the great complexity of social processes, one requires sufficient data, complex models, and strong computer processing capacity to make an ideally accurate and precise social prediction, which are the three dimensions of information limitations mentioned in the introduction. Due to these three bottlenecks, social scientists can hardly practice prediction. Instead, these scientists have shelved the ambition of prediction since the second half of the twentieth century. Since the data, models, and computing power required for accurate prediction were not yet available, the entire social science community, especially quantitative research, has focused on the relationships among variables. That is, based on limited sample data, unbiased estimations of the pairwise relationships between variables are obtained using statistical models. The delicate implication of this compromise is that social scientists no longer have unrealistic confidence in social prediction as the early pioneers did. Instead, these scientists deliberately confined their work to analyzing the pairwise relationships between variables (Hofman et al. 2017; Athe y 2018). In short, because of the bottlenecks of data, models, and computing power, most social scientists have long abandoned the scientific practice of prediction.
2.2 Revisiting Prediction

The abandonment of prediction has shaped the mainstream methods of quantitative research in the whole social science community. The primary efforts are spent determining the covariance between the independent variable X and the dependent variable Y through regression models. In other words, social scientists analyze whether the relationship between X and Y is statistically significant and has actual significance on economic and social scales based on certain statistical standards. They clarify whether and how the change of a unit of X is related to the change of Y. This
Y. CHEN ET AL.

correlation analysis, which focuses on covariance, cannot meet the ultimate academic mission of causal explanation. Thus, social scientists have started to use the analytical approach of parameter estimation to go beyond correlation analysis and reach causal inference. With the development of advanced econometric methods and the cautious application of experimental methods, some disciplines, such as economics, have shifted their mainstream quantitative analysis almost completely to causal inference based on the “counterfactual” framework in recent years, that is, they explore whether and how a change in X causes a change in Y through the observed social data (Pearl 2000; Rubin 1974). A similar disciplinary evolution occurred in sociology at the end of the twentieth century. Other disciplines such as statistics and econometrics provide ready-made methods and analytical models for causal inference in sociological analysis. Sociologists have contacted and introduced appropriate methods at an early stage (Morgan and Winship 2007; Brand and X ie 2007).

Can social scientists provide a satisfactory response to Max Weber’s emphasis on explanatory mechanisms and causality when the relationship between social index X and social index Y can be identified? Although social scientists are still concerned and worried about the invasion of advanced econometric methods into the discipline, scholars at the forefront of the discipline have given a clear and determined answer that the covariant research of correlation analysis and causal analysis is insufficient to constitute a social explanation in terms of science. Many social explanations confuse understandability with causality, which does not meet the standard of scientific interpretation. If social scientists expect their interpretations to be scientifically legitimate, they must evaluate them according to scientific standards; that is, predictions must be made (Watts 2014: 313). To make research more scientific, he stressed that it is necessary to sacrifice some seemingly straightforward and reasonable view, so social scientists have to make the right and necessary choices between satisfying but unscientific stories and unsatisfying scientific explanations.

How can Watts’ criticism be understood in relation to traditional quantitative methods in the social sciences? Watts directly engaged with Max Weber’s view that research on social life should provide an interpretive understanding of social action (“verstehen” in German) and, through this understanding, offer a causal explanation of its processes and outcomes (Weber 1968 [1921]: 4). Watts argued that interpretive understanding and causal explanation were distinct. If an explanation was causal, it could support prior prediction, whereas interpretive understanding only
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

needed to be reasonable and could be ex post. He emphasized that predictability was a necessary but not sufficient condition for establishing causal mechanisms and remained the most effective way to verify them. Yet many researchers overlook prediction or the improvement of predictive accuracy, claiming instead that prediction does not imply causality, that complex models lack generality, or that they offer little new insight. These concerns, however, miss the point: while prediction does not equal causation, causation can serve as a basis for prediction.

Watts’ criticism almost targets the general approach of all empirical research, but his exposition of the relationship between causality and prediction is clear and accurate, conforming to the classic concept of causality (Hempel and Oppenheim 1948; Mansk i 2007). In a sense, Watts’ view marks a rupture between the social sciences as empirical disciplines and the social sciences as part of the broader humanistic tradition. The tension between scientific and humanistic approaches has long existed across different fields (Chen 2017). Watts’ argument introduces more rigorous scientific standards for empirical research in the social sciences.

In summary, prediction is a central component in realizing the scientific aims of quantitative social science research. Among correlation, causality, and prediction, correlation is the prerequisite for causality and prediction, while causality is a sufficient but unnecessary condition for prediction. If there was causality, an event must have been predictable, but not vice versa. Causality and prediction are both probabilistic at the social level, and they are both powerful approaches to comprehending social affairs. These concepts share the same foundation and same direction, and both are valued by empirical social science. The problem is that the discipline has been in a state of under-preparation for prediction for many years, although quantitative social science research has developed rather mature methods and models for correlation and causal analysis. When the research goal is to provide a mechanical explanation of X with respect to Y, the traditional method to identify causality is sufficient. However, if the research goal was to predict the probabilities and intensities of certain phenomena in the future based on the existing data and methods (which is often the practical requirement of the social governance process for social scientists), traditional tools cannot achieve this task. Thus, the social prediction must be put on the agenda.

3 The Realization of Social Prediction

With the development of machine learning, the emergence of largescale social survey data and big data, and improved computer processing performance, the era of solving problems related to data, algorithms, and computing power and realizing social prediction has dawned. From the methodological perspective, the main approach to achieving social prediction is supervised machine learning.
3.1 Predictive Principle of Supervised Machine Learning

There are many specific methods for supervised machine learning, but the general model-fitting goal is quite different from the traditional model regression. The former category of methods aims at accuracy, that is, the difference between the prediction label and the real label is the smallest, while the latter type of procedure is meant to evaluate the impact of an independent variable on the dependent variable under the premise of controlling other variables (Athey 2018). Among numerous supervised machine learning algorithms, regularized regression based on linear models is widely used. Compared with the least squares model (OLS), the regularized regression model adds a penalty term into the regression coefficient. The unbiased estimation of the OLS regression coefficient $\beta$ is
\hat {\beta} _ {\mathrm{OLS}} = \operatorname{argmin} (y - X \beta) ^ {\prime} (y - X \beta) = \left(X ^ {\prime} X\right) ^ {- 1} X ^ {\prime} y
The regression coefficient of the regularized regression is
\hat {\beta} _ {\mathrm{OLS}} = \operatorname{argmin} \bigl \{(y - X \beta) / (y - X \beta) + \lambda \bigl [ (1 - \alpha) \beta^ {\prime} \beta + \alpha | \beta | \bigr ] \bigr \}

When λ is 0, the penalty term is 0, which refers to an unbiased OLS regression; when λ is not 0 and α is 0, an L2 regularizer $( { \textstyle \sum } P 1 \beta 2 J )$ is added to the parameter, where the term refers to ridge regression. When λ is not 0 and α is equal to 1, an L1 regularizer $( { \textstyle \sum } P \; 1 | \beta _ { \mathrm { j } } | )$ is added to the parameter, where the term refers to Lasso regression. The other cases are all elastic net regression. Therefore, ridge regression and Lasso regression can also be regarded as special cases of elastic net regression.

Here, we describe how regularized regression can obtain more accurate predictions than OLS. The error of a linear fitting of the model can be divided into three parts: bias, variance, and irreducible error. These

errors represent the deviation between the fitting expectation and the real value, the dispersion of the fitting value, and the inevitable system noise, respectively. The deviation of OLS is constantly equal to 0 due to its inherent least sum of squares of residual errors, whereas the regularized regression model reduces variance and overall error by introducing bias to improve the model’s prediction accuracy (Athey and Imbens 2016). The modeling of machine learning does not often consider theory. Generally, the inclusion of more variables helps to increase the prediction accuracy. Therefore, machine learning models can include seemingly unrelated variables and sacrifice the theoretical nature of the model. In general, there is a bias-variance tradeoff between introducing bias to improve the fitting accuracy of the model and continuing unbiased estimation to rely on previous theories, which directly reflects the difference between machine learning and traditional quantitative methods.

3.2 Redefinition of Social Prediction

Based on machine learning, we try to define social prediction in the context of contemporary social science. Thus, social prediction uses spatiotemporal data to demonstrate social phenomena or processes; machine learning based on appropriate algorithms can accurately quantify and measure unknown information to provide information and a basis for social decision-making and research. Machine learning encompasses both vertical prediction, which involves forecasting the future based on historical data, and horizontal prediction which uses sample data to make predictions about other data. Social prediction is an important part of computational social science. Computational social science is a new field of quantitative social science research that describes, explains, and predicts complex social phenomena and processes based on complex models and social computing tools. This field’s research methods of social computing include social network analysis, simulation modeling, machine learning, and big data analysis. Among these methods, the combination of big data, machine learning, and social prediction has special advantages. While the massive background information on observation objects provided by big data offers considerable convenience for model training, big data can provide outliers on a large scale. With the help of machine learning analysis technology, these outliers may contribute to theoretical innovation and policy implementation.

4 The Disciplinary Significance of Social Prediction

Since social prediction can be achieved through machine learning, what is its main value as an emerging research field and methodological approach for the development of the social sciences? Based on our understanding of the discipline and recent literature, we classify the value of social prediction into three dimensions: academic, governance, and contextual significance.
4.1 The Academic Significance of Social Prediction

Because machine learning can process complex and diverse information content for social science and generate variable forms for analysis, it expands the research horizon of social science. In brief, social prediction based on machine learning has disciplinary significance for social science research in the following five respects.

First, the latent indicators of interest can be obtained through prediction. There are two types of data that are difficult to obtain through traditional surveys or big data in social science research. One type is the “subjective latent indicator,” which often occurs because people are unwilling to disclose true individual information. The reasons include the sensitivity of the problem itself or social acceptance, such as personal unemployment, sexual orientation, venereal diseases, and religious beliefs. In the specific economic, social, and cultural context, this information is often deliberately hidden by respondents. At the social level, concealment prevents researchers or social governance officials from obtaining comprehensive, true, and accurate data about this type of information. The other problem is “objective latent indicators,” that is, there are objectively complex data measurements or heterogeneous group classification indicators that are difficult to detect directly. These latent indicators can be found by machine learning, which will provide new dependent variables or independent variables for academic research.

For the subjective latent indicators, as long as some people in our data provide these indicators truly and accurately, a social prediction based on machine learning can use the input data as a training set to accurately predict the people who are not willing to provide information or provide distorted information (in a sense, the result of this process can be regarded as a supplement to the missing values). The prediction accuracy
Y. CHEN ET AL.

depends on the size and independence of the samples and the optimization of the algorithm models. He et al. (2018) used Baidu search index to predict the regional distribution data of AIDS in China and employed the dynamic panel pooled mean group model, based on the heterogeneity hypothesis, because the prediction accuracy would be reduced using the dynamic generalized method of moments. This model could make a more convincing and credible prediction when uncertainty was resolved by machine learning based on larger samples. For the objective latent indicators, unsupervised machine learning (UML) is often used in variable generation. For example, in economics, unsupervised machine learning is used to analyze satellite images and generate measurements of data indicators for forest harvesting, environmental pollution, and nighttime lighting (Donaldson and Storeygard 2016). Studies in sociology classify and analyze government documents (Mohr et al. 2013) and academic texts (McFarland et al. 2013). In addition, research on social network using unsupervised machine learning has also garnered the attention of scholars.

Second, theoretical hypotheses can be generated via prediction. In traditional quantitative methods, the essence of the model is to include new main explanatory variables to test new theoretical hypotheses. In addition to theoretical intuition, whether to add variables to the model from a statistical perspective depends on stepwise regression, partial least squares, and the standard comparison of AIC and BIC. Scholars have summarized 21 varieties of traditional variable selection methods (Castle et al. 2009). However, with the machine learning method, some brandnew means could be adopted to examine and expand the influencing factors of the model. We can discover new explanatory variables and dimensions, and develop new theoretical hypotheses. This process aligns with the idea of “bringing theory back” advocated by big data researchers (Luo et al. 2018).

For the explanatory variables, if the effect of an independent variable X on the dependent variable Y is evaluated, Varian (2014) proposes using the same machine learning algorithm to fit and predict Y when the variable is included and excluded and comparing the difference between the two fitting effects. If the fitting effect of the model containing X is better, a theoretically hypothesized covariant correlation or even causal relationship between X and Y can be posited, and this hypothesis can be verified using traditional quantitative methods. At the level of the explanatory dimension (i.e., a set of explanatory variables that are highly correlated
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

conceptually and logically), machine learning can provide an important driving force for sociological imagination and realize the “precision difference analysis of grouped variables” method. The data can be labeled in advance, and all the variables in the data are combined and packaged into their respective explanatory dimensions without ready-made theoretical guidance, which is ultimately unified into the fitting process of machine learning. The prediction results of the same algorithm with and without an explanatory dimension are compared one by one. Thus, we obtain the predictive ability of an explanatory dimension for the dependent variable. Once a new explanatory dimension has a good ability to predict Y, we can examine the specific variables within this dimension and identify the most likely explanatory variable based on imagination and theory. In addition, the overall explanatory power or relevance of a new explanatory dimension to the dependent variables may trigger new thinking in the social sciences and even inspire new theories and hypotheses, that is, attempts to discover the overall influence of the new dimension.

Third, prediction facilitates the conduct of causal inference. In social science, the counterfactual framework, which defines the causal mechanism, is essentially speculation and simulation of the non-real world. Thus, when a certain influence is not applied or a certain processing factor is not changed, one asks what form the event will take. This problem is the precise problem at which machine learning is effective: constructing the state of an event that does not exist as accurately as possible with limited data (Athey 2015). Therefore, many studies have tried to apply machine learning methods to causal inference problems, especially in the counterfactual construction process and extensions of the selection model (Green and Kern 2012; Hazlett 2014; Imai and Ratkovic 2013).

For example, after the first-stage regression of the linear instrumental variable model, the endogenous explanatory variable X should be predicted, and the predicted value should be included in the main model (Chen 2011). The prediction process can be replaced by machine learning methods. Application cases include Lasso regression (Belloni et al. 2012), ridge regression (Carrasco 2012), and neural network methods (Hartford et al. 2016). Other examples are the prediction of propensity values in propensity score matching (PSM) and the logistic model used in the standard methods (Hu 2012). With machine learning methods, the model hypotheses and restrictions are reduced, and the causal effect estimation is stabilized. Existing application cases include the boosting method (McCaffrey et al. 2004), the neural network method (Westreich et al.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

2010), and the regression tree method (Diamond and Sekhon 2013). For another example, regarding the heterogeneity in causal effect (Xie et al. 2012), the machine learning method can also greatly improve the accuracy of the estimation, which demonstrates that we can make more accurate predictions of the counterfactual state of treated or untreated individuals without excessive hypotheses and constraints in the estimation process of the parameter model.

Athey (2018) predicted that, in general, machine learning technology would draw increasing attention to causal inference problems. In the context of causal inference in social science, the vast majority of counterfactual constructions can be completed by machine learning methods, and the difference between a counterfactual construction and an actual occurrence can be tested quantitatively. In the process of constructing counterfactuals, the results of prediction with machine learning ought to be reported as well, which was mentioned by the review of machine learning published in the Annual Review of Sociology (Molina and Garip 2019).

Fourth, data proliferation can be realized by prediction. In empirical social surveys, randomly incomplete or missing sample data is a common but aggravating problem. The traditional processing methods are either deleting samples or supplementing data. Deleting data would not only reduce the sample size but also destroy the original sampling design. The method of supplementing data relies on subjective factors, mean values, or the prediction of traditional regression models with comprehensive information, though this method is well developed (Allison 2009) However, quantitative models are not good at making accurate predictions, while machine learning can undertake this task. For instance, some scholars have tested the supplemental performance of different machine learning methods based on 15 datasets and found that the performances of support vector machines and Naïve Bayesian methods were relatively optimal (Farhangfar et al. 2008). Other scholars have tried to use a Gaussian mixture model to estimate the potential contribution of data and supplement data through an extreme learning machine method (a singlelayer neural network method) (Sovilj et al. 2016). Sovilj’s study evaluated six different datasets and found that the accuracy of supplementing values through machine learning is higher than the accuracy of traditional methods. Based on existing research, the estimation of missing data values should adopt an appropriate machine learning method to achieve the best
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED
fitting effect, or at least report the fitting effect of machine learning estimation and other methods, among which the optimal result would be chosen.

Fifth, the prediction could promote theoretical innovation. Machine learning can provide powerful methods and new perspectives for scholars, helping them expand their theoretical horizons and generate new academic knowledge. In the current research of machine learning in the field of social science, whereas the results given by the algorithm are not the goal of the research, they are a source of discovery that inspires scholars to develop and innovate at the theoretical level, to promote existing theories and to put forward new hypotheses. For example, Kleinberg et al. used the machine learning method to study the case texts of New York state courts (Kleinberg et al. 2017). They first trained the regression tree model to predict the decision of “bail or release” in New York state court cases and explained the contradiction between the model prediction results and the actual judgments through quasi-random experiments. The research shows that the results of recent cases significantly influence the judge leading to more severe punishment for minor offenses. This discovery reveals potential factors affecting the judge’s decision-making behavior from a new perspective and thus promotes the theoretical development of the social-psychological process of judicial judgment.
4.2 The Governance Significance of Social Prediction

It is one of the most traditional and basic topics of social science to predict economic and social processes and guide practice through research. However, neither an early intuitionistic prediction nor covariance research relying on traditional quantitative models can meet the real demands of economic and social prediction. At the forefront of contemporary social science, other disciplines have begun to explore the issue of social prediction. Among these disciplines, algorithm optimization and even prediction competition (to establish an open-source platform for different teams to participate and contribute algorithms to find the optimal machine learning model) have been applied in social governance, which is worthy of attention from policymakers and social scientists. Here are three cases closely related to social science.
First, this practice could benefit socially disadvantaged groups. Professor Salganik, a sociologist at Princeton University, and his
Y. CHEN ET AL.

colleagues used the big data of the “Fragile Families Challenge” project of Princeton University (the project tracks 5000 American children and obtains 54 million data points of their physical and mental health, cognitive ability, social-emotional ability, education and living conditions, family composition, family stability, and family economic status) to conduct an open-platform algorithm competition of machine learning with six aspects of the social results of children’s performances, personalities, and life difficulties. More than 150 teams from 68 universities and scientific research institutes in seven countries have submitted prediction algorithms. In addition to applying the results of machine learning models to community services, these teams conduct in-depth analysis of special case data on outstanding children growing up in disadvantaged families to provide a decision-making basis for improving the living standards of children in these groups.<sup>3</sup>

Second, we have research on social inequality. Scholars from Imperial College of Technology published a paper in Scientific Reports, in which they used in-depth learning of street image data to present and analyze social, economic, environmental, and health inequalities in urban areas (Suel et al. 2019). The team focused on four British cities, including London, Birmingham, Manchester, and Liz, and used 525,860 pictures of London (corresponding to 156,581 postal codes) as the training set. Using the government’s statistics on housing conditions, average income, mortality, and morbidity, these researchers made relatively accurate predictions of social stratification in the other three cities. This work’s significance lies in training computer programs with visual signal tags in images of some characteristics of urban life (such as the housing quality and living environment) to predict inequality in cities without relevant data.

Third, we consider public health governance. In 2016, American Economic Review published a paper on improving urban governance by algorithmic competition (Glaeser et al. 2016). The authors cooperated with the Boston municipal government, Yelp (the largest review website in the U.S.), and Driviendata (a well-known machine learning and data science competition platform in the U.S. that is similar to Kaggle and TopCoder) to train algorithms with comment text data on Yelp to predict

the possibility of violations of hygiene and health regulations of restaurants in the Boston area. The authors conducted out-of-sample tests of 23 submitted and complete algorithms and compared the predicted results with the actual results of 364 restaurants. Their results show that the efficiency of health inspections can be greatly improved by using the winning algorithm and machine learning to determine which restaurants are most likely to violate regulations and require inspection.

In many other fields, such as international politics, criminology, and public health, social prediction based on machine learning has also been employed. For example, Perry (2013) used the Random Forest method to predict the occurrence of violent conflicts in Africa. Berk (2012) used machine learning to predict the risk of crime in several studies. Kleinberg et al. (2015) used the Lasso regression model to predict which patients with medical insurance can obtain the most benefit from joint replacement surgery. To a large extent, these studies have opened up new areas of social exploration and provided important references and data templates for improving social governance.
5 The Paradigm Significance of Social Prediction

In the development of natural science, scholars in the scientific community use different paradigms in different stages (Kuhn 1962). In social science disciplines, an orthodoxy is similar to a paradigm in different historical stages. Therefore, social science has also undergone the development and evolution of its paradigm, which appears as a spiral rising from the conventional stage, through the crisis stage, and to the revolutionary stage ultimately culminating in a new conventional stage. When the development of social science steps into a specific stage and encounters problems that cannot be solved by the original methods, or new methods and information materials appear, a new paradigm will appear and gradually be accepted and recognized by the academic community. Certainly, the paradigm shift in social science research does not correspond to the kind of “paradigm revolution” described by Kuhn in the natural sciences, such as the subversion of Newtonian statics by relativity and the overthrow of Euclidean geometry by Riemannian geometry. Instead, social science presents a complex coexistence of the new and the old, as well as multiple dialogues.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

Kuhn defined the paradigm more clearly at the end of his research career and summarized its content as three nested logical levels. Kuhn suggested that a paradigm refers to a prescriptive consensus of ontology and epistemology, a set of general rules of a theory or model, and a specific problem domain of a symbolic nature (Kuhn 1977). The three basic paradigms of contemporary social research are the empirical paradigm, the interpretive paradigm, and the critical paradigm, founded by Durkheim, Weber, and Marx, respectively. In the past hundred years, the social sciences, especially sociology, have evolved from speculation to a coexistence of speculative and empirical work. This transformation reflects the central position of two fundamental paradigms, interpretation and positivism, as well as the complementary role of the logical and objective perspective of social realism in relation to the individual reality and subjective differentiation emphasized by social nominalism. Within the empirical paradigm, qualitative interviews based on the field and quantitative analysis based on data complement each other, but there are significant differences in the epistemology, research rules, and problem domains. For example, qualitative analysis focuses on the depth of individual experience and theoretical refinement, while quantitative research focuses on sample size, causal mechanisms, theoretical verification, and falsification and emphasizes scientific attributes (Popper 1962). Therefore, qualitative work and quantitative work, in essence, constitute the subparadigm within the empirical paradigm.

With the rapid development of social prediction based on machine learning, the basic paradigm of empirical work will be split into three pieces from the original dual peaks of qualitative and quantitative work to a trilogy of qualitative work, quantitative work, and quantitative prediction. Compared with the traditional quantitative mechanism (correlation and causality), the paradigmatic differences in social prediction are evident in the following aspects.

First, in terms of epistemology, the black-box mechanism is introduced into prediction. Compared with traditional quantitative research that pursues explicit, clear, and theoretical explanations, the epistemological absolutism of prediction is weakened. Second, in terms of the problem domain, the prediction does not focus on the correlation and causal mechanisms of the cause and result, but rather takes the accurate estimation of the target variables as the goal. Third, in terms of the research method, the prediction reduces the dependence on theory and the focus on the counterfactual framework and instead relies on
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

algorithms and data to train and test models. Fourth, in terms of the general rule, the prediction does not rely on the traditional hypothesis test rules and model identification techniques, such as the significance level of the regression coefficient. Instead, a series of new standards focusing on prediction accuracy are adopted, such as the F-score of accuracy and precision, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve with the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) as axes and the area under the curve (AUC) enclosed by the lower part of the curve.

Of course, if we adopt a more cautious attitude toward the understanding of a paradigm, it can be emphasized that the paradigm significance of social prediction lies in the fact that it has contributed to the subparadigm evolution of empirical research. In other words, the social prediction has experienced from qualitative work to qualitative plus quantitative work and then to a trilogy of qualitative work, quantitative correlation, and quantitative prediction.
6 The Ethical Implications of Social Prediction

The rise of social prediction has opened new frontiers for social science, but it also brings serious ethical challenges. These challenges do not only accompany technical progress but shape the very legitimacy of predictive research in social science. Three aspects are particularly important: privacy, bias, and the boundary between research and governance.

The first issue concerns privacy and consent. Predictive models in social research often rely on digital traces that contain sensitive personal information. The study using Baidu search queries to predict the regional distribution of AIDS in China illustrates both the promise and the risk (He et al. 2018). Search data provide timely signals of public health concerns, yet they also involve highly private queries that individuals never intended to share beyond the search engine. Even if such data are aggregated, the possibility of re-identification remains, raising doubts about whether participants retain meaningful control over their information. These dilemmas make clear that prediction cannot rely on technical efficiency alone; protocols of informed consent, data minimization, and secure handling are essential to preserve autonomy and trust.

The second issue is bias and inequality in predictive outcomes. Models trained on existing data inevitably mirror structural disparities. When Suel et al. (2019) used street-level images to predict socioeconomic inequality across British cities, the approach highlighted contrasts in urban living
Y. CHEN ET AL.

conditions, but it also risked fixing neighborhood reputations in ways that could stigmatize entire communities. Similar problems appear in crime and conflict prediction, where reliance on past records may reproduce earlier biases in policing or surveillance. These examples reveal that prediction is not a neutral reflection of society but an intervention that may reinforce disadvantage unless fairness tests and corrective measures are built into the research design.

The third issue concerns the boundary between academic research and governance applications. Work such as Glaeser et al. (2016)’s use of Yelp reviews to predict restaurant hygiene violations demonstrates how predictive models can improve efficiency in public administration. At the same time, the transfer of such tools into governance raises questions about transparency, accountability, and the risk of overreliance on algorithmic decision-making. Once models influence decisions with moral consequences, the line between technical guidance and normative judgment becomes blurred. In these contexts, social science must uphold its dual role as a provider of empirical tools and a critic of their use, ensuring that predictions are open to scrutiny and applied under conditions that respect social values.

In sum, the ethical implications of social prediction are inseparable from its scientific development. Protecting privacy, mitigating bias, and clarifying the boundary between research and governance are not optional concerns but necessary foundations for prediction to become a legitimate social science paradigm. By embedding these principles in both methodology and practice, social prediction can contribute to academic innovation and social welfare without compromising the trust on which the social sciences ultimately depend.
7 Conclusion

Prediction has always been an indispensable element of scientific methods. A prediction can verify and evaluate the applicability and effectiveness of existing theories. Although the process in which prediction drives interpretation has been widely used in physics and other natural sciences, it has not been widely used in social science. Indeed, the complexity of human society is much greater than that of nature, and the available data and computing tools in traditional social sciences are relatively lacking. In the past two decades, the rapid expansion of information and data in the network era has presented unprecedented opportunities for social
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

science. As early as 2009, Lazer et al. predicted in Science that the era of computing social science would dawn (Lazer et al. 2009; Lazer and Jason 2017). In the past ten years, the network has undergone significant development, and research has accumulated rapidly. In accordance with Lazer’s original expectation, a new wave is surging. Machine learning, which enables computers to process data in new ways, has been widely adopted. In summary, there is an urgent need for current academia to embrace machine learning and other trends, and this article intends to point out its future use.

Machine learning provides new assistance for the prediction research of social science and creates conditions for the formation of new paradigms in social science. This article first reviews the historical development of social prediction, discusses the current path of social prediction in relation to the principles and methods of machine learning, and provides theoretical considerations and empirical cases to demonstrate the value of prediction in social science. Machine learning is helpful in expanding the research horizon of social science, as it can obtain latent indicators, inspire theoretical hypotheses, generate causal inferences, realize data proliferation, and promote theoretical innovation. It presents a new paradigm in quantitative research for contemporary social research.

We fully realize that the data mining method on which social prediction relies cannot be perfect, and machine learning–based social prediction faces several fundamental limitations that must be acknowledged. A primary challenge lies in the “black-box” problem, whereby the internal mechanisms of algorithms such as deep neural networks remain opaque to both researchers and the public. This lack of interpretability may hinder social explanation, since understanding why a prediction occurs is as important as the prediction itself. Of course, the “black box” does not mean the model is completely unexplainable. An increasing number of interpretable machine learning algorithms are maturing, which can help us produce new theories from data and deepen the connection between causality and predictivity, as detailed in Chapters 6 and 7 of this book.

Equally critical is the sensitivity of machine learning models to data quality and bias. Unlike data generated in controlled laboratory settings, most social data arise from institutional processes, platform architectures, or self-reporting, which may neither be neutral nor random. For example, digital trace data may disproportionately represent younger, urban, or more affluent populations. Marginalized groups are often underrepresented or misclassified, making them particularly vulnerable to algorithmic
Y. CHEN ET AL.

misprediction. These imperfections can reproduce or even amplify existing social inequalities when fed into predictive systems. This sensitivity to the source data also points to a broader challenge: the issues of overfitting and weak generalizability. Models that perform well on historical or local data may fail when applied to new social contexts, undermining their reliability for long-term or cross-societal predictions. Overfitting to training data often yields deceptively high accuracy but poor real-world performance, limiting their value for long-term forecasting or cross-societal comparison. For social research, predictive models must therefore be contextualized and complemented by theory and qualitative insights rather than treated as universally portable tools.

Every method has its premises, assumptions, and limitations. The mission of social scientists is to ensure that these hypotheses are as close as possible to the specific research situation in a transparent, reasonable, and effective way and to make continuous progress on diminishing limitations. Therefore, Grimmer (2015) pointed out that data scientists should not only be computer scientists but also social scientists. Social prediction based on the black-box mechanisms of machine learning does not imply abandoning theoretical thinking and empirical knowledge; rather, these resources are essential for interpreting algorithmic results and dismantling opacity. In the process of dismantling the black box, the conclusions drawn from the black-box mechanism can and should be interpreted from the theoretical perspective and further verified by empirical methods. To address data quality and bias, social scientists should ask: who created these records and for what purpose? Which groups are overrepresented or absent? How do institutional practices shape what is observed? Such questions shift the focus from technical de-biasing to a deeper understanding of how data reflects and distorts the social world. Likewise, the problem of weak generalizability underscores the value of contextual knowledge. When a model that performs well in one setting fails elsewhere, this is not simply a statistical error but an insight from social science, revealing the boundaries of social processes and the significance of local conditions. The task of social science, therefore, is not to search for a universally perfect model, but to use theory to explain when and why models succeed or fail, turning limitations into opportunities for theoretical refinement.

New methods and paradigms will give rise to new problems and puzzles. In particular, the introduction of social prediction and machine learning may affect the theoretical depth and saturation of social science.
2 SOCIAL PREDICTION: A NEW RESEARCH PARADIGM BASED

Similarly, the social sciences could potentially lose their humanistic feelings and theoretical concerns or even become a pure data mining game. Such concerns are understandable, but they do not constitute grounds for rejection and exclusion. Excessive worry often derives from the lack of a comprehensive understanding of new methods and new paradigms, and the lack of confidence in the strong theoretical tradition of social science and the diversified expression of the humanistic spirit. Since its establishment a century ago, the social sciences have maintained their strong vitality and attraction with their open vision, tolerant mind, and interdisciplinary spirit.

However, these worries and doubts are not baseless. It is exactly this kind of vigilance rooted in the hearts of social scientists that has enabled the leaders of disciplines, advocates of paradigms, reformers of thinking, and innovators of methods to always maintain the spirit of academic reflection, respect, and perseverance of the theoretical tradition at every critical historical juncture. In this sense, excellent social science research must exemplify the rational use of advanced methods, combined with humanistic feelings and theoretical concerns. Humanistic feelings, theoretical concerns, and methods of the times are indispensable to the academic background, historical heritage, and contemporary pulse of social science. Research without human feelings and theoretical concerns cannot obtain historical respect and academic depth even if it uses powerful methods and data. Furthermore, research without scientific research methods cannot reach a real historical height regardless of how strong its theoretical consciousness and humanistic spirit are.

Therefore, like the introduction and emergence of every new thing and new field in the history of a discipline’s development, the introduction and emergence of machine learning and social prediction into the toolbox and thinking mode of social scientists will neither change the research merit of social science nor dim the traditional social research paradigms and methods. Causal inference in correlation research, big data, and computational social science represented by machine learning constitute three frontier quantitative research areas. Social scientists’ constant inquiry into causal mechanisms, continuous pursuit of the breadth and depth of social information, and unremitting exploration of social processes and the certainty of social phenomena together constitute the historical drive and endogenous power of these three frontier areas. Some of these three frontier areas have elaborated their research themes, while others have just emerged. As new branches of the social sciences,
Y. CHEN ET AL.
these fields will be nourished by the historical tradition of the discipline and thrive.

CHAPTER 3
Modeling Massive: Discovering Structure Using Unsupervised Machine Learning
1 Introduction

The social sciences’ engagement with culture dates back to the work of Max Weber and Émile Durkheim. Yet under the influence of Enlightenment rationalism, culture was long treated as subordinate to social structure and lacked the status of an independent explanatory variable. The “cultural turn” that began in sociology in the late 1970s and 1980s reshaped this view within sociology and beyond. As a branch of sociology, cultural sociology explored art, literature, popular culture, and media, while extending to issues such as social stratification and politics, reframing culture as a social force shaping the real world. Its influence also extended to anthropology, political science, communication studies, and other branches of the social sciences. In the context of the linguistic turn, globalization, and the rise of new media, language, meaning, and individual agency have gained new importance. Globalization disrupted traditional understandings of culture, and digital media transformed how culture is created and circulated (Poster 2010). These changes have prompted social scientists to adopt computational approaches to capture the spatial and temporal dynamics of culture and to analyze large-scale patterns that earlier methods could not address.
