With advances in machine learning, computer algorithms can now classify large-scale data and detect patterns that were previously difficult to observe. They enable the clustering of massive textual datasets, the analysis of themes and sentiments, and the identification of cultural explanatory variables that extend beyond traditional frameworks. In the era of big data, the use of diverse models and machine learning techniques has made culture both a subject of study and a source of theoretical insight. This development also gives new life to the cultural turn, which reaffirms the centrality of culture while moving beyond the limitations of extreme subjectivism and relativism.

This chapter begins with a historical overview of social science research on culture and introduces the classical methods of cultural study, represented by ethnography and qualitative content analysis. Then, with a contemporary focus, it introduces the application of emerging social computing methods in this field, using research from several important journals as examples. Finally, it introduces four methods for textual analysis through machine learning: LDA topic model, Word2Vec algorithm, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis.
2 Traditional Cultural Research Methods

As early as 1958, Raymond Williams (1958: 25), one of the founders of cultural studies, stated, “Culture is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language.” The scope of culture is extremely broad. It is as ubiquitous and relevant as the air, but when it comes to defining the concept of culture, it will be blurred, like in the mist. The academic debate on this concept has never stopped. Under the influence of the cultural turn, numerous disciplines are involved in cultural studies (e.g., anthropology, linguistics, translatology, history, etc.), and no broad consensus has been reached until now. However, William Sewell (2005: 156–157) argues that the basic categories of culture can be identified: culture exists either as a defining aspect of theoretical concepts in social life or as people’s concrete practices and behaviors. The former is a system of symbols and meanings, denoted as “culture” due to its abstract nature; the latter refers to the social practices of particular groups, denoted as “cultures” due to their actuality and their distinctions between groups (Geertz 1973; Sewell 2005: 164–165). However, the two categories are not contradictory, and the dialectical relationship between them counts

for much in the research of cultural theory. Many definitions of culture include these two categories. For example, one of the definitions of the word “culture” in the Oxford English Dictionary is “the customs and beliefs, art, way of life and social organization of a particular country or group” (Stevenson 2010).

Although different disciplines approach these two categories in their own ways, social scientists share a concern with social reality and do not see culture only as an abstract system of symbols. They seek to understand how culture takes shape and functions in concrete contexts. The relationship between culture and structure has long been a central question in the social sciences. Pioneers such as Karl Marx, Max Weber, and Émile Durkheim all grappled with this relationship, though each understood it in markedly different ways. Marx saw consciousness as inseparable from material existence, arguing that it reflects the real conditions of life (Fromm 1971: 19). Culture, despite its creative potential, is ultimately subordinate to structure. Weber, in contrast, stressed the role of ideas, beliefs, and values alongside material interests in explaining historical change. He described his approach as Kulturwissenschaft, meaning cultural studies in English (Eberle 2016). For Weber, meaning formation is tied to power and domination; culture is a meaningful form of social action, and sociology is the study of this reality, giving culture and structure equal standing. Durkheim differed from both. Early in his work, he viewed culture as a product of social structure. Later, he recognized the independent force of belief and ritual in shaping social life (Alexander 2003). He treated culture as a collective representation capable of transcending individual behavior and linked it to the organization of society and the division of labor.

Cultural studies within the social sciences have continued to draw on the theories and methodologies of early pioneers. For instance, the structural functionalism that dominated American sociology after World War II until the 1960s was influenced by Marx and Durkheim, giving the values representing culture a functional status subordinate to structure without further elaboration of their meaning. The Chicago School in the late 1960s, represented by Herbert Blumer’s theory of symbolic interaction, not only highlighted the constructive role of symbols for individual action but also achieved a revival of the interpretive paradigm. Another methodological contribution of the Chicago School is the development of grounded theory (GT), which informs its empirical research. As a qualitative research method, it runs counter to traditional positivism, and does
Y. CHEN ET AL.

not approach empirical facts by set research methods, but rather induces theories based on empirical facts, opening up another path for sociologists and anthropologists to study culture (Glaser and Strauss 2017). After structural functionalism lost its dominance, Weber’s theory is back in the limelight. His approach to interpreting the meaning-making process and his formulation of how meaning affects actions, practices, and institutions fit the new horizons of social science research, and have even influenced a part of post-structuralist and postmodernist theories, including the cultural turn in sociology.

Although culture was an important research object in sociology at the very beginning, it was not until the cultural turn occurred that cultural sociology was formally established as a new branch of sociology. The real appeal of establishing cultural sociology lies in making necessary corrections to the long-standing marginal role of culture in sociology, breaking the grand narrative of structural functionalism, and adjusting value judgments based on scientific rationality. Influenced by semiotics, phenomenology, and linguistics, the autonomy of culture was elevated to an unprecedented level in the early stage of the discipline’s establishment, and some scholars even believed that all social phenomena are composed of culture (Olick 2010: 97–108). Although the notion of cultural autonomy has since been reframed as a relative concept, the recognition of culture as a constitutive social force has been increasingly shared across the social sciences (2010: 99). As the interpretation of abstract cultural meaning becomes our focus, understanding culture in terms of other tangible things loses its meaning and is replaced by the study of how culture itself constantly reshapes the behavior of the real world (Sherwood 1993). After the cultural turn, culture came to be viewed not as a static element serving structural functions, but as a dynamic process in constant transformation. Consequently, space and time emerged as core dimensions of cultural analysis in the social sciences. At the theoretical level, the enduring question of culture is the relationship between the symbols, practices, and social structures that culture contains. How to strike a balance between structuralism and subjectivism is the constant goal of theorists such as Pierre Bourdieu and Anthony Giddens.

In the early years of cultural sociology’s emergence, its purpose and features determined its rejection of scientism and macro theory, as well as its special emphasis on experience. So far, qualitative research

methods, primarily based on field research (including participant observation and unstructured interviews), remain the mainstream approach in cultural sociology research. Among them, the ethnographic approach of anthropology is undoubtedly the best choice for cultural researchers when they aim to describe a certain kind of cultural practice. Both the Chicago School and the Birmingham School have made extensive use of ethnography, such as the fieldwork represented by the Chicago School. This trend is even more pronounced in the Birmingham School which specializes in cultural studies. For example, Williams applies historical ethnography to combine rural experiences in a series of literary works with his own experiences in The Country and the City (1973), adding life experiences to the images of rural and urban culture and giving culture a social significance. Similarly, Paul Willis in Learning to Labour (1977) used participatory ethnography, including listening, observing, and describing, to show how working-class youth reproduced structures of subordination through everyday acts of resistance. These studies illustrate how interpretive and experiential methods have shaped both cultural sociology and the broader social sciences in understanding culture as a lived and socially embedded pro cess.

Ethnography has long been central to the study of cultural practices, from everyday interaction to artistic production and consumption. When attention shifts from the process of production to the cultural object itself, experience becomes crucial to understanding its social meaning. Methods such as qualitative content analysis and discourse analysis, drawing on traditions in literature and art studies, allow researchers to examine how meanings are constructed through language, imagery, and form. When content analysis directly engages with the object, causality gives way to participation, and the observer’s perception becomes part of the process, revealing the internal logic and social meaning of the cultural form (Abbott 2007). By engaging directly with cultural texts and artworks, these approaches reveal how aesthetic experience connects to broader social structures and values. They also extend the interpretive tradition of cultural research, treating art and literature not merely as representations but as social facts with emotional and symbolic power (Bourdieu 1993; Abbott 2007; De la Fuente 2007).

From the above review, it is clear that cultural research in the social sciences combines both subjective and objective dimensions. It values interpretation and understanding while maintaining the empirical spirit of scientific inquiry. Methods such as ethnography, content analysis, and
Y. CHEN ET AL.

discourse analysis examine how cultural practices interact with social life. These qualitative approaches have at times been questioned for relying too heavily on interpretation, for offering limited causal explanation, and for struggling to capture how culture changes over time. In response, newer forms of quantitative cultural research have begun to address these limits. Rather than describing culture mainly in the manner of traditional anthropology or focusing on textual meaning as in literary studies, they treat culture as something that can be measured, modeled, and used to explain social outcomes. Social computing is central to this development. It makes it possible to move from local and small-scale observation to large-scale analysis of structure and stratification, opening new possibilities for the study of culture across the social sciences.
3 Computational Approaches in Cultural Research

Quantitative methods have advanced cultural research within the social sciences in two key ways: through innovations in statistical modeling and the emergence of computer algorithms capable of processing big data. With the introduction of advanced econometric models such as hierarchical linear models, non-linear approaches including logistic regression, and methods for causal identification, simple correlation analysis has evolved into causal inference, enabling clearer identification of relationships between social indicators (Chen et al. 2021). Yet for cultural research, the expansion of analytical tools alone is insufficient to transform its paradigm. When facing hard-to-capture cultural phenomena, algorithms are more objective tools than personal feelings, as they can transform the phenomena into data and models allowing culture to be causally analyzed together with other social phenomena and novel possibilities of cultural-structural interaction to be explored. With the help of cloud computing and cloud storage technologies, the data resources available to social scientists have expanded dramatically. For example, the 2019 version of Google Books has digitized more than 15 million books published between 1500 and 2019, forming a corpus of over 600 billion words, which is estimated to account for about 15% of all books ever

published in human history.<sup>1</sup> By analyzing it in comparison with realistic behavioral data, the impact of cultural meanings on social reality can be verified from a macro diachronic perspective, bridging the gaps in traditional methods. In Chen et al. (2020)’s study, examining the relationship between the frequency of suicide terms in books and actual suicide rates deepens understanding of the role of cultural and media autonomy.

Beyond classical causal inference, cultural research in the social sciences increasingly adopts mixed methods. The complexity of culture demands approaches that combine close interpretation with empirical analysis, connecting culture with society, subjectivity with objectivity, and micro behavior with macro structure. Bourdieu’s Distinction (1984) remains a foundational example: it integrates textual description, interviews, and participatory observation with the analysis of large-scale survey data using Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) to map social space and lifestyle. The richness of Bourdieu’s data and his use of non-traditional statistical tools provide a lasting methodological model for cultural social science (Holt 1997). Later scholars have extended this view, arguing that no single method or dataset can claim full objectivity and that the binary divide between qualitative and quantitative methods should be replaced with more integrated, multidimensional approaches (Majima and Moore 2009). While concerns persist about the reduction of cultural complexity through coding, researchers increasingly recognize that humanistic interpretation is not the only legitimate mode of cultural analysis (Lee and Martin 2015). The potential of computational and quantitative methods can therefore no longer be ignored.

The blurring of qualitative and quantitative boundaries has also driven the development of non-traditional descriptive analysis. Social computing, through big data and algorithms, allows culture to be measured and analyzed at scale. Interdisciplinary studies now use big data to explore social reality in cultural products. For example, researchers have compiled datasets of fiction across languages and periods to analyze gendered language, finding that collective terms such as person or people more often reference men than women (Bailey et al. 2022). Others have used probabilistic models to trace the evolution of love narratives in fiction, revealing that higher economic development correlates with more frequent representations of love (Baumard et al. 2022). At the macro level, machine learning has further expanded the analytic horizon. Machine learning algorithms were born for “how to learn to solve problems without explicit programming.” They can automatically update and upgrade empirical features of sample data to cluster or predict the data. Among the subfields related to machine learning, data mining and clustering are related to unsupervised machine learning, which can mine and cluster a large number of texts and images, helping us quickly understand the themes and features of these cultural objects without understanding and reading them one by one and greatly shortening the research time. Although some scholars worry that such methods overlook the aesthetic and interpretive dimensions of art, they provide a necessary complement to traditional close reading. As a form of distant reading, they help reveal long-term trajectories and recurrent patterns in cultural production that remain inaccessible through conventional methods.

Alongside methodological innovations in macro-level text analysis (Jockers 2013), Poetics, a leading journal of cultural studies, launched a special issue in 2013 that introduced topic models based on machine learning. The studies clustered textual themes and linked them to social factors such as author gender, nationality, and publication date, demonstrating how topics become measurable variables (Jockers and Mimno 2013). Another study compared the conceptual vocabularies of two academic communities to reveal how each constructs its understanding of the world (Marshall 2013). As scholars increasingly analyze largescale datasets from the Internet, social media, and digitized archives, the capacity to work with data at scale becomes indispensable (Mohr and Bogdanov 2013). Such approaches enable both macro-level analyses of cultural patterns and focused examinations of smaller cultural domains, extending the reach of traditional interpretive methods.

The emergence of social computing methods has brought culture and society closer together. In the era of big data, it is possible to accurately measure cultural behaviors, images, and texts, allowing them to be correlated with other traditional social indicators as an independent variable and tested for causality. These novel techniques help achieve the goal of the cultural turn in the new period, that is, to observe traditional social

4 Introduction of Unsupervised Machine Learning Methods

Text is a vital carrier of views, values, social activities, and historical traces of human society, and textual content analysis has long been a crucial method in cultural research. As archaeologists apply fossils to interpret history, textual content analysis researchers often collect and analyze various forms of written materials, such as books, newspapers, and poems, to explore social behaviors, cultural trends, and historical phenomena. Using machine learning methods to analyze textual materials can help social scientist avoid the challenges of subjectivism and relativism.

Textual content analysis often requires systematic, objective, and quantitative analysis. Traditional content analysis methods often require researchers to start from specific research questions. Then, they need to sample from the documents and quantify the document features by reading them manually according to a pre-drafted coding system. The limitations of this approach are as follows. First, the sheer size of the textual material makes manual reading impractical, and the errors that accompany sampling are equally difficult to avoid. Second, the researcher must determine the research question and coding method in advance, which means that the researcher’s awareness and experience could have a great impact. Along with more digitized information and more accurate and automated natural language processing algorithms, we can identify the latent cultural structure of massive amounts of texts from the historical perspective and explore cultural development at a macro level.

Text analysis based on machine learning is achieved through unsupervised machine learning, as it is suitable for unstructured data sets without labels. When the covariate matrix is available and the explained variable is not, the algorithm will calculate the distance between different samples based on the given covariate information, and cluster the samples. This section introduces four unsupervised machine learning methods for textual analysis: LDA topic model, Word2Vec algorithm, named entity
Y. CHEN ET AL.

recognition, and sentiment analysis. They can all be used to analyze the structure and contents to obtain further information about the deep connotation of the text, while each has its advantages. In addition to the case of Chinese poems presented in the section of the LDA, cases of other methods are in Chapters 10–13 of this book.
4.1 Topic Model

The LDA topic model is an important method for text analysis, which can automatically identify latent topic information in a large-scale text corpus and quantitatively measure the focus of the text. LDA is a three-level hierarchical Bayesian model for document topic generation with unsupervised machine learning techniques (Blei et al. 2003). The application of LDA is based on three nested concepts: the text set to be modeled (the “corpus”), an item in the corpus (a “document”), and a word in the document (a “term”). Thus, documents are nested in the corpus, and the terms are nested in the documents. This model assumes that the corpus contains multiple topics. Each topic is defined as the probability distribution of fixed words, whereas each document selects a topic with a certain probability, and a certain word is selected from this topic with a particular probability. A corpus is described as a probability distribution of potential topics, whereas each topic is a probability distribution of terms. Subsequently, data analysis is performed using the joint distribution to calculate the conditional distribution (a posteriori distribution) of the hidden variable (subject structure) given a specific observed variable (word in the document). The formula is expressed as follows:

with a simple co-occurrence analysis, the LDA topic model reveals the underlying semantic relationships between words, even if the words never appear together in a document. Unlike other topic cluster models, the LDA topic model uses a distinct mixed-membership approach that allows a document to span various topics, ensuring the accuracy of the analysis.

We take the analysis of ancient Chinese poems as an example. Through the LDA topic model, we discovered 10 topics in Complete Poetry Collection of Tang Dynasty (2011), which contains around 48,900 poems: (1) sorrow of parting evoked by the landscape; (2) women’s love and bitterness; (3) bosom friends across time; (4) Zen born from the forest and wind; (5) frontier of war; (6) idyllic leisure; (7) rites and music to praise; (8) seclusion as drifting clouds; (9) lessons from history; (10) immortal in Taoism. If the temporal dimension is introduced into the calculation of topic proportion, the panorama of cultural development and the features of different periods can be further examined, as shown in Fig. 1.

4.2 Word2Vec Algorithm

Word2Vec is Google’s open-source algorithm toolkit. It transforms unstructured text data into high-dimensional vector data, measures the similarity between words, and predicts the context (Yao et al. 2017). Word2Vec includes continuous bag of words (CBOW) and skip-gram algorithms, both of which are generated by a shallow neural network model, calculating and normalizing the cosine similarity between the input vector of the input word (the current word) and the output vector of the target word (the context of the current word). After the word segmentation, stemming, and stop-words removal, the two algorithms transform each word into a high-dimensional vector. The CBOW model takes the context of a certain word as the training input, the keyword itself as the training label, and predicts the central word through the context. On the contrary, the Skip-gram model takes a certain word in the sentence as the training input, and its context as the training label, and applies the input keyword to predict its context (Mikolov et al. 2013).

This section illustrates the application of the CBOW algorithm in the Word2Vec model, using the social concept polarization phenomenon in the “pseudo-environment” of the Internet as an example. The topic “which is more effective between traditional Chinese medicine and Western medicine” has been controversial in China’s Internet community. We analyzed this topic based on two data sources, one from China’s largest Internet Q&A community “Zhihu,” an equivalent to

Then, 735 articles related to traditional Chinese medicine and Western medicine were obtained from the “official account” of WeChat, a mini program for publishing long articles, totaling more than 2.34 million words, spanning from 2014 to 2021.

Each word is converted into a 256-dimensional vector during modeling, and the dimension of each word vector is reduced using Google’s embedding projector tool before mapping them into 3D space in different time periods. In this space, each point is a vector space position of a word. The denser the local point groups, the greater the difference between the semantics of the representative words, and the stronger the perspective polarization. 4.3 Named Entity Recognition

Named entity recognition (NER) is the tool for locating and categorizing important and proper nouns in a text, mainly including names of people, places, organizations, and time. As a fundamental technique for the automatic extraction of text information, NER, although simple, can accurately identify the subject, object, or adverbial in a sentence, and these entities often contain the most important information, such as time, place, and person.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

The tool used for this analysis is the Stanford Named Entity Recognizer, developed by the Natural Language Processing Group at Stanford University, which uses linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) sequence models (Finkel et al. 2005). This Java-based system uses CoNLL, MUC-6, MUC-7, ACE, and other named entity corpora for mixed model training. By utilizing one or more machine learning sequence models to label entities, it can automatically identify names of people, places, and organizations in sentences in a given corpus, and achieves outstanding performance in many applications.<sup>2</sup> The relevant research is further presented in Chapter 11 of this book.
4.4 Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment analysis involves analyzing, processing, drawing conclusions, and reasoning about sentiments in subjective texts. The text suggests various emotional tendencies among different people, which researchers can use to analyze the public’s views or evaluations of a specific issue. We conducted the sentiment analysis via Google’s Cloud Natural Language platform, which employs machine learning algorithms to reveal the emotional meaning of the text. The platform allows users to run sentiment analysis on uploaded texts through its application programming interface (API). After inputting text information, the model can determine the overall attitude expressed in the text, represented by a tone between −1.0 (negative) and +1.0 (positive). Scores in the negative range signify negative sentiments, while positive numbers denote positive sentiments. The greater the absolute value, the stronger the sentiment; the closer the number gets to zero, the more neutral the sentiment is (Garvey and Maskal 2020). The relevant research is further presented in Chapters 12 and 13 of this book.
5 Conclusion

Culture has long been a central concern across the social sciences. Since the cultural turn, two distinct approaches have shaped cultural research: on the one hand, qualitative researchers who focus on the hermeneutic approach emphasize the understanding and interpretation of cultural

meanings, hoping to present the interaction between society and culture in depth through fieldwork and literature analysis, but are inevitably challenged by relativism; on the other hand, quantitative researchers who believe in the positivism of social science are committed to data analysis to ensure the objectivity of cultural research, but they are limited to small samples and individual-level analysis, ignoring the magnitude and continuity of culture. The reason for this phenomenon is that the abstract culture at the macro level cannot be observed and analyzed through microscopic investigations. In addition, the vast number of cultural forms that have emerged as material entities, such as fiction, historical archives, media, government documents, academic journals, etc., only allows the researcher to scan a limited amount of material in a short amount of time. In this case, the contribution of big data and machine learning technology is to provide indicators of cultural volumes that are difficult to be exhausted by traditional qualitative research and cultural characteristics that are difficult to be measured by quantitative research. Thus, researchers can extract topic structures or cultural information from cultural histories or databases spanning a huge time–space scale, construct measurable indicators of cultural meaning, and explore how explicit social structures influence implicit cultural features in a macro-distant reading.

This chapter does not reject traditional methods in cultural research but rather emphasizes the importance of big data and machine learning in opening new directions for the social sciences. Given the unstructured nature of vast amounts of cultural data, big data computing, which specializes in text mining, has a natural fit with cultural research. We call for a synthesis of traditional qualitative methods and emerging machine learning technologies for analysis, a data-driven approach that draws on the visualization tools and indicator descriptions of big data to generalize and discover sociocultural patterns in texts and form theories, or a quantitative calculation of unstructured text to realize the operationalization of cultural hidden indicators and empirical tests.

Nonetheless, big data and machine learning pose substantial methodological and epistemological challenges for social scientists. Although algorithms operate autonomously, every stage of the analytical process remains shaped by human decisions. Critical decisions such as the selection and curation of the corpus, the specifics of data preprocessing, the choice of a particular model, and the tuning of its hyperparameters (like the number of topics) are all subject to the researcher’s discretion.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

Each of these choices can alter the results to some extent. Furthermore, the outputs of unsupervised models, such as topic clusters or word embeddings, represent statistical patterns that require informed interpretation. Assigning meaningful social labels to abstract clusters of words is a fundamentally hermeneutic act that reintroduces a significant degree of subjectivity. Also, the lack of a ground truth makes model validation a profound challenge. Unlike supervised machine learning, where a model’s predictive accuracy can be tested against known outcomes, there is no single correct thematic structure for a corpus. This makes it difficult to assess whether the result genuinely corresponds to meaningful, real-world cultural categories or are simply artifacts of the algorithm’s statistical assumptions.

Computational approaches also raise ethical and political concerns. The large-scale use of digital traces and cultural archives involves issues of privacy and consent, as individuals may not expect their expressions to be permanently stored or analyzed. Algorithms may further reproduce structural biases already present in the data. For instance, when topic modeling is applied to the Tang poetry corpus, the dominance of male literati and the scarcity of women’s voices and folk traditions mean that the results reproduce an already partial cultural record. When cultural models are extended beyond academia, they may also shape governance or platform practices in ways that constrain openness and diversity. These challenges do not diminish the value of computational approaches but highlight that methodological innovation must be accompanied by sustained ethical reflection and responsibility.

In an era of unprecedented cultural production and digital transformation, social computing offers significant potential to expand the scope of social scientific inquiry, reconstruct disciplinary discourse, and foster paradigm shifts. Yet its legitimacy depends not only on technical advancement but also on the social sciences’ capacity to uphold ethical standards, address bias, and remain critically engaged with the cultures and societies they seek to understand.

PART II
Measuring the Unmeasurable
CHAPTER 4
Unspeakable Violence: Predicting the Incidence of Intimate Partner Violence
1 Introduction

Domestic violence refers to violence or other abusive behaviors that occur within the household and includes violence against partners, children, teenagers, and the elderly. Recently, increasing worldwide research attention has been focused on a type of domestic violence known as intimate partner violence (IPV) (Garcia-Moreno et al. 2006; Adams et al. 2012). IPV is typically defined as any behavior, such as physical attacks, sexual coercion, psychological abuse, or controlling behavior, that causes physical, psychological, or sexual harm to others in an intimate relationship, which is usually a marital relationship (Krug et al. 2002; Stewart and Chandra 2017). Research has shown that women are more likely than men to suffer from domestic violence, most often perpetrated by their male partners (Swan et al. 2008). According to the World Health Organization, in 2018, approximately 30% of women worldwide had experienced physical and/or sexual violence from an intimate partner or husband in the previous 12 months (World Health Organization 2021). In addition, the stress and anxiety caused by lockdowns during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic have led to an impending crisis of domestic violence (Chandan et al. 2020). In China studies using local samples have estimated that the incidence rate of IPV ranges from 20 to 25% (Xu et al. 2005), yet a nationwide estimate has not been determined.
A crucial problem faced by researchers aiming to empirically analyze IPV is the large amount of missing data. This problem is particularly

pronounced in Asian societies, such as China, where traditional and patriarchal norms mean that women tend to conceal their partners’ violence toward them and are reluctant to report IPV experiences. This is consistent with feminist theory, which posits that domestic violence is the result of a patriarchal system that enables men to control women and thus strengthen their dominant position in society (Brookman et al. 2017; Hamberger et al. 2017). Thus, if a culture overemphasizes aggressive masculinity and patriarchal norms, there is an increased probability that domestic violence that occurs within this society will not be reported, especially violence experienced by women (Mshweshwe 2020). Previous research has determined that there are several reasons why domestic violence is not reported, such as concerns about privacy, a fear of reprisal or stigmatization, or a desire to protect the offenders. Consequently, substantial portions of data on certain types of domestic violence remain missing, which means that data analyses yield systematic underestimates of the number of domestic violence cases. Thus, it is challenging for researchers and policymakers to determine the real incidence rate of domestic violence.

Thus far, only survey-based analyses have been used to estimate domestic violence (Cui et al. 2012), with missing data problems addressed by the use of listwise deletion or various imputation methods, such as mean imputation and multiple imputation. However, listwise deletion and mean imputation have been criticized as leading to biased or less accurate estimates. For example, the multiple imputation method, which has been widely used, is based on a missing at random (MAR) assumption that may not hold for domestic violence data, as victims may be too ashamed to admit having suffered from domestic violence (Felson et al. 2002). To solve this problem, the current study used advanced machine learning methods to interpolate missing data and thereby obtained accurate estimates of the percentages of Chinese women who have suffered from domestic violence. Machine learning methods have been proven to be more powerful than other methods for obtaining missing data, as the flexibility and complexity of these methods enable them to capture higher-order interactions between data and thus generate better predictions (Pantanowitz and Marwala 2009; Jerez et al. 2010; He et a l. 2013). Thus, this chapter used six machine learning algorithms to analyze data from the Third Wave Survey on the Social Status of Women in China (TWSSSCW 2010) and to estimate the incidence rates of three types of IPV: physical violence, verbal violence, and cold violence.

2 Method
2.1 Survey and Sample

The data were obtained from the TWSSSCW 2010, the most recent nationally representative survey conducted by the All-China Women’s Federation and the National Bureau of Statistics of China. It included a wide range of questions on family, gender relations, health and wellbeing, and domestic violence (including IPV). The TWSSSCW 2010 used multi-stage random stratified probability-proportional-to-size sampling to ensure that its sample was representative of the general population at the province/municipality, street, and neighborhood levels. The survey comprised a sample of 26,166 respondents, but due to the research question of our study, we limited our sample to women and men who were married. Thus, the sample we used in our analysis comprised 23,597 married women and men.
2.2 Measures

Three types of IPV were used as the dependent variables, namely physical violence, verbal violence, and cold violence. In the TWSSSCW 2010, respondents were asked: “Has your partner beaten you?”, “Has your partner insulted you?”, and “Has your partner constantly ignored you?” Responses were recorded on a 4-point scale (“never,” “occasionally,” “sometimes,” or “often”). We dichotomized the three variables to measure whether respondents suffered IPV. As frequencies expressed as “occasionally,” “sometimes,” or “often” are similar and vague in meaning, we collapsed these frequencies into one category. Table 1 shows that 1.22% of men and 2.83% of women reported experiencing physical violence; 4.88% of men and 6.32% of women reported experiencing verbal violence; and 8.46% of men and 9.49% of women reported experiencing cold violence. The overall percentage of missing data was 6.95%. Figure 1 shows the demographic distributions of missing data on the respondents’ experiences of IPV. Respondents who were female, from urban areas, and had low education levels were more likely not to have supplied complete responses to questions on IPV than other female respondents, which suggested that IPV data were more likely to be missing from the answers of this subgroup of respondents.
To estimate the missing values, we analyzed the values of 611 variables from the dataset that covered a wide range of topics related to aspects

2.3 Imbalanced Data Problem

As shown in Tab le 1, the dataset was highly imbalanced, as only a small proportion of respondents reported having experienced IPV. For instance, in the case of physical IPV, there are 21,067 class 0 samples indicating that individuals were never beaten by their spouses, but the class 1 samples, which represent those who were beaten, total only 889, accounting for
4 UNSPEAKABLE VIOLENCE: PREDICTING THE INCIDENCE

approximately 4% of the class 0 samples. Similar imbalances were observed for verbal and psychological abuse. In the machine learning process, the majority class often dominates the learning process, making classifiers difficult to recognize minority classes. For example, if a learning algorithm were to adopt a simple approach and predict all 21,956 samples as class 0, indicating no spousal abuse, it would achieve an accuracy of 96%. However, this contradicts our goal of identifying genuine cases of IPV. Therefore, although ignoring the minority class is economical and efficient in algorithm processing of data imbalances, the resulting model bias in practical applications is immeasurable.

It is necessary to use strategies before applying machine learning algorithms to mitigate the degree of data imbalance, generally in two main directions: (1) increasing the number of minority class samples through oversampling and (2) reducing the majority class samples through under sampling. Since each method has its advantages and disadvantages depending on different application scenarios and data structures, we chose typical methods such as Random Over Sampler and SMOTE for oversampling, Random Under Sampler-ensemble and K-means for under sampling, and SMOTE-ENN, which combines both oversampling and under sampling, for model training. We then compared the performance of each model. The 21,956 non-missing samples were split into a training set and a validation set in a 70%–30% ratio, maintaining the original dataset’s distribution of two categories of IPV in both the validation set and training set. The training set was then resampled, and a Random Forest algorithm was used to train the classifier, with the validation set used to measure the classifier’s generalization effect.

Table 2 exemplifies the performance of models under different sampling methodologies using “physical violence” as a reference. In terms of evaluation metrics, we calculated accuracy, recall, confusion matrices, AUC values, ROC curves, and detection error tradeoff (DET) curves for a comprehensive assessment of each model. Accuracy (Acc) represents the proportion of correctly predicted samples out of the total samples, providing a straightforward reflection of model prediction effectiveness. However, it lacks significance in scenarios of imbalanced sample distribution. Recall (Rec), also known as the true positive rate, reflects the proportion of positive cases correctly identified among all actual positives. The confusion matrix visually contrasts the discrepancies between actual outcomes and predictions, where TN, FN, FP, and TP respectively stand for true negatives, false negatives, false positives, and true positives. The
Y. CHEN ET AL.

ROC curve illustrates the tradeoff between the true positive rate and the false positive rate across different thresholds, with the AUC ranging from 0.5 to 1, where higher values indicate better model performance. Similarly, the DET curve plots the false negative rate against the false positive rate at various thresholds, with a smaller AUC indicating a lower overall error probability and thus superior model performance. Since ROC and AUC are used to evaluate the overall performance of classifiers and are less sensitive to class imbalances, they are suited for the algorithms used in this study. In contrast, Rec is more informative than Acc when focusing on class 1 samples, especially when their number is significantly lower than that of class 0 samples. Accordingly, in this research, we prioritized AUC and Rec as the main evaluation metrics, supplemented by Acc and the confusion matrix, to select the best-performing machine learning classification model.

Regarding accuracy, the SMOTE algorithm performed the best, achieving accuracies of 0.96 and 0.95 in the test and validation sets, respectively; SMOTE-ENN followed closely but also showed good results with 0.95 in the training set and 0.94 in the validation set. However, the recall of SMOTE was only 0.33 in the training set and 0.16 in the validation set, and SMOTE-ENN also underperformed, as evidenced in the confusion matrix where these two algorithms frequently misclassified class 1 samples as class 0. This suggests that although these sampling models addressed the issue of sample balance, the trained models still tended to neglect minority class samples and erroneously categorize cases into

Therefore, in subsequent predictions, we employ the Random Under Sampler-ensemble method to train our models. We randomly select an equal number of majority class samples as there are minority class samples, combine them with all minority class samples, and train a classifier. This process is repeated 500 times, training 500 classifiers in total, and using these 500 base classifiers to predict each case, yielding 500 outcomes. Ultimately, a majority voting method is applied to adopt the most frequently occurring class from the predictions as the final classification for each case.

The Random Forest algorithm is a supervised machine learning method for classification. It generates an ensemble of decision trees, and these then vote for the most popular class. The growth of each tree in the ensemble is governed by random vectors. First, a random vector Θk is generated for the kth tree; it is independent of the previous random vectors Θ1,…, Θk−1, but has the same distribution. Then, a tree is grown using the training set and Θk, which results in a classifier h (x, Θk). After a large number of decision trees have been generated, these trees vote for the most popular class. Thus, a Random Forest algorithm is a classifier that consists of a set of tree-structured classifiers {h $( \mathrm { x } ,   \Theta \mathrm { k } ) ,   \mathrm { k } = 1 , . . . \} .$ where {Θk} are independent identically distributed random vectors and each tree casts a unit vote for the most popular class at input x (Breiman

2001). This can be expressed by the following formula:
H x = \arg \max \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} I (h _ {i} (x) = Y)
where $H ( x )$ represents the Random Forest model, $b _ { i } \left( x \right)$ is a single treestructured classifier, and Y is the output variable or target variable.

Constructing a Random Forest classifier involves tuning numerous hyperparameters. Although Scikit-learn provides default settings for this classifier, tailoring training hyperparameters specifically for the dataset can significantly enhance model performance. The objective of hyperparameter tuning is to balance the bias and variance of the classifier ensemble within reasonable limits. For Random Forest, increasing the number of decision trees (n estimators) can substantially reduce the overall model variance without affecting the bias and variance of individual sub-models, although there is a ceiling effect on performance improvements. Considering computational efficiency, we increased the number of sub-models from the default value of 100 to 500. For each sub-decision tree within the Random Forest, reducing the maximum number of features considered during splits (max features) introduces additional randomness into the model, which decreases the correlation between sub-models and enhances generalization capability, although too few features can increase the model’s bias. Furthermore, a deeper maximum tree depth (max depth) results in more complex sub-models, lowering the overall model bias but potentially increasing the variance among sub-models or leading to overfitting.

Thus, we employed a grid search method to identify the optimal hyperparameter settings within a specific range. We set the “maximum number of features” between 20 and 45 and “maximum tree depth” between 5 and 30, training a model at every five-unit interval, producing 36 different hyperparameter combinations. To avoid the randomness inherent in proportional division of test and validation sets, we applied a more rigorous ten-fold cross-validation approach. The selection criterion for the optimal model was based on the composite evaluation metric, the AUC value.

3 Results

Table 4 shows that the Random Forest classifier analyzed 1,641 missing cases of physical violence, of which 854 and 787 were classified as “No” and “Yes,” respectively. Thus, the incidence rate of physical violence was 7.10% in the data imputed via the Random Forest algorithm, which was greater than the rate (4.05%) in the original raw dataset (i.e., without imputation). Similarly, the Random Forest classifier analyzed 1,643 missing cases of verbal violence and classified 860 and 783 cases as “No” and “Yes,” respectively. This equated to an incidence rate of verbal violence of 13.74%, which was greater than the original incidence rate of 11.21%. Finally, the Random Forest classifier analyzed 1,645 missing cases of cold violence and classified 546 and 1,099 cases as “No” and “Yes,” respectively. This equated to an incidence rate of cold violence of 21.35%, which was greater than the original incidence rate of 17.95%.

5 Conclusion

In recent years, the problem of domestic violence, especially IPV, has received increasing attention from academics and policymakers worldwide, as it is regarded as an important predictor of couples’ health, well-being, and quality of life. However, missing data on certain types of domestic violence presents a substantial challenge for researchers performing IPV studies. The pattern of these missing data is missing
4 UNSPEAKABLE VIOLENCE: PREDICTING THE INCIDENCE

not at random because these missing data are largely related to IPV. For example, people may fail to disclose having suffered IPV due to concerns about privacy, a fear of reprisal or stigmatization, or a desire to protect the offenders. Therefore, the traditional methods used to deal with datasets that are missing data, such as listwise deletion and multiple imputation, are not suitable for dealing with datasets that are missing IPV data because these methods are based on missing completely at random or missing at random assumptions. Indeed, we found that the incidence rates of physical, verbal, and cold violence were underestimated if we performed listwise deletion of cases with missing values prior to analysis. Thus, we used innovative machine learning methods to predict the missing data on the incidence rates of three types of IPV: physical violence, verbal violence, and cold violence.

We therefore compared the performance of various machine learning methods and selected the optimal method—the Random Forest algorithm—to impute missing data. We found that analysis of datasets containing imputed data led to increased incidence rates of physical violence (7.10%), verbal violence (13.74%), and cold violence (21.35%), compared to those obtained from datasets without imputed data (4.05%, 11.21%, and 17.95%, respectively).

These results highlight the necessity and advantages of using machine learning methods to address the missing data problem in IPV research. This chapter reveals that more effective tools must be designed to enable the accurate estimation of incidence rates of domestic violence and demonstrates the need for more empirical research to further advance the understanding of IPV, using machine learning to obtain missing data.

CHAPTER 5
Hidden Identities: Predicting Sexual Minority Orientation Among Youth
1 Introduction

Across the globe, rights movements for sexual minorities have advanced at an unprecedented pace over the past few decades in Western countries and many other regions (Ghaziani et al. 2016). Despite this, individuals with sexual minority identities in most cultures are relegated to lower status and even marginalized as a distinct social group. Compared to sexual majorities, members of sexual minorities are segregated geographically (Gross 2012), socially, and psychologically, and are constantly exposed to the discriminatory tastes of the heterosexual majority (USAID 2014; Lee et al. 2016; Wang et a l. 2019).

While most of the existing literature on sexual minorities has been conducted in the Western world, research focusing on sexual minorities in China is relatively scarce (UNDP 2016). Owing to negative stereotypes and devaluation, sexual minority identities often result in antipathy (i.e., disgust), and even blame attributions and justification of unfair social treatment (O’Donohue and Caselles 1993; USAID 2014; UNDP 2016). Such long-standing stigmas and moral condemnation make individuals with sexual minority orientation reluctant to disclose their inherent sexual orientation, leading to a high percentage of missing values and downward-biased estimates in information obtained from traditional social surveys. For example, in the U.S., the relevant statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have shown that an estimated 4% of adults identify as members of a sexual minority.

However, if we look at items relevant to same-sex sexual behavior and same-sex attraction, the number of individuals who reported having samesex sexual behavior experience, and same-sex attraction has increased to about 8.2% and 11%, respectively (Gates 2011). This, to some degree, implies that the question relevant to sexual minority orientation may suffer from severe underestimation. A report from the American College Health Association showed that in 2006, 10% out of 33,000 undergraduates were identified as sexual minorities in the U.S. (Postsecondary National Policy Institute 2018). In China, the paucity of reliable data that can identify the sexual minority group and its associated needs contributes significantly to the invisibility of the sexual minority population in the eyes of academia as well as critical social programs (Cao and Lu 2014; Hu 2016; Xu et a l. 2017).

To address the challenges of estimating the size of China’s sexual minority population, this research, based on the Beijing College Students Panel Survey (BCSPS), aims to estimate the genuine percentage of sexual minorities among Chinese youth in Beijing using machine learning methods. We used Random Forest, an ensemble learning approach for classification and regression, to predict the sexual orientation of those who didn’t respond to the survey question. Given that the size of sexual minorities is considerably smaller than that of heterosexual people, the standard Random Forest classifier tends to be biased toward the majority class. To mitigate the bias, we adopted repeated random subsampling methods (Khalilia et al. 2011). To evaluate model performance, we compared the results of bagging, boosting, Gaussian Naïve Bayes support vector machine (SVM), and Logistic Regression classifiers. Results from multiple machine learning classifiers and different sets of covariates generally show that the actual percentage of sexual minorities among Beijing college students is nearly twice as large as that obtained from traditional social survey data, such as the BCSPS. Through our research, we paid particular attention to protecting individuals’ information security. All results that are presented in the paper reflect the group trend rather than personal traits.

2 Materials and Methods
2.1 Data

The analysis is based on the Beijing College Students Panel Survey (BCSPS) conducted by the Survey and Data Center of Renmin University in China. The first wave of data was collected in 2009. Using stratified random sampling, college students from 15 universities in Beijing were selected, with a response rate of around 93%. Since then, the follow-up surveys have been conducted each year until 2013. In the fourth-wave survey, there was a question relevant to respondents’ sexual orientation. It asked the surveyed college students to report their sexual orientation and provided four items to choose from (“heterosexual,” “homosexual,” “bisexual,” and “not sure”). As Table 1 shows, among the 4043 samples, 3684 students identified themselves as heterosexual and 115 identified themselves as sexual minorities (homosexual or bisexual), or belonging to a sexual minority. According to this, the percentage of sexual minorities among college students in Beijing is around 3.03% if we deleted 244 samples with missing values on sexual orientation (i.e., 156 declined to respond and 88 chose “not sure”). However, as mentioned above, many of the 244 students who did not explicitly respond to the question about their sexual orientation are very likely to be sexual minorities, given the lurking stigma toward sexual minorities in China (Wang et al. 2019).

The fourth wave of BCSPS contains 910 variables for 4043 respondents, providing comprehensive information about demographic characteristics, academic performance, and socioeconomic attributes, which offer us an opportunity to predict missing values on sexual orientation. 2.2 Imbalanced Problem

As shown, the dataset is highly imbalanced with respect to sexual orientation, which is unsurprising because the percentage of sexual minorities is much smaller than that of heterosexual people worldwide. In our data, the imbalance ratio is approximately 1:32 (115/3684), and the percentage of sexual minorities is 3.03% (115/3799). If one is using a standard
5 HIDDEN IDENTITIES: PREDICTING SEXUAL MINORITY

prediction algorithm, the highly imbalanced data may lead to underprediction of the minority group because most classifiers assume that training and testing data are drawn from the same distribution. In this vein, it is not easy to prepare appropriate data for training and testing, which leads to a biased prediction (Provost 2000). Taking sexual orientation as an example, if 99% of people declare themselves to be heterosexual, a standard machine learning algorithm (such as a Naïve Bayes classifier or a decision tree) can hardly do better than the 99% accuracy achieved by a trivial classifier that labels everyone as heterosexual. That is, when applying machine learning on highly imbalanced datasets, the built-in goal to maximize the accuracy of the learning algorithm will inevitably under-predict the minority class, as this is the “intelligent” solution for the algorithm. To address this, a common practice is to rebalance the training sets by resampling, boosting, bagging, or conducting repeated random subsampling (Japkowicz and Stephen 2002).

In this chapter, we applied the repeated random subsampling approach to address the imbalanced data problem. That is, we partitioned the training data into subsamples using 6-split, 12-split, 24-split, and 32-split of the original sexual majority respondents, respectively. By doing so, each subsample ends up containing a less imbalanced data set than the original one (the one with an imbalance ratio of around 1:32). For the 6-split subsample, the number of sexual majority participants is 614 (the original number = 3684/6). As a result, the imbalance rate is 1:5.34 (115:(3684/ 6)). Similarly, for the 12-split subsample, the number of sexual majority participants is 307, and the imbalance ratio is 1:2.67 (115:(3684/12)). For the 24-split subsample, the number of sexual majority participants is 153 and the imbalance ratio is 1:1.33 (115:(3684/24)). Finally, the 32- split subsample contains an equal number of instances from the sexual minority and sexual majority (115:115), with the imbalance ratio being 1. Note that the 32-split approach is 1:1-resampling, following Khalilia, Chakraborty, and Popescu (Khalilia et al. 2011) by partitioning the training data into subsamples with each subsample containing half the sexual minority and half the sexual majority, except for the last subsample (in some cases). We also experimented with repeated random subsampling by replicating sexual minority cases six, twelve, and twenty-four times. This approach reduced the imbalance in each subsample compared with the original dataset. However, due to the introduced repeated samples, the overfitting problem emerged, so we did not present the relevant results in this chapter.

In Random Forest, a forest itself consists of an ensemble of decision trees which could output a classification, where the output is predicted using the mode of observations in the terminal nodes. In this chapter, the splitting decision is based on the Gini index, a measure of node purity. It is given by the following formula:

where $P _ { k }$ is the probability of being classified as class k in a node. Thus, the Gini index takes values in [0,1], where 0 indicates that all elements are of the same class. In decision tree construction, splits are chosen to minimize the Gini index. The Gini index measures the distribution of class labels in nodes. A smaller value of the Gini index suggests a purer node. A split is valid only when the Gini index for a child node is less than that for the parent node.

Random Forest has the reputation of being insensitive to the training hyperparameters (Palmer et al. 2007); to choose the maximum number of features for a split, we followed standard practice by taking the square root of the number of our variables $( 1 8 \approx { \sqrt { 3 3 7 } } )$ for each individual tree. We followed the rule of thumb to set 50 as the number of trees for the Random Forest algorithm.
2.3 Sample Splitting

In this chapter, we developed an N-fold cross-validation using the whole available BCSPS data. We chose 6, 12, 24, and 32 (1:1) as split times $( T _ { i } )$ to create an upgrade trend for the sexual minority rate. For each splitting turn, we first separated the samples for learning $\left( N_{l}   =   3799 \right)$ and the samples for predicting $\left( N _ { p } = 2 4 4 \right)$ . And then, the learning sample was further divided into $N _ { l }$ sexual majority set $( N _ { l 0 } = 3 6 8 4 )$ and sexual minority set $\left( N _ { l 1 } = 1 1 5 \right)$ . For the sexual majority set, we randomly sorted the $N _ { l 0 }$ set and partitioned it into $T _ { i }$ subsamples. Every $N _ { l 0 }$ subsample has an equal number of unrepeated samples except the last $N _ { l 0 }$ subsamples of 24 and 32 splits (they contain 165 and 119 samples respectively). For the sexual minority set, the data points are sampled without replacement.

To generate subsamples for prediction, we combined each subsample from $N _ { l 0 }$ with $N _ { l 1 }$ . By doing this, each subsample of the sexual majority sample was selected once, while the sexual minority sample was selected $T _ { i }$ times. For each subsampling set, we randomly sorted the data and took

4 Conclusion

In the past decade, profound social transformations have caused the emergence of a broad sociopolitical climate that is gradually more accepting of sexual minorities in many countries (Lane 2007). Despite the overall shift toward reduced discrimination and greater acceptance, it would be premature to claim the imminent demise of societal stigma and individual prejudice against the sexual minority population. Being “invisible” in mainstream society becomes a living strategy for many sexual minorities in China. The perceived stigma may drive biased responses, particularly when using traditional survey methods, as sexual minorities often feel reluctant to disclose their sexual orientation, leading to a high percentage of missing values. To overcome such barriers, we adopt Random Forest imputation, a machine learning approach to infer the sexual orientation of non-respondents based on survey questions from BCSPS. After filling out those missing values, the percentage of college students with sexual minority orientation increased from 3.03% to 5.71%, which is a bit higher than the official estimation (2–4%) based on the first nationwide survey of sexual behavior in China conducted in 1998–99 (Wong 2015). The results remain consistent if alternative classifiers are adopted.

Regarding our result, one doubt may arise as we didn’t distinguish “not sure” and “refuse to answer” but simply took them as “missing value.” While different implications may link to these answers,2 this doesn’t challenge our findings. First, as respondents in the fourth-wave BCSPS are all senior-year college students, people who don’t understand the meaning of terms are rare. Second and most importantly, our models are trained to give the best prediction for samples’ sexual orientation without predefining their sexual preferences. If based on the training set, these models get the ability to predict an individual’s sexual orientation, then ideally, they can figure out whether an individual is a sexual/

gender majority or minority in any cases within the dataset. A valid prediction model independently predicts individuals’ sexual orientations without researchers’ influence.

Still, there are some limitations worth discussing. First, this analysis only provides a crude estimation of the percentage of college students with a sexual minority orientation without further differentiating specific types; especially, it does not capture gender minorities (e.g., transgender) and some subtypes of sexual minorities, namely pansexual or asexual (Suen and Chan 2020). Our coding scheme which only contains two values: 1-yes, 0-no, ensures that we still could capture those people but with lower precision. Considering the sensitivity of the sexual orientation issue, the data that involves sexual orientation is rare in China. Besides, most of the survey data relevant to sexual minorities are collected using the snowball sampling strategy; the data created are a non-probability sample which has no societal representativeness. BCSPS data is actually the only publicly available and regional representative dataset that has information about sexual orientation. It is one of the few data that has the potential to provide an accurate inferring of the sexual minority community, though the measurement of sexual orientation is far from ideal.

Second, extrapolating the sexual minority proportion in this analysis is based on the assumption that respondents reported their real sexual orientation. Note that due to the stigmatized social status of sexual minorities, respondents’ answers might be biased toward prevalent social norms, which are more acceptable to mainstream society. This means there may be some sexual minorities who deliberately hide their true sexual orientation by intentionally giving inaccurate responses. It is therefore likely that our estimation of the percentage of sexual minorities is still underestimated. In other words, our results provide a conservative estimation of the sexual minority of college students in Beijing. Nevertheless, as the BCSPS is a large-scale social survey with stratified random sampling and a clear commitment to protect respondents’ information security, sexual minorities generally have little need to deliberately pretend they are heterosexual people in an anonymous questionnaire. Furthermore, our robustness check by expelling samples who declared heterosexual preference but were predicted as sexual minorities in the first round shows little change occurred compared with the general findings.

Third, as the results show, the training accuracy is much higher than the validation accuracy, which implies that our Random Forest classifier may suffer from an overfitting problem. However, Breiman (2001) claimed that the Random Forest algorithm does not overfit, as it can generate an internal unbiased estimate of generalization error when more trees are added to the model. There is significant controversy surrounding this subject. Some other scholars have shown that as the forest building progresses, it is the generalization error variance rather than the bias itself that would decrease to zero in the Random Forest (Tang and Ishwaran 2017). In this research, by adopting a Lasso regression algorithm, we largely reduce the size of the variable sets for estimation, which, to some degree, has down-weighted bias arising due to an overfitting problem.

Finally, another potential source that may lead to biased estimation is the fact that our assessment is based on a one-item question: “What is your sexual orientation?” Considering the sensitivity of this question, substantial inaccuracies may occur. A more accurate estimate might be achieved by incorporating prevalent sexual orientation tests (including the Kinsey scale test, the Epstein Sexual Orientation Inventory (ESOI), Storm’s sexual orientation test with quadrants, and even list experience) into our approach. It is also worth noting that this study is limited to assessing the sexual orientation of college students in Beijing, but does not seek to estimate the number of gender minorities.

In spite of some deficiencies, the methods we used to predict the potential sexual minorities have undoubtedly been a breakthrough. Our effort helps increase the visibility of sexual minorities, which in turn will enhance the health and well-being of the sexual minorities and serve to protect their rights, which are so important in achieving equality in society and before the law.

PART III
Developing Theories
CHAPTER 6
Computing Grounded Theory: Algorithm-Based Approach to Deriving Theories
1 Introduction

Quantitative analysis was previously a general designation for the analysis and research of numerical data (Scott and Marshall 2009: 538). But it has been increasingly framed in a single dimension with the deductive method as logic, theoretical (hypothesis) verification as purpose, statistical inference as the paradigm, especially the binary separation of qualitative and quantitative studies. Undoubtedly, the method of hypothesis testing has shattered the pure philosophical speculation involving unsocial phenomena. But it seems to gradually lose the initiative of theory production and development. To be specific, new concepts and theories are constantly observed, discovered, and refined by qualitative researchers, thus forming the “precursor” of the theoretical development frontier. On the contrary, quantitative researchers can only conduct post hoc statistical tests on existing theories or hypotheses derived from the literature and from researchers’ own interpretive assumptions. Quantitative researchers focusing on Karl Popper (2005)’s definition of science tend to overlook the value of data and models for directly enlightening theory and the application possibility of inductive logic for quantitative research since they get indulged in self-appreciation of the importance of falsification testing in most cases.

Is there a new methodological path through which quantitative researchers can, like their qualitative counterparts, directly contribute to the development of theoretical hypotheses rather than merely performing
© The Author(s) 2026 Y. Chen et al., Machine Learning in Social Science, [https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-6465-1\_6](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-6465-1_6)
Y. CHEN ET AL.

post hoc statistical tests? Large quantities of unsubstantiated or even absurd hypotheses may be produced from brainstorming variable lists randomly or even via the pairwise correlations of $N \times ( N - 1 )$ variables in ergodic form. Moreover, problems such as quantitative restriction, selective combination, and multicollinearity of control variables cannot be addressed through the implementation of the cyclical tests for various X –Y combinations based on the traditional regression model. As a result, the direct application of data and models in the direct midwifery of theory has been considered impossible among quantitative scholars for quite a long period of time.

However, with the abundance of social survey data on a large scale and the application of methods such as machine learning in social science research, possibilities have been discovered. In this chapter, a generation method for quantitative theory was proposed based on large amounts of data and machine learning models (algorithm model). In practical terms, quantitative analysis was conducted on a series of X to Y predicting capabilities through supervised machine learning for the given Y and a large number of explanatory variables X. Many factors with strong predictability can be explored and filtered using the logical correlation between causality and predictability, which is directly referential for the theoretical hypothesis. In addition, Y attempts to be prepared with one or more new factors that have potential theoretical value, further helpful for social scientists to generate, develop, and revise theories. As a typical method for computational social science, its logical foundation has achieved the same result by the core principle of “grounded theory (GT),” a famous method for qualitative research. Data were coded and interpreted by breaking the preconception of theory, and without any theoretical hypothesis, so that the generation path from empirical to theoretical research can be opened by breaking the logic of “deduction verification.” It is named the computing grounded theory (CGT).
2 Limit of Falsification
2.1 Hypothesis Testing and Scientific Ring

The development of quantitative social science research has expanded a century from the initial simple data description to contingency tables, and from various regression models to causal inference methods. In the past four decades, the fundamental model for quantitative social
6 COMPUTING GROUNDED THEORY: ALGORITHM-BASED

science research was built on the basis of questionnaire data. And the multiple linear regression was adopted to statistically infer whether explanatory variables are correlated or causal with the explained variables. This development process from formation to maturity is a process during which research paths are constantly solidified, and the traditional quantitative study is fast developed. That is, the relatively standardized “template” format has been adopted by mainstream social science journals at home and abroad. A traditional quantitative article that conforms to the standard should be composed of problems, references, assumptions, measurements, data, methods, analyses, and conclusions, with these closely interlocked parts forming a connecting link between what comes before and what goes after. In fact, Wells and Picou (1981) also made similar conclusions regarding the hypothesis-testing model upon analyzing the contents of the American Sociological Review (1936–1979). Furthermore, the conventional paradigm of quantitative research is not unique to sociology but is also widely applied across other social sciences such as economics, political science, and psychology. In these fields, quantitative analysis typically follows the principle of statistically testing theoretical propositions by falsifying their corresponding null h ypotheses.

Testing existing theories is not the entirety of theoretical work in the social sciences. In Scientific Logic in Sociology, Walter L. Walla ce (1971: 18, 23) proposed the concept of the “scientific ring,” arguing that social research advances through a continuous, reciprocal cycle of theory construction and empirical testing (Fig. 1). Although the traditional quantitative paradigms of hypothesis testing apparently center on the right half of the “scientific ring,” the process of theoretical construction to testing is a complete path followed by social science research institutes. And theoretical construction has seemingly become an exclusive mission of qualitative research, while theoretical verification is taken as a pattern by quantitative research due to the distinction formed between quantitative and qualitative research. Therefore, qualitative research is utilized for the proposal of theories as it is considered “inductive,” “understanding,” “humanistic,” and “historical context,” whereas quantitative research featuring “deductive,” “objective,” “positivist,” and “of natural law” are for theoretical verification. Quantitative research, however, tends to be assumed under the limitation of existing common senses of theories and research, leaving it challenged by “the verification of common senses with complex methods” and “the mediocrity of research topics” in most cases.
Y. CHEN ET AL.
