Research on Chinese BL fiction investigated gender politics constructed by BL fandom groups. As an epitome of neoliberal feminism, BL authors and readers explored their subjectivity, while also resisting or conforming to official discourse and state authority (Tian, 2020b). When discussing the cultural attributes of Chinese BL fiction, researchers mostly regarded it as a modern or postmodern counterculture against Confucianist cultural norms (Chang & Tian, 2021), while paying less attention to its possible patriarchal remnants in the traditional culture and clan system. In addition, the relevant literature primarily adopted qualitative methods, such as interviews, questionnaires, and textual analysis of representative works. Although their conclusions have greatly enriched our understanding of gender perspectives in BL novels, their research objects were always within their visible range, causing them to easily ignore works that were not popular but did have a certain impact on the author and the reader.

Tracing the origin of BL fiction, Japanese BL fiction had two characteristics, namely the Western story background and tragic plots (Mizoguchi, 2015:26-27). These aligned with the pursuit of supreme beauty and sensory pleasure under aestheticism. Following two decades of growth, Chinese BL fiction has already departed from its Japanese ancestor and developed its own tastes. As an article in The New York Times stated, BL fiction in China is too large to be considered a subculture in comparison with its Japanese counterpart (Tatlow, 2014). Besides, owing to the Chinese government’s anti-pornography campaign, nowadays, no sexual scenarios appear on legal websites (Yang & Xu, 2017). The resulting

BL fiction has already become an increasingly prosperous womencentered culture in China that involves millions of women authors. We adopted unsupervised machine learning text analysis methods to analyze the titles and introductions of 72,548 Jinjiang’s original BL fiction pieces from 2003 to 2019. These analyses answered two questions: (1) What topics and contents do Chinese women BL authors prefer? (2) How do the gender concepts of Chinese culture affect the topics and contents of BL fiction?
2 Gendered Perspective

Elaine Baruch (1991:9) stated in her work Women, Love, and Power that great love literature could help us look for the transcendence of gender polarization and disrupt the hierarchically structured male/female binary system. In a sense, BL fiction is “great love literature” from its readers’ and authors’ perspectives. This genre can be considered a breakthrough of the “male gaze,” which constructs the “female gaze” through consuming male erotica (Meyer, 2013).

The majority of studies about male-male romance have suggested gender, especially the impact of gender description on readers’ intention and their identity (Yi, 2013; Nagaike & Suganuma, 2013). For the
Y. CHEN ET AL.

former, scholars such as Pagliassotti (2008) found that the “pure love” gender-absent dimension in the stories, which avoided one-dimensional characters of women and heterosexual “boring narratives,” was the primary attraction for the audience. Furthermore, Zsila et al. (2018), using an online survey, proved that sexual titillation, visual imagery, and aesthetics explained readers’ preference for BL fiction.

Other researchers have focused on the authors’ intentions conveyed by the text of the fiction. When Jenkins (1992: 191) researched slash fiction, similar to BL fiction in China, he considered that the transition of these stories from male homosocial desire to homoerotic passion was an exploration of alternatives to traditional masculinity. Since BL fiction was often associated with women’s literature, Takemiya (1993), a Japanese BL manga artist, believed that BL works negated the subservient gender role imposed on women, helped women liberate themselves from the oppression of male power, and facilitated feminist ideals. A Chinese scholar went further by invoking Michel Foucault’s constructivism to argue that women created a heterotopia through BL to compete for political space and resist patriarchy (Zheng, 2016). These studies presented the feminist significance of BL fiction.

However, recent studies have increasingly analyzed the anti-feminist features of BL stories. For example, Zhou, Paul, and Sherman (2018) studied the heterosexual romantic ideal in BL fiction and found that power differences persist in relationships between men. In particular, the fixed couple of seme (the attacker in Japanese, referring to the penetrator in sex) and uke (meaning the receiver in Japanese, referring to the penetrated in sex)3 imitates the typical male-woman relationship that produces unequal power. Han (2020) also highlighted that Chinese BL authors often allow male protagonists to behave like heterosexual women in the male-male relationship, while women were absent in these relationships. This phenomenon suggests that the burden of sexual objectification cannot disappear easily. “The male gaze would not be simply inverted to produce a straightforward female gaze” (Burston & Richardson, 1995: 32), which means the female gaze could not consume the other gender as

Although there are controversies surrounding the feminist features of BL fiction, it is undeniable that power-related issues remain crucial in the study of gender within BL fiction, not only as a reflection of gender power against patriarchy, but also as a manifestation of resistance to authority and mainstream culture. As Foucault (1979: 48) points out in The History of Sexuality, pleasure and power are linked by complex mechanisms and devices of excitation and incitement while they seek, overlap, and reinforce each other. When women BL authors enjoy their erotic desire through the two male protagonists, their pleasure is also associated with power. Indeed, some researchers considered that gender power and political power could work together. From the authors’ side, Xu and Yang (2013) focused on a particular branch, father-son incest, which, in their perspective, reflected the resistance of Chinese women authors to the “authoritarian” government. From the government’s side, Bai (2022) analyzed the regulation of pornography in BL works and pointed out that this seemed to be objective censorship that was contextually and structurally gendered. However, interpreting any narrative about imbalanced power relationships solely as a political metaphor might be unfounded. At the very least, an alternative explanation could be that BL works on legal websites, which do not contain any substantial political implications due to self-regulation. Consequently, for the unseen political threat of BL works, the government endeavored to reduce the pornographic content inside rather than simply ban this genre.

Shifting from a political focus, given China’s rich ancient history, systematic ethics, and literary heritage, it is likewise reasonable and theoretical to hypothesize that the traditional culture may have greatly influenced women’s writing. Considering that Chinese BL fiction is embedded within Chinese culture, some long-standing patriarchal values—including the importance of marriage and the continuity of a clan through reproduction—may help to explain the content of BL fiction. Therefore, the context of Chinese traditional culture should be explored when analyzing gender power in Chinese BL fiction’s literary creation.

3 Data and Methods

We implemented text mining methods to explore the unstructured text data of BL fiction. This methodology was chosen for the following three reasons: (1) We planned to obtain an entire picture of Chinese women BL authors’ literary creation, which could only be achieved with largescale text analysis, and any part of the data enables further representative studies. (2) Compared with questionnaire surveys and qualitative thematic analysis, text mining of Chinese BL fiction is more objective in exploring the fiction topics and gendered expressions in the fictional stories. (3) Different from quantitative methods that use computer programs to search texts for keywords, the LDA topic model and word vector technology of text mining methods explore the meaning of the text by fully considering the relations between terms (DiMaggio et al., 2013).

We selected JLC as the data source, which is the largest and most well-known online platform for BL fiction creation in China and globally. Various studies have used cases and data from JLC. Several have focused on the site’s profit model (Jiang and Kuang, 2016), whereas others have examined the feminist implications for Chinese women’s literature (Feng, 2009). This website features strong interactivity. Since its fiction is mostly serialized, readers’ preferences strongly influence the story’s completion. Like sponsors, online reading communities offer authors emotional and financial incentives through comments and rewards (Tian and Adorjan, 2016). Their support even forms a “gift economy” that provides authors with the opportunity to contract with JLC and publish commercially, thus earning both popularity and commercial benefits (Wei, 2014).

To deal with the sample selection problems that may exist in previous studies and include works with lower visibility in the study, we analyzed titles and introductions of all 72,548 BL fiction pieces published since the foundation of Jinjiang in 2003. To make our topic more focused, we excluded fan fiction, so only original and stand-alone stories were entered into the database. We counted the number of Jinjiang original BL fictional works by year, as shown in Fig. 1. This number increased every year, save for a slight decrease between 2014 and 2016 due to the Chinese government’s most extensive anti-pornography campaign.

Due to the data protection protocol of the paid main body on JLC, we could not extract and archive all complete texts of the 72,548 BL fiction pieces. Rather, we explored the information-rich titles and introductions (written by the author and containing a blurb and a plot synopsis) to

Similar to a “vestibule,” they provide the reader with the choice of either stepping inside or abandoning the text. Currently, online fiction is typically mass-produced and formulaic. When readers search for fiction, titles and introductions are essential in attracting readers through quick scanning and picking. More importantly, titles and introductions written by the authors can precisely capture what the author intends most to express, which is more efficient and precise in collecting the genderrelated attitudes of the authors than the complete fiction texts. That is, the authors have already presented us with the plots and highlights of their stories, which are obviously better than those acquired using other methods such as machine learning.

The topics of BL fiction reflect the author’s preferences and interests, which focus on a macroscopic level. Consequently, topic choices reveal the level of relevance to Chinese culture and social reality, as well as the aspirations projected by women authors onto the male protagonists. Therefore, we applied the LDA topic model to cluster the topics using fiction titles

4 Topics in Chinese BL Fiction
4.1 Synchronic Analysis of Topics

To explore the topics within BL fiction and the associated cultural information, we applied the LDA topic model for unsupervised clustering analysis of story titles and introductions. Since the number of topics is a significant parameter for the model, we trained the model with an even number of topics, ranging from 6 to 50. After a comprehensive evaluation of each topic’s connotation and extension, the differentiation degree between topics, and the study purpose, we selected a 10-topic model for subsequent analysis, which grouped all words under ten topics. Since words under the same topics are highly related, we summarized their features and named them.

Table 1 highlights the ten topics and words with the highest values for each topic, as analyzed by the LDA topic model. The more value a word has, the more frequently it appears and the more relevant it is to the topic. Furthermore, we eliminated words without substantive semantics, such as hehe (an onomatopoeia of laughter) and liangzhi (two). Since the introduction contains both the blurb and the synopsis, the ten topics are not entirely about plots. Among them, topic 10 contains story tags and is a functional topic through which authors mark their works and categorize them into various types to allow readers to find them easily. Considering that our aim was to study the plot of BL fiction, we will not discuss Topic 10 in detail below.

Among topics related to plots, Topic 1 and 2 both focus on sweet love. Topic 1 is a campus topic. The words “xiaoyuan” (campus) and “laoshi” (teacher) clearly indicate that the campus is the setting of the BL stories. Other words highlight that the love experienced on campus is pure and dreamy, such as “zhuma” (childhood sweetheart) and “wenrou” (tender). Similar features apply to Topic 2. It is named “fairy tale” since it has words such as “wangzi” (prince), which appear as the Westerner’s appellation, as well as “meigui” (rose) and “baise” (white) that describe love

Topic 3 is about the one and only love in Chinese myths, which further puts imagined romances in the heterosexuality-like pattern. According to Radway’s (1991) research, a successful heterosexual story should only focus on the love between two single protagonists. Similarly, Mizoguchi (2015) considered that the BL protagonists would only love each other and foils could never really intervene in their relationship, which was different from the ordinary gay couples in reality. In this case, it is hard to argue that BL authors have completely broken the heterosexual norms. Moreover, Chinese legends can add to the fatalism of the BL relationship, such as reincarnation, a Buddhist concept representing the repetition of birth, life, and death. The reincarnation words “qianshi” (previous life), “jinsheng” (present life), and “qiannian” (one thousand years) indicate that the protagonist’s soul incarnates into another person, who will fall in love with his former gay lover again, thereby achieving an eternal “love myth.” While still within a similar framework to heterosexuality, Buddhist karma adds new excitement to the love story. Also, the ability to “become a god” in Taoism, a Chinese indigenous religion, helps form a unique aesthetic rooted in Chinese religious culture.

The BL fiction involving Chinese myths predominantly contains ancient scenes, similar to Topic 4, which is based on the Chinese feudal dynasties, narrating the fight for the throne and the defense of the frontier. Words such as “jiangjun” (general), “huangdi” (emperor), and “jiangshan” (state power) highlight the struggle for the throne and the defense of the frontier, revealing a strong sense of nationalism. Compared with “god” related Topic 3, Topic 4 reveals more about Confucianism, advocating the realistic ideal of the “human” world, but not directly describing contemporary China, thus avoiding possible political innuendo. Besides the influence of China’s long history, it appears that women authors’ preference for this topic is rooted in their desire to participate in male-dominated fields, such as war and leadership. Women authors expect power beyond romance here, which embodies the close relationship between sexual pleasure and power pointed out by Foucault (1979:48). One possible explanation for why authors do not directly tell women’s participation in power is that it was proven unrealistic in patriarchal history. A queen, for example, rarely occurred in China’s actual history, so women chose to describe power in the relatively equal love between men. In this case, the existing gender division of labor remains
10 MODELING GENDER CONSCIOUSNESS: WOMEN AUTHORS’
unbroken. By projecting their power ideal onto men, women authors harvest both career and love at a minimal cost.

Topic 5 also includes the idea of love, and to some extent is a variation of the fantastic Chinese myths topic in reality. This topic portrays happiness within reach in daily life; therefore, it is named “daily happiness.” Words under this topic, such as “rensheng” (life), “shenghuo” (to live), and “xianshi” (reality) refer to reality; “xingfu” (happiness), “yongyuan” (forever), and “yisheng” (all one’s life) represent the authors’ view on happiness, which is having love and the only lover forever.

Topics 6 and 7 continue to tell stories in reality. Topic 6 includes words on dramatic love, such as “gouxue” (dramatic), “zhagong” (unfaithful seme), and “tishen” (substitute). The money disputes that involve CEOs, the messy relationships between both sexes, and the disloyalty related to unfaithful seme, all result in conflicts and thus form dramatic stories. Topic 7 is relevant to the entertainment industry. “Laoban” (boss), “mingxing” (celebrity), “dianying” (film), and “yanyuan” (actor) present romantic stories among stars, highlighting women authors’ preference for celebrity. Money, beauty, and fame entangled with sensory stimulations are the fundamental concepts in this topic, which allow authors to break through mediocre heterosexual norms and pursue an extraordinary life.

Topic 8 is about games, involving words such as “youxi” (game), “wangyou” (online game), “mowang” (dark lord), and “siwang” (death), where the protagonists must survive in killing games. Topic 9 describes a fantastical otherworld. Words such as “weilai” (future), “diqiu” (the earth), and “jiqiren” (robot) belong to science fiction; “Jingling” (elf) and “yaoguai” (monster) depict mysterious creatures. As Ni (2020) said, although the Chinese government’s censorship cleared the pornographic contents, authors shifted their interests to construct scientific discourses and achieved great commercial success. This topic reveals that Chinese BL writers have acquired a revolutionary consciousness, enabling them to engage in dialogue with the wider social world and its future. Besides, the otherworld they create is a utopia of gender since it makes where the same-sex relationships can be more reasonable and the equal love between protagonists would naturally emerge as they fought together.

5 Diachronic Analysis of Topics

After analyzing each topic, we studied the proportions of BL fiction under specific topics in the total number from 2003 to 2019, as shown in Fig. 2. As we planned to analyze how the plots changed over time, the story tag topic was excluded from this analysis.

Fairy tales, daily happiness, and fantasy topics had a downward trend. The daily happiness topic accounted for about 45% of the topics in 2003, though decreased, it still accounted for nearly 18% of all topics in 2019. Its decline was relative to the rise of other topics. Compared with daily happiness, the fairy tale topic accounted for just 11% in 2003. After a decline of over 2%, its proportion was under 9% in 2019. In addition, the fantasy topic slightly declined from approximately 12% to 8%. Since the fairy tale topic is traditionally Western, and the fantasy topic also contains certain Western elements, the decline in their popularity suggested that authors’ preference for Western settings was also declining.

In contrast, campus, Chinese myths, dramatic love, entertainment, and game topics increased. Among them, the campus topic had the largest proportion, increasing from 10% to nearly 20%. This suggests that youth love has increasingly become a favored topic for BL authors. Besides, the

Lastly, the ancient China topic had retained a proportion of over 8% between 2005 and 2019. Its share, along with the rise of the Chinese myths topic, proved the ongoing popularity of China’s native stories.

The above topic analysis formed the panorama of Chinese BL fiction. Chinese women authors prefer surreal BL stories, including reincarnation, ancient China, game, and fantasy topics. Even seemingly realistic topics, such as campus and entertainment, still involve dramatic turns and a dream-like atmosphere. Furthermore, the fantasy world in the past or future eliminates the obstacles, creating a paradise of love and freedom for gay men.

This fantasy world is almost departed from the influence of Japanese BL fiction. First, Chinese authors are free from the dependence on Western settings. Although Western elements still exist in Chinese BL stories, diachronic analysis reveals that their proportion is decreasing, while topics such as reincarnation and ancient China remain popular. Through local legends and religious thoughts, Chinese BL fiction has remained rooted in traditional Chinese culture. Besides, unlike the necessary tragedy in early Japanese BL fiction, Chinese authors also prefer relaxed stories. For instance, “wenxin” (warm and sweet) ranks high in the synchronic analysis of the story tag topic, and daily happiness even becomes one of the ten topics. Therefore, currently, Chinese authors have changed both features of Japanese BL fiction.

The above topic analysis formed the panorama of Chinese BL fiction. With the disappearance of Western elements in the most popular quarter of BL fiction, the Chinese BL world has departed from Japanese works. Unlike the necessary tragedy in early Japanese BL fiction, Chinese authors prefer relaxed stories. For instance, “wenxin” (warm and sweet) and “HE” (happy ending) both rank high in the synchronic analysis of the story tag topic. Therefore, Chinese BL novels have gained a strong cultural subjectivity.

Chinese women authors prefer surreal BL stories because the fantasy world in the past or the future eliminates obstacles, creating a paradise of love and freedom for gay men and for themselves. However, while gaining freedom in fantasy, Chinese women are bound by the “love myth.” The formation of a myth indicates the separation of Chinese women BL authors from reality. They choose to describe the fictional relationship between men as similar to heterosexuality rather than their real

heterosexual identity, which is an escape from their gender role. In addition, although conveying the desire for power, they only tend to project such ideals onto the male roles, not daring to overturn the existing patriarchy. To further examine those ideas, we will analyze women authors’ perceptions of gender in the next section.
6 Gender-Related Contexts in Chinese BL Fiction
6.1 Synchronic Analysis of Contexts

Following the analysis of Chinese BL fiction topics, we proceeded to examine contexts related to gender and same-sex relationships through word vector technology, totaling 39,619 discrete words, which reflect how related concepts are discussed. We removed words that lack semantic significance and character names, like zhende (really) and jiju (very), listing hanzi (Chinese characters), pinyin (Roman spellings of Chinese characters), and English translations.

The words directly related to gender are women and men. In Chinese, two pairs of words could represent women and men; these words are “nvren” (the common term for women) and “nanren” (the common term for men), as well as “nvxing” (the biological term or the term used in written language for women) and “nanxing” (the biological term or the term used in written language for men). We analyzed the two pairs of Chinese gender names, respectively.

Table 2 presents words related to women. In the entry of “nvren” (woman), “tongqi” (homowife) ranks first. This term represents gay men’s heterosexual wives, whose role is to reproduce and allow gay men to be accepted by Chinese society (Bie & Tang, 2016). However, their husbands deprive the marriage of love, exposing them to intimate partner violence. According to the raw data, homowives predominantly appear as shadowy presences in the story background. Instead of empathizing with their suffering, authors apply them as a tool for gay men to realize their sexual orientation (“he realized that he was gay after marrying a woman so his wife became a homowife”) or as a child-bearer (“even though he married a woman and had a child, he could not forget the man he loved most”). Authors sacrifice homowives to reduce Chinese gay men’s moral pressure, social stress, and the pressure to continue the clan.

Compared to “nvren,” words close to “nvxing” (woman) reflect the coexistence of negative and positive attitudes. According to the raw data, the relationship between “yiduan” (heresy) and women is that “not marrying a woman is a heresy,” revealing the rejection of same-sex relationships in mainstream Chinese society. In contrast, “qishi” (discrimination) was predominantly used in sentences like “do not discriminate against women,” representing kindness to women.

The woman-related contexts reveal Chinese BL authors’ strong demand for heterosexual marriage. Although they describe unconventional gay men, they still regard marriage as the most standard and accepted criterion for them, and the same-sex relationship in the story has nothing to do with their own lives. This craze for marriage is a reflection of the thousand years of patriarchy, indicating that the women authors are still spokespersons of Chinese traditional ethics and moral discourse.

Among the words close to “nanren” (man) in Table 3, some have occurred in the entry of “nvren” (women), such as “tongqi” (homowife), “daguanggun” (stay single), and “muzi” (mother and son). Along with the newly appearing term “hunsha” (wedding dress), these words prove again that marriage is the primary task even for roles in BL fiction.

The clan concept rooted within Chinese traditional culture mainly explains Chinese women authors’ intentions. Reproduction has always been essential in maintaining the prosperity of the clan, as well as a vital means of maintaining filial piety; having no descendants is the gravest offense against filial piety (Luo, 2008). Therefore, motherhood is considered a major role for women, so the clan concept is closely entangled with patriarchy, and men can never be certain of their masculinity until they become fathers (Webb and Judith, 1999). The patriarchal values of “must-have offspring” explain why Chinese BL authors are interested in marriage and reproduction issues, although gay men cannot conceive children naturally. Considering same-sex marriage and surrogacy are illegal in China, BL authors either let women become homowives to bear children, which sustains the imprisonment of women’s gender roles in the patriarchy, or empower gay men with the ability to conceive. When the clan continued, male-male love became socially acceptable in China.

Paradoxically, pregnant gay men’s stories also result in feminist awareness. These authors could have written heterosexual love stories, but only a very heterosexual-like pattern of same-sex relationship, where women do not exist, would free them from patriarchal constraints. When women endow their physiological features to men, they can reexamine the ability to get pregnant and other features (without being oppressed by the patriarchy) and escape objectification through the male identity. This can be the first step toward feminism, as Kaja Silverman (1992: 389) put it, “for a female subject to re-encounter femininity from within a male body is clearly to experience it under different terms—to live it no longer as disenfranchisement and subordination, but rather as phallic divestiture, as a way of saying ‘no’ to power.” However, although transferring women’s characteristics to men frees women, it results in their absence. Women become more dispensable after the reproductive function is no longer exclusive to them. This phenomenon reflects the passive resistance by women in a patriarchal society: avoiding discussing the root of their oppression, which is their physiological capacity to get pregnant.

Since BL fiction involves a romance between gay men, we chose the Chinese expression of same-sex relationships, “tongxinglian,” to analyze whether women authors’ descriptions of this group were linked with reality or were all fantasies (see Table 4). Table 4 includes many words related to marriage, such as “jieguohun” (have ever been married), “hunyin shenghuo” (married life), and “hunyin guanxi” (marital relations). Although same-sex marriage is illegal in China, it has always been

7 Diachronic analysis of contexts

After analyzing the overall entry for each keyword, we selected six words in Tables 2, 3, and 4 to track frequencies from 2003 to 2019. We focused on the diachronic changes in words that reflected the influence of traditional Chinese culture and society. Reflecting the dilemma of gay men’s marriage in reality and the effect of filial piety on gay men, the word “Tongqi” (homowife) connecting women and the gay community merits close inspection. Similarly, “chuye” (the night one lost virginity) and “chuanzongjiedai” (continuity of a clan) relate to fertility, reflecting the shackles of traditional ethics on women in China. As for men, “shuangxingren” (intersex) is an important finding, which transfers women’s physiological features to men. Also, “Shengyu nengli” (reproductive ability) can describe men’s ability to get pregnant. These two words both reveal the emphasis on reproduction in Chinese culture. In terms of same-sex relationships, “hefahua” (legalization) means that the identity and marriage of gay people are legally recognized, highlighting BL authors’ attention to reality.
In addition, we divided the word frequency of one term in a certain year by the total word frequency of the year to achieve a specific value, as shown in Fig. 3.

The top half of Fig. 3 reveals the frequencies of three words, namely, “tongqi” (homowife), “chuye” (the night that loses virginity), and “chuanzongjiedai” (continuity of a clan), all linked to the keyword “nvren” (woman). “Tongqi” only occurred after 2010, meaning that BL authors have increased their attention to homowives, a vulnerable group in reality. However, the word frequencies of “chuye” and “chuanzongjiedai” declined, indicating that the stereotypical ideas of women

The trend of “shuangxingren,” another word for men, was very similar to “shengyu nengli” from 2012 to 2018, implying that men’s ability to reproduce in BL stories did relate to intersex people, especially their physiological feature that allows them to fall pregnant. Furthermore, “hefahua” refers to same-sex relationships, whose curve rose after 2013. After the Taiwan judiciary proclaimed that the current civil law did not make gay marriage unconstitutional in 2017, the discussion on legalizing same-sex marriage reached its peak, representing the reality of BL fiction.

This chapter illustrates the impact of Chinese culture, which both inspires BL fiction plots and influences the gender perspectives of women authors. They are contradictory when discussing gender issues. They allow gay men to fall pregnant, hoping to shatter the traditional gender ideologies, but patriarchal ethics make them deliberately ignore women’s roles. Hence, Chinese women fail to break the shackles of the clan concept within BL fiction, and the extreme emphasis on reproduction brought by thousands of years of Chinese patriarchy still imprints on Chinese women’s cultural creation.
8 Conclusion

In the previous two decades, the number of Chinese online BL fiction pieces has increased rapidly. Through the LDA topic model and word vector technology, we drew three main conclusions on the content of BL fiction. (1) Chinese women BL authors prefer surreal topics in the history and future, as well as the dreamy “love myth,” which owns more heterosexual features than the real LGBTQ group. (2) Chinese traditional culture powerfully influences BL fiction, creating a distinct aesthetic style and strong nationalism. Besides the inspiration from Chinese history and myths, the patriarchal clan concept also makes BL authors focus on marriage and reproduction issues. (3) Chinese BL fiction reveals the paradoxical nature of women authors’ gender perspectives. They want to feel power through the male protagonists’ “equal love,” and even transfer
10 MODELING GENDER CONSCIOUSNESS: WOMEN AUTHORS’
pregnancy to the intersex group. However, they avoid discussing their own gender, which means that they are still unable to escape the shackles of patriarchy.

Chinese online BL fiction remains in a state of contradiction. The authors created male-male romances but were distant from gays in reality; they expressed women’s desire for love but lacked women characters. Eve Sedgwick (1985) pointed out that the male homosocial desire and homosexual desire both have a necessary relationship to misogyny, and we found that even within the fictional male-male romances written by women, misogyny remained. For instance, women who were closely associated with Chinese gay men, homowives, were ignored by early authors. As Toril Moi (2008: 268), who emphasized the significance of women’s writing, stated, “to turn women into second-class citizens in the realm of literature is to say that women’s experiences of existence and of the world are less important than men’s.” Though the stereotype of women in Chinese BL stories has been reduced, the awakening of Chinese women authors remains incomplete.

In addition, BL authors are also attempting to change the currently marginalized roles of women. For example, in Heaven Official’s Blessing (2018), the most popular BL fiction on JLC, a powerful goddess character subverted the traditional image of the god of wisdom. In ancient China, only men were allowed to take the imperial competitive examination; hence, the god of wisdom in Taoism has always been depicted as male. This goddess of wisdom changed the patriarchal tradition and broke through the former gender roles of Chinese women as mothers and wives. Although such women characters cannot be protagonists in BL fiction, and the discussion on women is not the story’s core, it still represents gratifying progress.

BL fiction is produced within a specific social and historical context. In today’s Chinese society, with the market expansion of BL-adapted TV drama and animated works, Chinese BL fiction is developing. However, as BL forms a larger cultural industry, various questions will arise, such as the impact of pornographic elements on children and the hindrance of patriarchal culture to feminism. After thousands of years of sexual repression, Chinese women’s desire has awakened, but the patriarchy remains an invisible net, limiting their transformative efforts. In this case, BL fiction becomes a woman’s utopia. In the world of male-male romance, women can enjoy consuming men, albeit momentarily. Women return to reality;
Y. CHEN ET AL.
they will only find that this incomplete awakening means deeper bondage since they have eliminated their own living space.

In the postmodern narrative, the boundary between fact and fiction is blurred (Brinkmann, 2009). BL fiction seems to remove women’s existence, but even the most fantastic and bizarre plot cannot escape their life experiences. By discussing Chinese women BL authors’ literary creations, this research has made two main contributions: (1) Theoretically, this chapter opens up a new perspective of Chinese traditional culture and ethics for the feminist study of BL fiction. The discovery of heterosexual relationship patterns and men’s reproduction content both make the conclusion that BL women authors are still bound by patriarchy more convincing. (2) Methodologically, machine learning methods enable a comprehensive examination of JLC, helping to understand this cultural creation without thoroughly reading all the texts. It also avoids the omission of niche works. Since writing can provide the author with valuable experience, niche works also allow us to explore the perspectives and preferences of an audience with obscure tastes. Meanwhile, this chapter has certain limitations. We could not include full BL fiction texts in the model, so we hope to explore them and compare BL fiction to other related genres in future research.

CHAPTER 11
Modeling Ideology: A Distant Reading of Marx/Engels Collected Works
1 Introduction

Scholars in the relevant field have proposed introducing quantitative methods into the study of the history of Marx’s thoughts to provide an empirical and scientific tool and a new dimension of thinking for the deepening analysis of classic texts (Zhang 2012). With the continuous digitalization and internet-based development of classic Marxist literature, a digital research path has been formed (Ji and Liu 2018). In recent years, the quantitative analysis of text, facilitated by computers and algorithms, has been integrated as a fundamental method into the research paradigms of text analysis, transforming traditional text analysis based on understanding and interpretation. With the maturity of machine learning techniques, especially natural language processing algorithms, quantitative text analysis is no longer limited to simple manual coding and word frequency counting. Various analysis techniques, such as topic analysis, semantic analysis, and network analysis, have led to breakthroughs and added value in the application of machine learning techniques. There have been some exploratory studies using the machine learning technique in sociology, political science, economics, psychology, and other areas of the social sciences (Grimmer and Stewart 2013; Klüver 2009; Pauwel s 2011; Stubbs 2005), offering useful examples for understanding the reliability, validity, and application methods of this technique.

Comparatively speaking, quantitative text analysis is more macroscopic, deductive, and objective, while qualitative methods are more interpretive, inductive, and exploratory. Marx and Engels wrote a vast number of works, but it is the grandness, richness, and complexity of their thoughts that make it difficult to acquire a micro-level and holistic understanding of their doctrines across space and time. As analyzed above, under an analysis framework dominated by segmented and interpretative methods, introducing machine learning methods into the analysis process of the works of Marx and Engels and re-reading these intellectual heritages of Marx and Engels “distantly” on the basis of full-text reading and large historical spans may bring a different perspective to the study of Marxism. Thus, this chapter is a new attempt to quantitatively analyze the texts of Marx and Engels using computational research methods.
2 Data and Methods

The Marx/Engels Collected Works (MECW), a collection of English translations of the works of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, was used in this study. It consists of 50 volumes and is compiled based on the second Russian edition of MECW published by the Institute of Marxism-Leninism of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) and the German edition of MECW published by the Institute of Marxism-Leninism of the Central Committee of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), and printed by Lawrence & Wishart from 1975 to 2004. This compilation contains more than 5000 manuscripts written by Marx and Engels during 1835–1895, including: their works on philosophy, history, politics, economics, and other areas (vol. 1–27); Marx’s The Capital and related manuscripts (vol. 28–37); and their letters (vol. 38–50). It is the most complete publication of the works of Marx/ Engels in English. The main content and covered period of each volume are shown in Table 1.

The quantitative text analysis method based on machine learning was used in this study. It is a method for analyzing unstructured text data and extracting information from these texts in a quantitative way by capturing the relationships between words. When analyzing the holistic and historical properties of Marx and Engels’ texts, the LDA topic model was employed. For the practical and communicative properties, a named entity recognition (NER) method based on the Stanford Named Entity Recognizer was used.

blocks.content: Written material generally centers on specific topics/themes, which represent the elements that frequently appear in the text, including propositions, habitually used words, or contextual meaning. Topic analysis is the process of mining, describing, comparing, and reproducing these topics. The probabilistic topic modeling with LDA was used here, which can automatically identify the hidden topic information in a large text corpus through relational analysis of word meaning (that is, the co-occurrence of words). Moreover, NER is the algorithm of locating and categorizing important and proper nouns in a text, mainly including names of people, places, organizations, and time. In this study, the realistic attention to different countries in the texts of Marx and Engels was measured through recognizing the country names in the works or articles of Marx and Engels, and the social/relation network of Marx and Engels was also constructed by recognizing the people’s names in their letters. See Chapter 3 for an introduction to the LDA topic model and NER algorithm.
3 Contents and Structure

The overall word frequency in volumes 1–50 of the MECW was first counted. To avoid situations where the same English word has different forms, all words were lemmatized. Figure 1 shows the top 100 high-frequency words after removing some meaningless function words. The larger the size of a word, the higher the frequency of its occurrence. Overall, capital (appearing 34,858 times) and value (appearing 32,625 times) are the two words that appear most frequently in the MECW, followed by production (appearing 18,384 times), work (appearing 17,785 times), and money (appearing 15,366 times). Many high-frequency words in the MECW are related to surplus value or labor,

such as commodity (appearing 14,626 times), surplus (appearing 11,177 times), profit (appearing 10,795 times), price (appearing 10,304 times), worker (appearing 10,224 times), exchange (appearing 8646 times), and wage (appearing 7633 times). High-frequency words related to Marxist politics include power (appearing 9659 times), class (appearing 8797 times), war (appearing 8083 times), government (appearing 7487 times), party (appearing 6413 times), and movement (appearing 5055 times). German (appearing 11,733 times) and French (appearing 8896 times) are also frequently mentioned in the MECW.

Table 2 displays the 10 topics identified by LDA, along with the 25 words that have the highest probability or are most representative under each topic. For each work in the MECW, every word can be categorized as a topic, and the distribution of the content of the work over each topic can then be calculated. In some cases, there may be no words under a certain topic in the work, then the proportion of this topic is 0. Or, if there are many words in an article on a certain topic, then this article can be a representative work on this topic. An article can cover multiple topics or focus on a single topic. The name of each topic is summarized and extracted by considering all the keywords presented by the topic. In general, the topics revealed by the LDA topic model include: labor and surplus value, society and history, revolution and party, military and violence, trade and economic crises, class and rights, politics and editorials, international workers’ organizations, nature and science, and “others” (which is difficult to summarize its specific meaning and thereby not analyzed in detail in this study).

Topics 2 and 9 both fall into the category of Marxist philosophy, with Topic 2 focusing more on the philosophical worldview of Marx and Engels, and Topic 9 more on the views of Marx and Engels on nature and science. Topic 2 relates to the basic views of Marx and Engels on the world and society and the laws of their development: terms such as individual, society, form, history, and development are directly related to the relationship between human and society and the historical development stage of human societies; terms such as political, property, produce, principle, religion, law, and relation refer to the elements of the socioeconomic base and superstructure, trying to reveal the general laws of social development; terms such as right, spirit, freedom, and mass correspond to the Marxist view of history on the roles of the mass and the realization of the kingdom of freedom; and terms such as criticism, object, and contradiction embody the methodological principles of the Marxist worldview. Topic 9 centers around the discussions of Marx and Engels on nature and science: terms such as motion/move, form, process, and change directly refer to Marx’s opinion that matter is in constant motion; terms such as nature/ natural, atom, heat, energy, earth, animal, light, weight, quantity, physics, chemistry, and organic reflect the attention of Marx and Engels to natural sciences including physics, chemistry, and biology and the influence of natural sciences on their view of nature; terms such as force, product line,

Topics 1 and 5 relate to Marx’s discussions on the capitalist system and the law of its development. Topic 1 mainly focuses on the theory of labor and surplus value. Its terms concern Marx’s expositions of the core concepts of the capitalist mode of production and basic economic laws, such as capital, money, circulation, commodity, market, value, price, production, exchange, surplus, value, profit, capitalist, worker, employ, wage, material, cost, rate, and productive. The terms of Topic 5 are mostly related to trade and economic crisis, such as trade, increase, price, wage, amount, market, machinery, export, and so on, and refer to excess production capacity, insufficient consumption demand, and the contradiction between expanding production and weakening purchasing power of the people caused by the capitalist mode of production; terms such as class,
Y. CHEN ET AL.

capitalist, and employ refer to the manifestations of the basic contradictions of capitalism in class relations; and terms including bank and crisis concern the economic crisis resulting from this basic c ontradiction.

Topics 3, 6, and 8 are Marx’s discussions on class, revolution, and the dictatorship of the proletariat, describing the nature, conditions, and laws of development of the struggle for the liberation of the proletariat. Topic 3 focuses on revolution and party, including both socialist and bourgeois revolutions. Revolution is the term that appears most frequently and is also the most important word in this topic. Terms such as war, party, army, movement, force, struggle, and interest show Marx’s programmatic guidance for the proletariat to form parties, launch armed and violent revolutions, and fight for their own interests; and terms such as constitution, bourgeoisie, republic, king, empire, election, and prince relate to the anti-feudal capitalist revolutions fighting for democracy. Topic 6 is about Marx’s theory of class and society. The first four most important words in this topic are class, worker, bourgeoisie, and peasant. Proletariat also appears in this topic. Terms such as land and property correspond to Marx’s relevant discussion on the standards of class division; words such as right, interest, and force reflect the class struggle. Topic 8 discusses the establishment of international workers’ unions in the works of Marx and Engels. Terms such as council/committee, international, association/ alliance/federation/league, worker, party, and communist refer to Marx’s basic view that the proletariat must unite internationally, establish international communist organizations, and use their international solidarity to fight the bourgeoisie; terms such as rule, Geneva, delegate, pamphlets, and meetings refer to the organizational principles, programmatic documents, and daily activities of the international federation of w orkers.

Topics 4 and 7 relate to the discussions of Marx and Engels on military and politics. The core vocabulary of Topic 4 is basically related to military and armed affairs, including terms such as army/troop/battalion, war/battle, force, attack, enemy, infantry, artillery, and soldiers. This topic explores the series of theoretical viewpoints developed by Marx and Engels on war, the army, violent revolution, and other issues, which were formed after reflecting on the wars of the nineteenth century and reflect the concerns of Marx and Engels regarding the realities of their time. Topic 7 mainly refers to politics. Terms such as government, treaty, ministry, police, official, cabinet, parliament, power, law, and court have obvious political and legal references; and terms such as newspaper, debate, and tribune indicate that this topic mainly relates to Marx’s political

editorials published in newspapers and periodicals that lashed out at the malpractices then.

With topics being detected, we further explored the proportion of each topic in the MECW. Since LDA can categorize each term in each document into a topic according to the optimal probability, the proportion of the terms assigned to each topic in the total words of the MECW was calculated. The results are shown in Fig. 2.

It can be seen that, in the MECW, expositions on the capitalist system and its law of development account for the largest proportion, up to 41%. The discussion on labor and surplus value accounts for 32% of the total content, and the discussion on trade and economic crisis accounts for 9%. The discussion at such great length can be directly attributed to the three economic manuscripts of Marx and the three volumes of The Capital compiled based on them. The discussions of Marx and Engels on class, revolution, and the dictatorship of the proletariat account for the second-largest proportion, approximately 23% of the total content. The discussions on class and revolution account for 9% and 10%, respectively, and the discussion on the formation of international workers’ organizations accounts for 4%. The content related to Marxist philosophy accounts for about 14% of the MECW, including the discussion on society and

history (12%) and the discussion on nature and science (2%). The discussion on military and violence accounts for 9% of the total content, and the topics of politics and editorials account for 8%.

In 1913, Vladimir Lenin outlined in his work “The Three Sources and Three Component Parts of Marxism” that Marxism could be divided into three components: Marxist philosophy, Marxist political economy, and scientific socialism. Through the quantitative analysis of the basic content of the main works of Marx and Engels, these three components do form a corresponding relationship with the topics of the classic texts of Marxism. The result of the topic analysis shows that, through textual counting, the overall exposition of the classic texts of Marx and Engels is an encyclopedia covering philosophy, politics, economics, military, law, society, etc.; the organic integration of the principles of the Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism; a multi-level theoretical system from abstract to the concrete level that includes worldview and methodology, the basic laws of human social development, and different stages of human social development; a comprehensive discussion from theoretical deduction to realistic criticism unifying theory and practice.

It is worth noting that our topic categorization of the MECW is not an artificial dismemberment of the overall writings, dividing Marx’s thoughts into different branches or sub-categories. On the contrary, we intend to view all the focal points in the MECW generally from a macro perspective and understand the most comprehensive and complete theoretical implications from the original texts of Marx and Engels. From the perspective of analysis methods, the LDA topic model uses words as the analysis unit and categorizes words into different topics; therefore, each work may have multiple topics. Meanwhile, the words under each topic are not mutually exclusive, and the same word may be assigned to different topics due to different contexts. This can avoid an either-or division of the contents, and ensures an organic and holistic analysis of the classic texts of Marx and Engels.
4 Development of Marx and Engels’ Thoughts

Marx and Engels are not only the founders of Marxism, but also its developers, while Marxism is constantly supplemented, enriched, and developed along with the changes in Marx and Engels’ thoughts. A historical investigation of the development process of Marx and Engels’ thoughts in the background of historical development, which implements
11 MODELING IDEOLOGY: A DISTANT READING OF MARX/

the unity of theory and history, and theory and practice, can facilitate our re-understanding and summarization of the lessons and laws from the emergence and transformation of Marxism under specific conditions and understanding the internal logic of the development of Marx and Engels thoughts.

Based on the above results, we further introduced the time dimension into the topic analysis. We divided and counted all the texts in the MECW year by year according to when they were written. For each year’s texts, each word was assigned to a topic by the trained LDA topic model according to the context, and then the proportion of the words in each topic in the total text content of the year was calculated. A proportional distribution of each topic in the total text of the year was finally obtained to show the diachronic changes in the writing focuses of Marx and Engels. Figure 3 illustrates the topic changes in the texts written by Marx and Engels from 1835 to 1895, presented as a percentage stacked area chart.

Most works prior to 1847 fall into the philosophical category, focusing on philosophy, worldview, nature, and science. During this period, Marx focused on criticizing and transforming classical philosophy, discovering historical materialism, and founding Marxist philosophy. Marx’s doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature (1841), Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right,

captions.content: Fig. 3 The percentage stacked area chart of diachronic changes in the writing topics of Marx and Engels

blocks.content: Y. CHEN ET AL.
Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Holy Family (1844), The German Ideology (1845–1846), and The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) were all written during this period.

In the first half of the 1850s, under the influence of the revolutions in real life, Marx and Engels mainly focused on three topics: “revolution and political parties,” “military and war,” and “politics and law,” and wrote a large number of editorial articles that pointed out the shortcomings of the times. Since the bourgeois revolutions broke out in Europe in 1848, the proportion of the treatises of Marx and Engels on revolution, military affairs, and politics has grown rapidly and reached a peak, reflecting the influence of the objective situation of revolutionary development on their thoughts. During this period, Marx and Engels not only conducted theoretical analysis and summarization of the lessons from the European revolutions in 1848, but also made real-time comments and analyses of the wars that occurred in reality. They wrote The Class Struggles in France, 1848–1850 (1849–1850), The Peasant War in Germany (1850), Revolution and Counter-Revolution in Germany (1852), The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1851–1852), Revolutionary Spain (1854), The Armies of Europe (1855), and other articles, mostly published in the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, New York Daily Tribune, and Die Presse.

In the second half of the 1850s, focusing on the two major themes, “labor and value theory” and “trade and economic crisis,” Marx and Engels accumulated their systematic theoretical works on political economy that analyzed the capitalist system and the laws of its development. Between 1857 and 1868, as capitalism underwent steady post-revolutionary development and experienced periodic economic crises, Marx shifted his writing focus to economic research. The discussion on the theory of value and basic contradictions of capitalism was the main content of his writings during this period. The three manuscripts of The Capital were written during this period.

From the 1860s to the 1870s, the writing focus of Marx and Engels shifted to discussing the dictatorship of the proletariat, aiming to enrich and develop the theory of scientific socialism. Their works during this period centered on the three themes, “class and society,” “revolution and political party,” and “international workers’ organization.” Back to the historical background of this period, the 1860s, the proletariat’s growth with the development of capitalism led to surging labor movements. There were labor strikes in the UK, France, and Germany. And
11 MODELING IDEOLOGY: A DISTANT READING OF MARX/

from a global perspective, national liberation movements against colonial rule and democratic movements against feudal rule were surging, such as the national unification movements in Germany and Italy, the uprising in Poland, the Civil War in the U.S., and the Taiping Rebellion in China. When labor movements and national movements collaborated, Marx and Engels actively participated in analyzing and guiding revolutions in various countries. In 1863, they founded the International Workingmen’s Association, endeavored to enhance the international unity of the proletariat, and published a large number of guiding opinions. In the 1870s, with the establishment and failure of the Paris Commune and the establishment of the German working-class political party, as the leaders and mentors of the international proletarian revolution, Marx and Engels, based on their experience in guiding labor movements and related reflections, wrote The Civil War in France (1871), and Criticism of the Gotha Program (1875), making scientific predictions on the development of communism and fighting against the opportunistic ideological trends such as Lassalleanism and Proudhonism in the labor movement.

In their later years, Marx and Engels returned to the study of history and natural philosophy, focusing on philosophical topics and summarizing and sublimating the thoughts of Marxism once again. It can be seen that the topics of philosophical worldview and natural sciences once again peaked in the works of Marx and Engels from 1875 to 1888. The ideas of the revolutionary mentors evolved from theory after decades of revolutionary practice. During this period, Marx conducted in-depth studies of the evolutionary laws of prehistoric society, especially the development of Indian society, and made notes on anthropology. At the same time, he extended his research on world history, especially European history, and made notes on history. Engels wrote Dialectics of Nature and Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy to systematically explain the Marxist view of nature, worldview, and methodology. The works of this period further enrich and develop Marx’s research on the relationship between humans and nature and the laws of development of human society.
From the historical development process of Marx and Engels’ thoughts, the following characteristics were summarized.

First, the writing themes of Marx and Engels are clearly related to the time period in which they compiled their works. The distribution of the topics in the works of Marx and Engels is not evenly distributed over time. Marx and Engels focused on different themes in different periods.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

In general, the early works of Marx and Engels are mainly philosophical; their works in the middle period mostly focus on the political economy of the bourgeois revolution and the nature of capitalism; and the works in the later period are devoted to the study of proletarian revolution, scientific socialism, and human history.

Second, the works of Marx and Engels contain an internal development logic that moves from practice to theory and then back to practice. After their initial discussion on historical materialism and dialectics in the early years, Marx and Engels revisited these topics following their practical experience in the real world for half a century. Meanwhile, the theory of surplus value came into being just after the failure of the European Revolution in 1848 and before the leadership of the Paris Commune, reflecting the theoretical and practical cycle of Marx and Engels from reflecting on reality to returning to reality.

Third, the themes of the works of Marx and Engels are the organic unity of concrete history. Although the works of each period have a clear topic emphasis, they are not disconnected from each other. Basically, the works of Marx and Engels in each period related to multiple themes. The historical materialism, theory of surplus value, and scientific socialism of Marx and Engels interact with each other and advance as a whole in the course of historical development.
5 Realistic Concerns of Marx and Engels

The works of Marx and Engels are not lofty theories confined to academic studies. Since their emergence, they have been deeply rooted in, serving, and developing in practice. Marx once said, “all social life is essentially practical…The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways, the point, however, is to change it.” Marxism was born under the waves of capitalist development and the workers’ revolution. It has been tested, enriched, and developed during its attention to reality, and continuously applied in the social practice of guiding the social revolutions of the proletariat to realize its historical mission. When writing their classic texts, Marx and Engels drew on the development status and practical problems of various countries, reflecting distinct practicality and realistic concerns. Therefore, it will provide us with a better understanding of the formation process of Marxism arising from practice and returning to practice by exploring the realistic attention to countries in the classic texts of Marx and Engels.

The number of mentions of different countries by Marx and Engels in the writing process can directly reflect the scope and intensity of their realistic attention. The changes in such numbers of mentions on a yearly basis can intuitively reflect the shift in the attention of Marx and Engels to real society. Therefore, we have identified all the country names in the texts of Marx and Engels through the NER method and counted their frequency of appearance. Figure 4 shows a heat map to indicate the number of mentions of the countries/regions in the world across vol. 1–37 of the MECW. Moreover, five representative countries, England, Russia, America, India, and China, were selected to count the changes in their frequency of appearance. Data of two consecutive years were smoothed to draw the percentage stacking area chart for them (Fig. 5).

It can be observed that Marx and Engels primarily focused on the realities of most countries in Europe, Asia, and North America. The focus was on Britain, France, and Germany in Europe, Russia, and India in Asia, and the U.S. Attention was also paid to several countries in Latin America, Africa, and Oceania, indicating a very wide perspective. European countries were the most important ones. England received the most attention, being mentioned a total of 4648 times, followed by France and Germany. Known from the diachronic data of England, a representative country in Europe, Marx and Engels paid great attention to this country during the country’s Chartism (1842–1848), the later period of the European Revolution (1852–1856), the writing period of economic manuscripts (1861–1865) and the arms race period in the early 1890s (1890–1892). It indicated that Marx and Engels concerned themselves with real issues such as the European bourgeois revolution, labor movement, capitalist development, social status, and imperialist invasions.

Marx and Engels demonstrated a particular interest in Russia, mentioning it 3078 times in their works. Over time, there were four distinct peaks in the degree of attention, occurring around 1854, 1866, 1875, and 1889, respectively. The first two heated discussions coincide with the Crimean War in Russia and the anti-Russian national uprising in Poland, respectively. In the 1870s, Marx even taught himself Russian to give a very detailed discussion of the forms of land ownership in Russia. At that time, Marx and Engels no longer paid attention to Russia due to current affairs, but studied Russia’s development path as a complete field, and explored the particularity of the Russian labor movement and socialist revolution. In fact, some of Marx and Engels’ works were first published and disseminated in Russia. Marx and Engels paid great attention to issues
11 MODELING IDEOLOGY: A DISTANT READING OF MARX/

such as the history of imperial colonial diplomacy in Russia, tsarist autocracy, serfdom, the village land system, and the revolutionary situation of the working class. Their ideas also had significant reverberations in Russia.

Marx and Engels paid attention to the U.S. mainly around 1862 and in the late 1880s. Around 1862, when the American Civil War broke out, Marx and Engels conducted a profound analysis of the reasons for the War, its tactical strategies, and the American slavery system situating distant America within their capitalist analysis framework. A series of reviews was written, such as The Writings on the American Civil War. The peaks of attention in the late 1880s were attracted for two reasons. The first peak corresponds to the strikes in Chicago. The labor movement in the U.S. reached its climax during this period and had a profound impact on socialist movements worldwide. Engels paid great attention to the working class in the U.S. He not only went to the U.S. in person, but also publicly set Labor Day to commemorate this movement in the U.S. at the founding meeting of the Second International. The second reason is the development of the American capitalist economy. After the Civil War, the U.S. capitalist economy experienced rapid development, marked by several trends and changes that foreshadowed its future growth, including credit accumulation, joint-stock companies, and trusts. To further improve his theory of political economy, Marx closely followed the new changes in the American economy, and even came up with the idea of revising The Capital and compiling his theory of credit using the U.S. as a model. Engels directly made new research on these phenomena, trying to provide a scientific basis for the proletariat to develop new struggle strategies.

Regarding Eastern countries, Marx and Engels mainly focused on India and China, mentioning 1152 times and 369 times, respectively. Over time, the focus on both China and India shifted in the 1850s, related to colonial aggression, the Second Opium War, and the waves of movements against Western colonialism in China and India during this period. On the one hand, Marx paid more attention to China and India out of his thinking on the historical destiny and future of the backward countries and eastern societies. On the other hand, the anti-feudal Taiping Rebellion and the Second Opium War broke out in China in 1851 and 1856. Meanwhile, India experienced a national uprising against British colonial rule in 1857. Marx and Engels analyzed the political and economic structures of the colonizers and colonies from a global and historical
Y. CHEN ET AL.
perspective, and began to explore the internal relationship between proletarian revolutions and movements, and national liberation movements in the oppressed regions.

According to our analysis of the realistic concerns of Marx and Engels, we can see that Marxism is not founded on the investigations or analysis of certain countries. Instead, Marx and Engels, with a very broad vision, investigated and analyzed countries with different geographical locations, social backgrounds, and political systems by taking into consideration the East and the West, the colonizer and colonized countries, the bourgeois revolution and national liberation movement, the labor movement and peasant uprising, the land, and economic systems and other aspects. As Marx and Engels repeatedly pointed out, their theories are not dogmas, but guides for action. Marxism is constantly being enriched and developed through the practice of various countries, and is constantly tested and realizing its own historical mission in this process. The basic principles of Marxism are not a one-sided generalization based on particularity, but a universal science sublimated on the basis of a comprehensive overview of the world. It is this practicality, which is closely integrated with the masses and the specific conditions of the times, that determines the scientific nature and vigorous vitality of Marxism.
6 Social Networks of Marx and Engels

A social network refers to a structure consisting of social relations. It reflects the social relations between actors. Marx and Engels’ thoughts are not isolated, but came into being and spread in the collision and communication with other thinkers’ thoughts. Vol. 38–50 of the MECW contains a total of 3957 personal letters of Marx and Engels. Compared to the treatises, the letters have a clear address. The correspondence reflects a person’s social network to a certain extent. So, these letters can reflect the dissemination process of debate and influence among Marx, Engels, and other contemporary thinkers. In general, the letterhead and the closing part contain specific information about the writer and the recipient. If a third person is mentioned in the body of the letter, then this person is likely to have some kind of social relationship with both the writer and the recipient; or at least be someone that the writer or the recipient knows in real life, or a public figure that both of them pay close attention to.
Therefore, if two names appear at the same time in a letter, there must be some intersection of them in life, work, or thought, which can reflect
11 MODELING IDEOLOGY: A DISTANT READING OF MARX/

the social networking and interaction of Marx and Engels. We automatically identified the person’s names in each letter using the NER method as a node in the network analysis. If two person names appear at the same time in a letter, a set of co-occurrence relationships is recorded as edges in the network. Gephi, a network analysis software, is used to draw a global social network of Marx and Engels with figures appearing more than 20 times in their letters. As shown in Fig. 6, the size of a node reflects the frequency of appearance of a person’s name in all letters; the connections between the nodes reflect the co-occurrence between the figures, and thicker lines indicate more co-occurrences between nodes and thereby closer social tiers. The obtained social network contains a total of 1079 nodes and 2973 edges. The diameter of the network is 3, the average path length is 1.968, and the average clustering coefficient is 0.859. To better present the information, we selected the persons’ names that appeared over 160 times and the edges with two names that co-appear over 120 times to draw a local detailed social network of Marx and Engels (Fig. 7).

In the social network of Marx and Engels, there were many activists of the labor movement and followers of Marxism. As revolutionary mentors, Marx and Engels guided them in establishing the workers’ parties and leading the workers’ movement. August Bebel and William

As close friends and comrades-in-arms of Marx and Engels, they jointly promoted the dissemination and development of Marxism, as well as the integration of Marxism with the specific revolutionary practices of various countries.

There were also many representatives of opportunism and revisionism in the social correspondence network of Marx and Engels: Ferdinand Lasalle and Jean Baptist von Schweitzer, the representatives of the Lassalleans; Mikhail Bakunin, a Bakuninist representative; Pierre Joseph Proudhon, a Proudhonist representative; Edward Bernstein, a revisionist representative; and some other representatives of petty bourgeoisie socialists, Gottfried Kinkel, Henry Mayers Hyndman, Giuseppe Mazzini, Julian Harney, August Willich, and Karl Blind. Most of these figures were activists in the international labor movement who had followed Marx in the early days or were close friends of Marx. However, their non-radical petty-bourgeois ideas on how to lead the working class diverged from

those of Marx and Engels. They even severed relationships with Marx and Engels.

The families, doctors, and working partners of Marx and Engels also corresponded with them actively. Marx and Engels co-occurred most frequently, up to 23,238 times, reflecting their intimate revolutionary friendship. The frequency of Marx’s co-occurrence with his eldest daughter Jenny Marx, his second daughter Laura Marx, his youngest daughter Eleanor Tussy Marx,<sup>2</sup> and his sister Louise Juta is 794 times, 686 times, 722 times, and 335 times, respectively. The social co-occurrence network also unveils that Engels’ doctor and friend, Edward Gumpert, whose name co-appeared with Engels 418 times. In his letters to Engels, Marx often asked him to consult Gumpert for advice on illness treatments (Henderson 1976). At the same time, Marx and Engels had very good relationships with Joseph Weydemeyer and Ernst Dronke, the editors of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, and Charlie Anderson Dana, the editor of the New York Daily Tribune.
7 Conclusion

This chapter undertakes a macro-level and distant reading of volumes 1 to 50 of the Marx/Engels Collected Works (MECW) quantitatively. Ten major topics were identified with their proportions determined in the works of Marx and Engels through the LDA topic model, making an objective and comprehensive statistical description of the basic content and writing focuses of the MECW from a macro perspective. Through a diachronic analysis of the changes in topic proportions, we viewed the research focus shift of Marx and Engels and the social background factors behind it in the grand spatiotemporal context, and understood and investigated Marx and Engels’ thoughts by placing them within their historical background and its own development logic. Meanwhile, we examined the concerns of Marx and Engels regarding the fate of different countries and regions, and analyzed their realistic concerns in practice. Finally, by analyzing the social network within the letters of Marx and Engels, we revealed the social network of Marx and Engels, understood them in a three-dimensional manner, and tentatively explored the dissemination process of their thoughts. This chapter is an exploratory application of
2 Tussy was the nickname given by Marx to his youngest daughter, Elena Marx.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

machine learning methods in the textual research of the works of Marx and Engels. Compared with traditional textual criticism or hermeneutic textual research, this chapter provides a new perspective. It makes contributions in ensuring a macro-level, deductive, and objective analysis of the MECW and explaining the theoretical, historical, and practical logic within the thoughts of Marx and Engels.

This chapter also has several limitations. First, it mainly relies on computers to present quantitative and objective results of textual analysis, which may not be as in-depth and active as qualitative text analysis methods in terms of interpretation. Second, our analysis, which treats the word as a unit, can divide certain fixed phrases or important collocations during counting, and this can lead to simplification or misinterpretation of some words due to polysemy and the inability to restore the context. Third, due to space and time constraints, we provide a relatively rough distant reading and overview of the MECW from a single perspective, without focusing on a specific problem or providing more detailed analysis methods and angles. Fourth, the interpretation of the results of textual analysis is data-driven, deductive, and speculative. Further theoretical and practical evidence-based tests are needed to ensure the scientific and objective nature of the interpretation.

“The weapon of criticism cannot, of course, replace criticism of the weapon, material force must be overthrown by material force, but theory also becomes a material force as soon as it has gripped the masses.” The purpose of our study is not to summarize and interpret thoughts contained in the vast texts of Marx and Engels through one study. Instead, it intends to prove that the quantitative text methods introduced into the research on classical theoretical works is an approach that is parallel to the previous research and can facilitate the capture of the macroscopic context of a theory. Moreover, new sparks may fly out during the collision between computer algorithms and texts. We call for more in-depth and valuable quantitative text analyses to be on the agenda. For example, by quantifying text thoughts as variables, we can explore the relationship or causality between them and other social indicators; or, by calculating text similarity, we can explore the transformation process of Marx and Engels’ thoughts in two periods, or its connections and differences with other thoughts; or, by further expanding the content and time span of the Marxist textual analysis data, we can explore the position of Marxism in the long historical process.

CHAPTER 12
From Barbarism to Civilization: The Evolving Image of China in International Cinema
1 Introduction

Ever since Joseph Nye (1990) popularized the concept of “soft power,” the approach to power through attraction, rather than coercion, has gained increasing acceptance among academics (Zhang and Wu 2019). As a kind of soft power, the national image could play a vital role in international politics. Jervis (1970: 3, 6) argued that a national image allows a country to exercise influence without incurring the high cost of changing its main policies, making the desired outcome more useful than a significant increase in military or economic power. A country is like a brand; its image and reputation are part of its strategic capital, which is why China considers its national image a new “battlefield” to develop its capability of international communication after decades of rapid economic development (Ding 2011).

More often than not, a country’s self-image construction fails to achieve the desired effect, for the reason that the national image is not entirely determined by the subject of the image. Hegel (1975: 7) states that an image is the sensuous existence of a particular significance, including intuition, sensibility, and symbol. According to Boulding (1959) a country’s national image is built on a combination of the country’s self-cognition and other bodies’ cognition of it within the international system. The image may even be distorted in other countries’ depictions, especially through cultural and artistic works.
