For China, the most significant economic and political strategic issues in the country, such as the trade war with the U.S. and the Taiwan issue, all have a shared connection to the national image, so the perception of other nations and its underlying reality will influence the future of China’s development and reform (Ramo 2007: 12). In this case, exploring the formation and change of China’s national image becomes a top priority. Mainly, three directions lie in its research field. The first is the study of China’s long-term national image changes, which helps to understand the historical facts behind the interactions between China and other countries (Xie and Page 2013; Zhu 2019). The second is the study of the Chinese government’s construction of its national image, where most studies are based on specific events, such as the Beijing Olympic Games and the China-EU Cultural Festival (Brownell 2013; Maags 2014). The third category takes the perspective of other countries, examining the image of China in a variety of foreign and domestic media, like films and newspapers (Greene 2014; Birama and Röschenthaler 2017; Zhu and Ji 2018). The integration of these three directions points to China’s position in world affairs.

Descriptive analysis of images helps to understand trends, policies, causes, and effects, making it the basis of all research. However, among all kinds of studies, few studies measure the change of image itself accurately, either due to the lack of data or the fact that no uniform and convincing results could be drawn. Most existing studies focus on individual and single-country surveys, which often lack a sufficient time span, geographical scope, and sample size (Page, Rabinovich, and Tully, 2008). To make up for these deficiencies, we began by choosing film as the medium to carry the image of China, for the reason that film can communicate more directly between the subject and the audience, better conveying the connotation contained in the image (Monaco and Lindroth 2000). Second, we obtained a huge sample size of 4,927 Chinarelated films via the world’s most popular and authoritative film source, the Internet Movie Database (IMDb), while machine learning methods process text analysis objectively and comprehensively. Lastly, to draw strong conclusions, Granger causality test was used to determine the potential relationship between the emotional changes of China’s image and the macro-level socioeconomic factors. The above methods analyzed the image of China over the century and around the world from three aspects: content, sentiment, and determinants. The methods used fill the
12 FROM BARBARISM TO CIVILIZATION: THE EVOLVING
gaps of both quantitative and qualitative literature and lay a foundation for future mechanism analysis.

“Representations of films are interpretations (Malcolm 2004: 101),” The purpose of this article is to extract the representations through big data and machine learning methods and show the image of China as an interpretation. This “image” carries with it the filmmakers’ real-time views of China, so to present it is to interpret its historical and political implications. On this basis, we can know the effect of various factors on the formation of this image, including comprehensive national strength and international relations. Its change is due to the accumulation of various historical factors, so the time of over a century is of great significance. One could glimpse the trend of China’s soft power in the world and look to the future from the past.
2 Films and Image of China

Film was invented at the same time that China was forced to open to the outside world in the late nineteenth century. At that time, China had become a semi-colony and undergone exploitative practices related to colonialism. Coinciding with the rise of the film industry, the cinematic image of China seen across the globe, therefore, became closely related to the development of modern China and its diplomatic relations with other countries.

A significant amount of literature discusses China in global films. For example, Gina Marchetti and other scholars examine the depiction of China to judge China’s status in global film culture and the connection between such cultural exchange and politics (Marchetti and Lu 2018). Since Hollywood nearly dominates global cinema markets, most literature studies the relationship between Hollywood and China. Literature on early films focuses on Hollywood’s stereotypes of the “Orient,” while articles on contemporary films explore how the rise, transition, and social context of China have affected the Hollywood film industry (Chung 2006; Gries et al. 2015; S u 2016). Their limitations are similar to those of the national image literature: the time range of these studies is limited, and they primarily conduct theoretical rather than empirical research.

Representations of China in Hollywood films have undergone several changes. For instance, films about China in the early twentieth century such as Daughter of the Dragons (1931) featured tenebrous and uncanny scenes, coupled with evil characters like Fu Manchu, and portrayed the
Y. CHEN ET AL.

“Yellow Peril” and China’s barbarism. During World War II, films like The Good Earth (1937) showed China’s uncivilized status and garnered the sympathy of Western audiences (Meyer 2006). The 1960s witnessed the emergence of films with anti-Communist topics, and the 1970s saw the popularity of Kung Fu films starring Bruce Lee. By the twenty-first century, works such as Kung Fu Panda (2008) and Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps (2010), began to highlight China’s cultural and economic power.

Postcolonialism and postmodernism are often used by scholars to interpret the image of China in world cinema (Marchetti and Lu 2018). Especially early films, produced in the West and later introduced to the East, bore colonialism’s imprint. Gramsci (1992: 233–238) wrote of colonialism as the unapparent hegemony of one form of culture over another. Edward Said developed the above arguments for Orientalism (1978) and stated that the remote and strange Oriental World in Western artworks is artificially created to manifest the West’s cultural superiority (Mamdani 2005; Sai d 1995). Moreover, Orientalism is an agent of “discourse” as defined by Michel Foucault, as it is highly social and “a political actuality of great and significant moment” (Said 1995: 247). This kind of cultural expression affects the East, even interfering with the way the East sees itself.

Chinese cinema is experiencing a kind of “re-Orientalism,” which is evidenced in films like Hero (2002), which is remarkably close to the Hollywood aesthetic. Like many other Eastern artists, some Chinese filmmakers depict Chinese culture from Western perspectives, thereby submitting to Western cultural hegemony (Mendes and Lau 2015). Additionally, the editors of IMDb, the database used in this chapter for the quantitative research, have their preferences. Due to Western identity and ideology, they prefer films with Western perspectives. For these reasons and because the number of Chinese films within the sample size is relatively small (accounting for 15.4% of the 4,428 films examined), we can largely regard these representations of China as formulated according to an outsider’s perspective, especially the West’s.

It is worth noting that films inevitably use rhetorical devices to exaggerate reality. The international media system is shaped by idealism, so the art and culture it conveys always has an ideological shadow, which explains stereotypes of China that remain in Hollywood films (Said 1993: 309). With the help of big data research, we hope to suggest that film has become an integral player in the cultural interactions between countries

and continues to shape China’s national image in ways that are constantly evolving.
3 Data and Methods

A country’s national image is an abstract cultural idea based on a group of general and ambiguous cognitive concepts spread through a social cognitive structure. Traditional methodologies, based on sampling and questionnaires, have difficulty accurately measuring such an amorphous concept. Recently, with the increased digitization of data, especially regarding the maturation of machine learning and its applications, as well as natural language processing technologies, text analysis has become a breakthrough for measuring cultural ideas.

In this study, we used the text data from IMDb’s plot synopses of China-related films as the source for analysis. Founded in 1990, IMDb is an online film database that maintains a record of film plots, casts, lengths, production regions, release regions, and reviews. As of June 2020, IMDb had collected 6,534,894 works, involving 552,366 films, making it a high-quality source of data for academic research.1 Currently, this database is being applied by scholars in literature, communication studies, sociology, and other related fields. Inquiries into this data have yielded an assessment of the relationship between film popularity and geopolitics, a comparative analysis of writing styles and metadata characteristics through film reviews, and an examination of the features of the most influential films in film history (Dodds 2006; Otterbacher 2013; Canet 2016). These studies have inspired further research projects, which can capitalize on this data to explore sociocultural issues.

There are other well-known film databases, such as Rotten Tomatoes, but its main feature is to review and evaluate films, rather than an archive or a search engine.<sup>2</sup> When it comes to older movies (especially before the 1950s), Rotten Tomatoes may not provide this study with accurate information about the movies, including film plots and regions of production and release. Hence, we chose IMDb as the primary data source.

To research how China is represented in these films, we set retrieval conditions, selecting films before 2020 with “China” and “Chinese” as keywords. Thus, the content of works retrieved under this condition is about the country China or the elements related to China. After removing duplicated data and missing values, a total of 4,428 China-related films from around the world are obtained, including 682 films made in China. According to the agenda-setting theory, Western perspectives might bias editors against China, affecting their choice of China-related films. In this case, audiences may be influenced to accept what the image of China “should” be rather than what it “actually” is McCombs (2005). This study wants to explore the “should” images produced in this mechanism.

We used web crawler technology to grab film titles and plots from IMDb. Such information directly reflects the basic plot-setting of each work, which has informed the content analysis of this study to gauge how China has been portrayed in global films. We also obtained information regarding the film’s regions of production and release dates to further explore how these factors have impacted the international perception of China. Accurately measuring how China has been portrayed in these films depends on whether the plot descriptions of China can be effectively mined. Since film titles and plots are classified as unstructured text data, we mainly applied the text mining method based on machine learning in this study. To intuitively measure the main situation-setting of “China” and “Chinese people” in films from around the globe, we adopted word embedding technology to predict the contextual information of “Chinese” and “China.” Then, we adopted the LDA topic model to explore how cinematic portrayals of China vary around the world, as the interpretation of images differs across different cultures. Finally, we applied sentiment analysis to calculate the general tone of relevant films in various global regions and measure audiences’ overall attitude toward China. See Chapter 3 for an introduction to the relevant models mentioned above.
Contexts in Films Related to China

We first analyzed the trend of China-related films over time and found that China-related elements were incorporated into films beginning in the 1890s in Fig. 1. A small peak appeared around 1912 when the Republic of China (ROC) was founded, suggesting that the increase in films might be closely related to immense political events. In the early years of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the number of films involving China
12 FROM BARBARISM TO CIVILIZATION: THE EVOLVING

remained low, a likely product of the PRC’s diplomatic isolation and onesided foreign policy during this period. It was not until 1971 that the PRC returned to the United Nations and began to establish diplomatic relations with Japan (1972), the U.S. (1979), and European countries respectively. These events are probable causes of an increase in the number of films made about China in the 1970s. After the nation’s leader Deng Xiaoping renewed the Open-Door Policy in 1978, the PRC began to welcome foreign involvement and investment in the country, deciding to go global. In 2001, the PRC joined the World Trade Organization, embracing the world on a broader scale. Since then, the PRC has played an increasingly important role in the international arena, and the number of China-related films has also shown exponential growth.

It is worth noting that the number of China-related films is also closely tied to the political histories of Hong Kong and Taiwan before 1997. These regions were more open to the world than the PRC at the time and thus served as important windows into China. As two of the “Four Asian Dragons” alongside South Korea and Singapore, Hong Kong and Taiwan experienced rapid economic growth and the commercialization of their film industries, which partly explains the increase in China-related films produced between the 1970s and the 1990s. Taken together, the international community’s impressions of these regions and

5 Topics of China-Related Films

To better delineate China’s national image, we applied the LDA topic model to cluster all the plot summary texts. They also analyze the trend of variation in film topics over time. Since the number of topics is a crucial parameter, topic coherence, an indicator that measures the internal coherence of the topics in the model, is selected as a reference. The higher its value, the higher the polymerization degree of topics in the model. We chose a range of 5 to 50 topics and trained topic models every five steps for evaluation. Figure 2 shows the results. We finally used 10 topics to train the model.

Table 4 presents the 10 topics and the top 20 keywords that appear most frequently in relation to them. When naming the topics, we referred to the major keywords related to the topics. The top 10 topics are: daily life (23%), kinship and friendship (17%), crime (16.6%), culture (10.6%), suspense (8.7%), love (7.4%), war (6.6%), art (3.8%), business (3.7%), and food (2.6%).

Topics of daily life, kinship, and friendship account for the largest proportion of the data set, reaching 40%. Like the first two categories, love, though relatively small (7.4%), also relates to fundamental matters of human life. The most relevant words connected to the topic of

On the other hand, it shows Westerners’ great interest in the feudal royal power system of ancient China.

Finally, topics of business and food account for relatively small proportions of the sample set, about 3.7% and 2.6%. The business topic is associated with terms such as “CEO,” “agreement,” “producer,” and “lawsuit,” which refer to business practitioners and practices. The related keywords for food include “food,” “chef,” “restaurant,” and “Chinatown,” revealing the global influence of Chinese cuisine.
The results of the above topic clusters are static, meaning they do not account for how these data may have fluctuated over time. To explore

topics concerning China from a more dynamic perspective, we further studied how these topics have changed proportionally since the invention of cinema. We defined the annual value of each topic as the average proportion of all the text data they retrieve from the plot synopses of films released in that year. We also incorporated values of the next three years for data smoothing and added the trend line, as shown in Fig. 3.

The topics of crime, war, and suspense represent the dark side of China’s image to some extent. The top part of Fig. 3 shows that the proportions of all three topics have presented downward trends since the 1970s. This period coincides with the course of China’s economic reform, which began with the renewal of the Open-Door Policy in 1978, together with the “peaceful development” policy in 2003. China has developed a prosperous domestic economy, improved social governance, and increased foreign exchanges. According to the Law Yearbook of China, since 1978, the crime rate in China has actually shown a rising trend. Therefore, world cinema has reduced the number of crime-related films, probably due to China’s new image formed through foreign exchange and economic development.
The bottom part of Fig. 3 shows the trend fluctuations of four topics: daily life, kinship and friendship, love, and culture. By focusing

The frequency of these four topics appearing in China-related films has increased during the past 50 years, which stands in sharp contrast to the downward trends seen in the top part of the figure. In addition, the topics of art, business, and food fluctuated significantly in the early years, but their trend has been relatively stable recently. These results suggest that the image of China depicted by foreign films has changed from the violent and conspiratorial one to the tender and cultured one.

Many topics appear in China-related films, ranging from daily life, suspense, to history and culture. Despite the variety of topics, the audience has a preference for specific topics in different periods, such as crime films in the early twentieth century and love films in the twentyfirst century. When combined with the historical background, it can be inferred that a country’s image, if relatively negative in the world, will become a stage for suspense films. When its economy prospers and society becomes stable, stories about daily life will occur naturally.
6 Sentiment Analysis of China-Related Films

By conducting a sentiment analysis of these data sets, we were able to more directly investigate the evolving portrayals of China in international films. After calculating the average sentiment score of China-related films per year, we were able to chart how this score has changed since the inception of cinema, as shown in Fig. 4.
We applied political and diplomatic factors to analyze the fluctuation of sentiment scores in recent years.

First, the sentiment score before 1900 had an abnormal peak, which was due to the limited number of films. From 1900 to 1949 (the year of the founding of the PRC), China experienced chaotic internal affairs resulting in a fluctuating emotional tone. The valley from 1919 to 1926 was a typical example. When the government of the Republic of China was not long established, warlords constantly fought with each other and the masses lived on the edge of starvation. Hence, China was often depicted in Western films as a suffering and powerless nation. In contrast, the sentiment peaks of 1928–1930 and 1945–1948 were related to the end of tangled warfare among warlords and China’s victory in the Resistance Against Japanese Aggression.

blocks.content: However, the film is inevitably influenced by the subjectivities of the filmmakers, which can create disparities between cinema and the world it represents. This divide was especially stark during the early 1900s. In films like Broken Blossoms (1919), the Chinese were depicted as sickly and indecisive. Though its cause was related to China’s waning national power in that period, prejudices against Chinese people were more likely due to the Western anti-Chinese feeling, which could be traced back to the Boxer Uprising and the U.S. implementation of the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882.

Another typical case occurred during the Resistance Against Japanese Aggression from 1937 to 1945, when the sentiment score of international films was still on the rise in the face of constant domestic wars and poverty. This was because the outbreak of World War II caused the international community to become sympathetic toward China. The image of poor and hard-working peasants in The Good Earth (1937), for example, inspired the missionary spirit of salvation. Some scholars believe that the goodwill garnered by The Good Earth even won a more favorable Far Eastern policy for China from the U.S. government during World War II,
Y. CHEN ET AL.
showing interdependence between international media and global politics (Flynn and O’Neill 1993: 57).

After the founding of the PRC, stereotypes gradually became more complex ideological factors and continue to lead to emotional fluctuations. In the 1960s, the U.S. “Red Scare” against the Communist Party spread all over the world, making the PRC’s image appear evil, which is also revealed in Fig. 4 (The Vatican 1965: 16). In the 1970s, the friendly interactions between the PRC and the rest of the world, such as the PRC representing China at the United Nations and the establishment of diplomatic relations between the PRC and Western countries, boosted the sentiment score of China-related films, which peaked in 1978.

Then, the Tiananmen Square incident in 1989 impacted the international views of the PRC. The valley in the 1990s was probably related to the incident, as well as the frequent diplomatic friction between the U.S. and the PRC, such as the U.S. linking the PRC’s human rights performance to the most-favored-nation treatment in 1993 and bombing the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade in 1999. Due to these political factors, China’s positive image of a rapidly growing economy and a prosperous society was not fully reflected in world cinema. It wasn’t until 2001, when China acceded to the World Trade Organization, that the sentiment score soared again.

After 2010, the sentiment score declines again, which might be related to the positioning of China by the international community, especially the U.S. Since China overtook Japan to become the world’s second-largest economy in 2010 and the Obama Administration began the “Pivot to Asia” strategy in 2012, the post-9/11 honeymoon between the two countries against terrorism was over. The U.S. tended to respond to China’s growing national power with both engagement and deterrence (Harris and Trubowitz 2021). It suggests that ideologically driven action plays a crucial role in shaping the national image.

Considering the varying perceptions of China may differ across different political systems, relations with China, geographical locations, and cultural traditions in different countries, we further analyzed Chinarelated films in the U.S., Russia, and Japan. Figures 5, 6, an d 7 reflect trends in the number of films made and the sentiment score over time in these three countries. The U.S. has 2,165 films, accounting for 48.9 percent of the data set, while Russia has 23, and Japan has 125.
The three figures show that the U.S. started producing China-related films first and produces them most frequently, while far fewer films about

The sentiment scores of China-related films in the U.S. and Russia are generally the opposite. Around 1996, the sentiment score of U.S. films reached a low point and then continued to rise, showing a V-shaped trend. On the contrary, the Russian films’ score peaked in 2000, then continued to decline, reflecting an A-shaped trend. The trends were tethered to the relationship between the U.S. and Russia. Japan’s attitude toward China is closely related to Japan’s historical origins and the wars between the two countries. After World War II, from the 1950s to the early 1960s, Japanese films maintained a relatively positive emotional view of China. After that, the sentiment score dropped sharply and did not recover until the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1972. During this period, Japan feared the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance, the PRC’s military strength, and the Communist Party’s military threats (He 2009). We further quantitatively examined the economic factors that could potentially influence the tone of films since 1950, as the data of economic variables in the first half of the twentieth century are not available. Based on previous literature (Xie and Page 2013), combined with existing data resources, this chapter proposes the following hypothesis:
Hypothesis 1: After 1950, China’s domestic and international economic conditions have positive impacts on the emotional tone of the image in the films.
Y. CHEN ET AL.

We applied China’s gross domestic product (GDP) to represent China’s economic power, and import and export value (IEV), foreign direct investment (FDI), and inbound tourism (IT) to represent international economic communications. All of these variables are collected from the China Statistical Yearbooks. We took the logarithms of GDP, IEV, and FDI, and calculated the three-year moving average of sentiment scores. Due to the difficulty in obtaining early data, the available years for each indicator vary. Starting from the earliest year of each indicator, we conducted a Granger causality test to verify if using the history of these time series could help to predict the emotional tone of China-related films.<sup>3</sup> The results are shown in Table 5.

Model 1 and Model 2 reveal the relationship between fd\_lnGDP and fd\_SS from 1954 to 2019. Model 1 is significant at a confidence level of 99%, so fd\_lnGDP is considered to be the Granger cause of fd\_SS. Model 2 is not statistically significant, so the null hypothesis cannot be rejected. The results indicate that China’s economic growth is conducive to a positive portrayal of China in international cinema; however, there is not enough evidence to prove that the rise in sentiment score explains the economic growth. Therefore, there is a one-way association between China’s economic power and the emotional tone of films.

According to Models 5 and 6, there is also a one-way connection between fd\_lnFDI and fd\_SS from 1986 to 2019, indicating that a significant increase in foreign direct investment can lead to a rise in the sentiment score at 95% confidence level, but the reverse relationship does not exist. Moreover, Model 3, Model 4, Model 7, and Model 8 show that there is no existence of Granger causality between fd\_lnIEV and fd\_SS, and also fd\_IT and fd\_SS. The emotional tone of China-related films is not significantly related to import and export value and inbound tourism.

So far, Hypothesis 1 has been partially verified. China’s domestic economic strength positively influences the emotional tone of its image in the film. In terms of the international economic environment, only foreign investment has a positive impact on the tone. The possible reason is that foreign direct investment acts as a weather vane. 7 Conclusion

By processing word vector technology, LDA topic model, and sentiment analysis, this research has obtained the following conclusions. In general, China’s image in world cinema is influenced by its overall national strength, including economic power and diplomatic ability. Meanwhile, Hollywood has been the foremost producer of China-related films and
Y. CHEN ET AL.

holds a vital role in setting cinematic narratives, topics, and perspectives. Therefore, the relationship between China and the U.S., who owns Hollywood, is particularly critical in all foreign relations. The opinions expressed in Chinese films about China differ according to the historical context within which they were made. Representations will vary depending on major sociopolitical events that bear a global impact.
The image of China in international films can be divided into five stages.

First, before World War II, few films were produced about China. Influenced by China’s waning national power and the deep-rooted Orientalism, the Chinese were often imagined as sickly and barbaric in films during this time.

Second, during World War II, topics of war and love were on the rise. Filmmakers began to show the suffering of Easterners and the selflessness of Westerners. The attitudes toward the Chinese in these films turned to sympathy.

Third, due to the change of regimes, the image of China in international films fluctuated greatly between 1945 and 1975. Fears of the Communist Party and the Sino-Soviet alliance caused stereotypes to resurface, and the PRC was portrayed as a scheming entity that sought to rule the world.

Fourth, after 1975, with the thawing of relations between the PRC and other countries, a cinematic focus on daily life, kinship and friendship, and love in China increased. Since the PRC renewed the Open-Door Policy and the economic take-off of Hong Kong and Taiwan, the international community has turned the spotlight on the common Chinese people’s lives.

Fifth, since the beginning of the twenty-first century, films related to China have witnessed sharp growth. This is not only because China’s increasingly prominent position has attracted international films’ attention, but also because China’s cultural strength has improved. More films made in China have been exported abroad. In terms of subject matter, most films are related to Chinese culture, daily life, and love, resulting in a high sentiment score. This shift reveals that nowadays, the proportion of China’s image influenced by politics is decreasing, and international films present a more approachable, open, inclusive, and positive image of China.
From the barbarian to the schemer to the civilized great power, China’s image in international films conforms to these representational trends to
12 FROM BARBARISM TO CIVILIZATION: THE EVOLVING

an extent. However, it does not entirely accord with reality. As an art product, film does not simply convey reality. It can also distort it. Thus, in the development of China’s image, it is evident that China’s national strength and its relationship with the outside world significantly shape certain aspects of the image, while the filmmakers’ ideology determines the remainder. This image is not the product of such a simple binary distinction but a complex and multi-layered system of influential factors, including national strength, interests, status, and diplomacy.

Besides drawing descriptive conclusions, quantitative analysis can also verify the propositions of cultural theory. Orientalist misapprehensions were especially evident before 1975, when the seemingly bizarre Oriental world portrayed in the film was exploited as the “other” that could best reveal the uniqueness of the West, and the sentiment score showed a relatively negative trend throughout this era. However, with the rise of the Chinese economy since 1978, Orientalism is declining but still hides in several recent films, like Disney’s live-action film Mulan (2020). Its core concept of “being loyal, brave, and true” is separately picked out from Confucian classics and pieced together, while the Chinese seldom put these three words together. It is more like a constructed spirit by the West than the true belief of the Chinese. Such works will collide with nationalist films exported from China. Although the outcome is unknown, it is sure that Western filmmakers will not ignore Chinese audiences’ views since China has grown to be the world’s second-largest film market.<sup>4</sup>

According to Said, “culture is a sort of theater, where various political and ideological causes engage one another” (Said 1993: xvi). As a form of soft power, the cinematic image is produced when ideology interacts with social reality and holds great significance for a nation’s self-identity. Due to the complexity of factors, it is difficult for us to analyze the mode and degree of this interaction comprehensively. This article mainly examines the impact of China’s GDP and foreign direct investment on the tone of China’s image, supplemented by the analysis of other factors. We hope to explore the formation mechanism of the national image in future research and provide data support and inspiration for scholars in sociology, international relations, communication studies, and other areas of the social sciences.

CHAPTER 13
A United Tale of Three Regions: A Century of China on Screen
1 Introduction

Films represent both the film industry and pieces of visual art. The film industry has thrived in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR, and Taiwan, Province of China since it was first introduced to China at the end of the nineteenth century (Lu 1997). The films from the above three regions have developed in different directions and, while they are mainly independent, each region exerts some influence on the others (Tan 2020). The differences and changes in the sociopolitical environments of the three regions have created complex contexts for the films they have produced. The history of film in China began with the Shanghai film industry, which experienced significant growth before 1949. After the founding of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in 1949, the Communist Party of China ruled Chinese mainland and the Nationalist Party of China occupied Taiwan, while until 1997 Hong Kong was a British colony, which explained the reason that the three regions and their films took very different paths. However, with the reforms and the opening up of Chinese mainland, collaboration between the three regions has increased since the 1990s. A golden age for the Chinese film industry is emerging.

The diverse histories and cultures of the three regions have given rise to distinct film styles. However, their films share the same cultural roots and show robust national features. Some scholars have argued that the Chinese have used the Western concept of the nation-state to participate in the international order and to resist the West (Berry and Farquhar

2006: 2). Therefore, an analysis of China’s image as evinced in the films from the three regions may elucidate the process of China’s cultural connection with the Western world.

A national image is shaped by both objective and subjective factors. According to Kenneth Boulding (1959), a country’s national image represents the amalgamation of its understanding of itself as well as outsiders’ view of the nation. Thus, the subjective impression is pivotal to the interpretation of a national image. The cognitive subject belongs to a specific society, and individual impressions must bear the brand of the local culture, as is particularly evident in Hong Kong and Taiwan. As former colonies, Hong Kong and Taiwan were influenced by the states that dominated them. A separation between “self” and “the other” was thus bound to appear in their standpoints vis-à-vis China.

Films can integrate national images into specific plots and pictures, thus denoting one of the most vivid ways to express such cognitive representations. The audience effects model of agenda-setting theory states that media such as films influence audience perceptions; in turn, audience feedback modifies the focus of these media (Erbring et al. 1980; McCombs 2005). In reality, in the era of the Internet, editors of leading Western websites place selected films about/from China on their online platforms, and this selection governs Western audiences’ initial view of China. The cinematic portrayals of China subsequently enable a second construction, the outsiders’ view of China. The two processes reflect the media’s influence on audience consciousness. Understanding the choice of film topics and the expression of ideas facilitates the study of the process through which the Western mind forms its impression of China.

This chapter conducted a comprehensive analysis of China’s image in the Western world using big data. In doing so, it covered a century of films produced in the three regions mentioned, thus signifying a novel deconstruction of China’s film history; it also represents a pioneering use of context analysis methodology. Traditional film studies have focused on case analysis (e.g., Lu 1997; L i 2016; Ye h 2018), but the conclusions deduced from specific instances cannot guarantee objectivity, generalizability, and comprehensiveness. In this study, the above issues were resolved using the Word2Vec toolkit, LDA topic model, and Google’s sentiment analysis model to study the synopses of pre-2019 film plots on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). A spatiotemporal analysis framework was constructed to explore changes in the conception of China in

the content, topics, and sentiments of films from Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan.
Background

When describing Chinese films in the past, scholars usually constructed a linear historical narrative to explore a unified and coherent national boundary (Yoshimoto 1991). However, the grand conceptual construct of China actually comprises varied content types such as multiple spoken languages, former colonies, and religious affiliations (Berry and Farquhar 2006). The emergent notion of the Chinese-language film thus transcends the singular nation-state narrative, encompassing all types of local or global cinematic renditions related to the Chinese language (Sun 2016). However, some scholars have argued that viewing Chinese films through the lens of a Western cultural system could cause their “de-China-lization” (Li 2016), which means abandoning Chinese cultural connotation to cater to Western understanding. Chinese films face the challenge of balancing globalization and nationality as they attempt to establish a new subjectivity.

The confrontation between globalization and nationality is particularly evident in Chinese mainland. Since the founding of the PRC, filmmakers have made great efforts to resist foreign cultural invasion. Films have thus become a crucial political component of nationalism (Lu 1997) and a powerful instrument in promoting socialist ideology. Following the launch of reform and opening-up in the late 1970s, a new generation of directors, including Zhang Yimou, described a charming and barbaric East in films such as Raise the Red Lantern (1991). Although narratives that showed the eeriness of the East achieved massive success in the West, postcolonialists were highly critical of these renditions (Li and Wang 2009). The situation changed again as China entered the twenty-first century: the economy and the film industry in Chinese mainland soared together. Some films, such as The Wandering Earth (2019), combined a Hollywood narrative style and national confidence with mature film technology, expressing the ambition to dominate the international order and successfully constructing a China-centric subjectivity.

A former British colony, Hong Kong’s early films followed British practices of live entertainment and included vaudevilles and cabarets (Yeh 2018: 6). The Hong Kong film industry was the first of the three regions to commercialize, producing many comedies and kung fu films in the
Y. CHEN ET AL.

1970s, when films starring Bruce Lee became immensely popular worldwide. For instance, movies such as Way of the Dragon (1972) were set in a foreign country and represented “ethnic Chinese.” They showcased a powerful national character by portraying the development of Chinese kung fu, and attained global fame as they defended Chinese identity. As an urban center representing ideological confrontations, Hong Kong has always avoided politics and prioritized entertainment, which helped the tide of consumerism sweep through its film industry. Nevertheless, consumerism could not dispel the identity-related dilemma of the colonized, and numerous films continued to discuss this issue after Hong Kong’s return to the PRC. For example, Port of Call (2015) described the integration of Chinese mainland residents into Hong Kong society, showing that this region still sought its identity through the story of “the other.”

The portrayal of China is more complicated in Taiwanese films than in films originating from Chinese mainland. As a former Japanese colony, Taiwan belongs to the Chinese mainland-Taiwan-Japan cultural triangle, and its colonial history and postcolonial context have caused an identity crisis (Li and Wang 2009). Homi Bhabha’s (1994) postcolonial theory posits that the colonist’s culture creates a continued pain in the colony, forming a hybrid culture. Taiwanese filmmakers have validated their identity through just such a cross-cultural construct. Directors such as Hsiao-Hsien Hou and Edward Yang contemplated Taiwan’s turbulent history in the 1980s, exhibiting an intense nativeness and discovering a narrative path between Chinese and Western cultures. However, in establishing its nativeness, Taiwan emotionally and culturally distanced itself from the mainland. Films like Cape No.7 (2008) manifested this de-China-lization and even evoked nostalgia for Japanese culture, revealing the lingering presence of the ghosts of the Japanese colonial period.

Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan share their origins but have taken different paths. Their cultural expressions of China have thus diverged under the joint influence of various factors, including the economy and politics: Chinese mainland has embarked on the socialist path, Hong Kong has an affinity with Great Britain and the U.S., and Taiwan leans toward Japan. Faced with the West, however, all three regions have been forced to demonstrate their distinctiveness as “the other.” According to Bhabha (1990: 294; 1994: 34), the problematic boundaries of modernity are sketched out in these ambivalent temporalities of the nation-space. This ambivalence has evoked an irreversible
13 A UNITED TALE OF THREE REGIONS: A CENTURY

inclination to construct cultural differences that can revise the history of critical theory. Therefore, the trend toward globalization drives the need to grasp the cultural distinctions within a nation. After a long cultural collision with the suzerain state, the former colony generates new power through mimicry and finally achieves cultural hybridity.

As a vital aspect of postcolonialism, numerous ideological and social forces have informed the impression of China expressed in the films of the past 70 years. It is challenging for theoretical studies to accurately compare the discrete features of the films from the three regions and to understand their changes over time. Therefore, using big data analysis and machine learning methods, we explored the transformations observed in the image of China in the films produced in Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan over the last century from a postcolonial theoretical perspective.
3 Data and Methods

Traditional methods using questionnaire surveys cannot accurately measure a country’s image, which is diffused through an entire society and entails both subjectivity and universality. However, based on massive content, the current capabilities of unsupervised machine learning open the door to new methodologies. Natural language processing technologies enable the analysis of an extensive range of content and provide a more accurate measure of cultural concepts for social science disciplines.

As the data source, we selected the plot synopses of China-related films from Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan collected via IMDb. Founded in 1990, IMDb is a high-quality international online database of films, providing information including film plots, casts, regions of production and release, ratings, and reviews. As of June 2020, the IMDb collection consisted of 552,366 films. The database has been widely used in scholarly research. For example, researchers have applied statistical models to classify the sentiments expressed in film reviews (Tripathy et al. 2016) and to predict the popularity of future films (Abidi et al. 2020). Film reviews have also been used to study the attitudes of audiences toward elite values (Ridderstrøm 2018) or to explore the politicized role of humor (Ridanpää 2014). New quantitative and qualitative research breakthroughs have been reported using large datasets such as IMDb.
This study used the terms “China” and “Chinese” as keywords to screen pre-2019 film data from the three regions, aiming to determine the
Y. CHEN ET AL.

image of China. All of the selected films articulated an idea of China for international audiences. Some of the films involved multi-regional collaborations; thus, to avoid duplication, the first region where the film was made was considered the standard of judgment. After removing error values, 1047 relevant films were found: 682 from Chinese mainland, 261 from Hong Kong, and 104 from Taiwan.<sup>1</sup> For historical and political reasons, we mainly compared the films of the three regions between 1949 and 2018. We used web crawler technology to grab titles and plot synopses from IMDb, reflecting the plot and setting of each film. Furthermore, information about each film’s region of production and release year was compiled to explore the process of transforming China’s image, as well as the factors related to the films’ social contexts.

The 1047 films selected from IMDb showed a multidimensional image of China. The quantitative analysis performed in this study endeavored to address three aspects of the main topics of the films from the three regions. We examined their mentions of China or the Chinese people; their specific propensities to treat particular topics; and their positive or negative attitudes in describing China. We used text mining in the analysis because film titles and plot synopses represent unstructured textual data.

First, for the contextual measurement, we used word embedding technology to predict the contexts associated with the term “China.” Google’s open-source toolkit, the Word2vec algorithm, can turn unstructured textual data into high-dimensional vector data. The similarity between words can be measured, and the context can be predicted by calculating the distance between the high-dimensional vectors.

Second, for topic analysis, films have changed according to the historical development of the different regions. The special relationship between Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan in the past has left the regions with closely related, yet very different, images of China. The films produced in the three regions often feature their preferred topics or events in their descriptions of China, and the LDA topic model can help tease these out.

Third, for sentiment analysis, we applied sentiment analysis to calculate the overall sentiment score of the relevant films from a more abstract perspective. Sentiment analysis entails the use of opinions or emotions (affective states) in the examination, cognition, and inference of subjective texts. The text hints at the varying feelings of different people. Researchers can use the trends that are discerned to analyze the public’s views or evaluations on a specific issue using two methods of analysis: the sentiment dictionary can be used to assess the rule matching method and the sentiment classification task can be set up based on the sentiment dictionary and text features.
4 Contexts in China-Related Films

Figure 1 reflects the changes in the number of China-related films from Chinese mainland (navy), Hong Kong (orange), and Taiwan (red) from 1950 to 2020. It illustrates the number of China-related films originating annually from Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. The number of films produced in Chinese mainland was relatively low for the three decades following the founding of the PRC, possibly due to the immaturity of film technology and the Cultural Revolution. Following China’s reform and opening-up, the number of films increased explosively, given the context of a booming economy and the need to build national confidence.

China-related films peaked in Hong Kong and Taiwan in the 1970s and 1990s, respectively, likely due to the cognitive reconstruction of the concept of “China” by their citizens. These periods coincided with turning points in relations between the two regions and the mainland. In 1971, the PRC resumed its lawful seat in the United Nations, prompting people in Hong Kong and Taiwan to pay attention to China’s position and build on China’s legacy in their films. The Sino-British Joint Declaration that returned Hong Kong to the PRC in 1997 was announced in 1984. Hong Kong, which had been ruled by the UK since 1841, re-examined its relationship with the mainland. This reassessment was directly reflected in films made in Hong Kong, and the number of relevant films increased in the following decade (1985–1995).

The results of Word2vec reveal that “single” denotes the term closest in films made in Chinese mainland to the focal word. In terms of specific context, “single” is mostly combined with “child” and “mother,” revealing the films’ preference for family-related settings and their attention to the one-child policy and single mothers. 5 Topics of China-Related Films

Although the films of the three regions influence each other to some degree, we postulated that the topics covered by the films would differ due to their respective social backgrounds and political environments. Bringing out these distinctions would facilitate understanding of the three regions’ national identities. The LDA topic model was deployed to perform unsupervised cluster analysis based on the corpus of film synopses. After considering the overall length of the text and the model’s actual effect,<sup>2</sup> the model with five topics was selected for the analysis.

Table 2 presents the top 20 words with the highest frequency corresponding to each topic after excluding words with no practical significance. The topic of war accounts for nearly 20% of the films, while films on kung fu and crime represent around 10% of the total. The topic of rural and urban has the lowest share in all three regions at less than 5%.
Figure 2 compares the proportions of kung fu (navy), kinship and love (orange), rural and urban (red), war (blue), and crime (green) topics in Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan.

Meanwhile, the distribution of topics in the three regions also differs. To ensure the robustness of the results, we performed an analysis of variance (ANOVA) and least significant difference (LSD) tests on the proportion of film topics in the different regions. The detailed results are shown in Table 3.

First, the proportion of films about kinship and love in Chinese mainland is significantly higher than that in Hong Kong and Taiwan. Films from Chinese mainland on this topic account for 55% of the total, 4% and 5% higher than Hong Kong and Taiwan, respectively. Therefore, mainland Chinese films tend to focus on everyday contexts and depict the feelings, social relations, and destinies of characters at the micro level. There are also significantly more films about rural and urban issues in Chinese mainland and in Taiwan than in Hong Kong, which is more modern and

In addition, the long-standing household registration (Hukou) system that divides the mainland Chinese population into urban and rural residents with strikingly different living conditions and social welfare support schemes may have led to more films depicting both the conflicts and the connections between rural and urban areas.

Second, most Hong Kong films focus on kung fu and crime. Table 3 shows that the number of Hong Kong films about kung fu (15%) is significantly higher than that of mainland Chinese films (11%), while the proportion of crime films in Hong Kong (12%) is greater than that in the mainland (9%) and in Taiwan (9%). The film industry in Hong Kong showed increased commercialization and marketization characteristics in its early stages of development, resulting in the flourishing of high-drama action films. Thus, kung fu and crime films in Hong Kong were of high quality and well received both at home and abroad. In addition, as a former British colony and an international port city, the Hong Kong film industry learned from the crime films that were popular in Europe and America.

Third, Taiwan’s proportion of war films is around 23%, slightly higher than the percentage of Chinese mainland (22%) and significantly higher than that of Hong Kong (20%). Taiwan has not been the main battlefield of any modern war, but it does show a preference for war stories in its films, especially the AJW. The Taiwanese share China’s historical
13 A UNITED TALE OF THREE REGIONS: A CENTURY

memory of wars as an aspect of their ethnicity. Thus, a group of patriotic filmmakers in Taiwan uphold the ethnic, kinship, and geographical relationships between Taiwan and the mainland through military films set in various modern wars (Chen 2008). However, Japan colonized Taiwan from 1895 to 1945, and many Japanese elements therefore persist in Taiwanese films, partly validating Homi Bhabha (1994)’s postcolonialism.

The above analysis primarily focused on the different proportions of major China-related topics in the cinema of the three regions, examining them at a static level. Films favor different topics at different times, depending on their social contexts, meaning that the topics prevalent at any given point may change. Thus, the topic of war is used as an example to introduce time, allowing for a dynamic comparative analysis.

Some war films are filled with nationalist emotions, stimulating anger toward aggressors, nostalgia for the homeland, and sympathy for the tragic destinies of victims. Some films about war raise crisis awareness, strengthen historical identity, and enhance social unity. Other war-related films construct fantastic images of heroes, showcasing their wise decisions. The three regions commonly give wars significance against the backdrop of historical efforts and the consciousness of these efforts to transform China into a modern nation-state. According to the Western ethos, only countries with such consciousness may claim their rights in the international arena (Duara 1995: 4). Hence, war is a topic suitable for discussion in all Chinese regions. War films are often based on historical facts and influenced by political, diplomatic, and other social characteristics. The distribution of this topic, as shown by the proportion of films dealing with it, was extracted by year. To smooth out extreme values, the moving average was calculated using the proportion values from the previous three years. Missing values and curves are plotted in Fig. 3.
Figure 3 reflects the changes in proportions of China-related films on the topic of war in Chinese mainland (orange), Hong Kong (navy), and Taiwan (red) from 1950 to 2020.

First, victories in war often lead to peaks in the number of war films in certain periods, such as in the 1950s in Chinese mainland. China was able to end its long history of war and establish a new nation after its victory in the AJW in 1945 and the Chinese Civil War (CCW) in 1949. Filled with joy, the people praised their war heroes and their new life, and this pride and happiness were reflected in the films of that era. The proportion of films on this topic rose significantly and peaked at 33% in 1954, right after the Korean Armistice Agreement was signed in the Korean War
Y. CHEN ET AL.

blocks.content: (KW), which the PRC considered a victory. Similarly, the proportion of war films peaked in Chinese mainland around 1985 and 1995, the two years coinciding with the 40th and 50th anniversaries of the victory in the AJW. With the exception of a peak at nearly 24% in 2009, which met the 60th anniversary of the founding of the PRC, the proportion of war films in Chinese mainland has mostly remained below 22% since the beginning of the twenty-first century. During this period, the mainland’s economy was growing rapidly, and its films’ focus on peaceful development may have led to a reduction in the number of war films.

Second, international circumstances significantly influenced the extent to which this topic was highlighted in the films made in the three regions. War films often fulfill the political function of building nationalist feelings, which may explain the peak achieved by war films in the 1970s in Taiwan, when it confronted diplomatic turmoil. The United Nations ended Taiwan’s membership in 1971. In 1972, Japan severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan, triggering a series of severances involving 27 countries. Japan then became the main object of resentment for Taiwan (Li 1997). War films reshaped historical memory at that time. The Taiwanese authorities hoped to relieve people’s disappointment and
13 A UNITED TALE OF THREE REGIONS: A CENTURY

anxiety and rebuild national confidence through such films. The proportion of Taiwanese war films reached its highest level, about 28%, in 1978. In contrast, war films declined to a low level (approximately 20%) in Chinese mainland during the late 1970s and early 1980s, a fact that could be associated with the establishment of diplomatic relations between the PRC, Japan, and the U.S. At that time, Chinese mainland needed to show an attitude of avoidance and restraint toward war.

Third, the war film curve of Taiwan reflects the change in its identity. Taiwan’s attitude toward Japan and the AJW reflects these temporal shifts. Lee Teng-hui, who was strongly pro-Japanese and pro-American, was elected Chairman of the Kuomintang (KMT, or Chinese Nationalist Party) in 1990. He visited the U.S. in 1995 as the leader of Taiwan and broadcast his support for Taiwan’s independence. From 1995 to 2000, the proportion of war films continued to decline, reaching a low of 13% in 2000. Taiwan’s sense of identity with China weakened during his tenure, and the trauma of being colonized subsided. Instead, postcolonial nostalgia was evoked, and a new culture with a pro-Japanese color gained prominence. War films fell out of favor in Taiwan as a result. However, the proportion of war films was relatively high after the turn of the twenty-first century, especially under KMT rule between 2008 and 2016 when it rose to more than 22%. In contrast, the number of war films fell when the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) came to power and advocated Taiwan’s independence (e.g., 2000–2008, 2016–present), perhaps because of the attitude toward the PRC of the administration concerned. Currently, the KMT aspires to normalize relations with the PRC, whereas the DPP advocates for the opposite, calling for a distinctive national identity for Taiwan.

The people of Hong Kong demonstrate relatively little interest in war films compared to those in Chinese mainland and Taiwan, perhaps because Hong Kong films have long been marketized and are less subject to political influences. Few war films have recently been produced in Hong Kong. In 2011, for example, the proportion was only 13%. The reason is presumably that the region’s war history is gradually receding, and therefore young audiences have no memory of war.

6 Sentiments of China-Related Films

The sentiment analysis of a text directly reflects the general positive and negative tones of films from the three regions. Figure 4 demonstrates that the general average sentiment scores of films made in the three regions are all greater than 0, implying that China is positively viewed in all three regions. Table 4 shows the results of the ANOVA and LSD tests on the sentiment scores in the three regions. No significant difference is found between the scores of Chinese mainland and Taiwan at 0.16 and 0.17, respectively. Hong Kong has the lowest score (0.03) with far fewer sentiment factors. We calculated the moving averages of the scores for the three regions by year and drew curves to accurately reflect the changes in the sentiments of the films produced in each region (Fig. 5).
Figure 4 compares the average film sentiment scores of Chinarelated films in Chinese mainland (navy), Hong Kong (red), and Taiwan (orange).

blocks.content: The sentiment scores calculated for the films from the mainland are intricately related to China’s political and economic circumstances. In the early days of the PRC, film sentiment in Chinese mainland was very low, ranging from −0.2 to −0.1. Subsequently, the political movements from 1958 to 1978 prompted particularly high positive sentiments in mainland films. For example, the films of 1959 reached the highest sentiment score of 0.32, a level almost 1.8 standard deviations above the average value
Y. CHEN ET AL.

(0.10).<sup>7</sup> However, as political bubbles such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution burst by the 1980s, the moods depicted in the films also turned sour: the score was −0.01 in 1982 and −0.1 in 1986. Often dubbed “Scar culture,” many of the films of this period focused on tragic destinies and traumas, reflecting the distortion of the national spirit and the deterioration of interpersonal relationships. Since the late 1990s, with the return of Hong Kong and Macao and the economic boom, the sentiment score of films produced in Chinese mainland has risen significantly, reaching 0.24, about 1 standard deviation above the mean, in 2001. This increase reveals the exploration of subjectivity by mainland films, which explains their optimistic and nationalist sentiments.

A complex and changeable cross-strait relationship has been forged between Taiwan and Chinese mainland due to their shared historical and political contexts. The early Minnan people who migrated to Taiwan, the Japanese colonial government, and the later Republic of China administration regarded Taiwan merely as a small island on the edge of their territories, deeming it far less critical than the mainland (Berry and Lu 2005: 4). Given the influence of different policies, such contrasts present diverse social and cultural states, as well as varying opinions and sentiments.

Taiwanese films produced during the period of martial law (1949–1987) were anti-Communist but not anti-China, exhibiting a “low-highlow” trend in their sentiment scores. In 1949, the KMT retreated to Taiwan and implemented a strict martial law policy. Films were used as ideological tools for political propaganda and were increasingly controlled by the KMT government. A substantial number of films made in Taiwan in the late 1960s portrayed hatred toward the mainland, and their corresponding sentiment scores were also very negative. For example, the scores from 1967 to 1974 were all lower than 0. In the mid-1970s, the focus of Taiwan-made films shifted from an anti-Communist to an anti-Japanese stance because of the diplomatic turmoil at the time. Resentment over the severance of diplomatic relations with Japan was expressed through the memory of the victory in the AJW, which created the growing sentiment toward China seen during this period, reaching 0.35 in 1976, approximately 1.5 standard deviations higher than Taiwan’s annual average score. The sentiment scores declined in the late 1970s,

and their low values continued into the 1980s, reaching a low of −0.04 in 1983. Taiwan’s film industry began to produce anti-Communist films such as Message to Compatriots in Taiwan (1979) as it constructed a cultural orthodoxy in the context of the mainland’s Taiwan policy.

The KMT government announced the end of martial law in 1987. The same year, the isolation of the two sides of the strait ended. The sentiment scores rose rapidly immediately after the period of martial law (1987–1990), reaching a local peak of 0.25 in 1993, almost 1 standard deviation above the mean, reflecting both sides’ desire to communicate. The Taiwanese could visit relatives on the mainland and see the thus-far imagined China. The higher sentiment scores of Taiwanese films in the late 1980s to the early 1990s may partly be attributable to this ability. After martial law ended, cinema no longer had the power to construct its version of China’s reality; rather, it instinctively revealed Taiwanese feelings.

Since the 1990s, the emotional changes noted in Taiwanese films have been closely tied to the region’s power politics. Cross-strait relations fell to a freezing point in 1995 following Lee Teng-hui’s remarks on Taiwan’s independence. The 1995–1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis made the situation even tenser, which explains that the sentiment scores of Taiwanese films related to China touched a nadir of only 0.02 in 1996. However, after the crisis, the sentiment score of Taiwanese films rose sharply, holding at about 0.38 from 1999 to 2001. In 2000, the DPP came to power for the first time, and Chen Shui-bian was elected Taiwan’s leader. He reiterated Taiwan’s independence, as well as carrying out several de-China-lization policies such as constitutional reform, corresponding to the downward trend of the sentiment scores in that period. The result is evident in the downward trend of film sentiment scores from 2001 to 2004, which reached a low of −0.1 in 2004. Then, in 2008 the KMT candidate, Ma Ying-jeou, was elected Taiwan’s leader. At the same time as he promoted a peaceful exchange between Taiwan and the mainland based on the 1992 Consensus, from 2009 the sentiment score rose, peaking at 0.33 in 2012. Tsai Ing-Wen (member of the DPP) has been in power since 2016 and has stoked hostility between the two sides of the strait. Consequently, the moods of the films show a downward trend again, even as the overall sentiment remains positive.

Hong Kong and the mainland have made different journeys and developed distinct social environments, creating separate emotional cognitions and cultural expressions. This separation is reflected in Hong Kong films,
Y. CHEN ET AL.

in which sentiment sometimes moves in the opposite direction to that of the mainland. Hong Kong’s economy was booming in the 1960s and 1970s, while the opposite was true of the political and fiscal environment on the mainland. Some Hong Kong leftists launched an armed uprising against the British colonial government in 1967, but this drive gave rise to Hong Kong’s aversion to nationalist ideology. It may have contributed to the negative sentiments toward China from 1967 to 1974, with sentiment scores below 0. The PRC and the UK issued a joint declaration in 1984, agreeing to the return of Hong Kong’s sovereignty to the PRC in 1997. The significant changes they were facing caused anxiety among Hong Kong people. In the words of author Leung Ping-kwan (2012: 243), “what most people worried about in the 1980s was losing their existing way of life and the obliteration of the existing culture.” This assertion may explain the emotional low points registered in Hong Kong films from 1987 to 1995, most of whose values were negative, with a low of −0.11 in 1994. The increasingly frequent exchanges and growing cooperation with the mainland after the turn of the century led to progressively more positive feelings toward China in Hong Kong films. During this time the sentiment score rose, reaching 0.25 in 2011. However, the mood turned negative again because of political protests such as Occupy Central with Love and Peace, and in 2018 the sentiment score was just 0.03.

The above analysis, to some extent, showed that there are many factors influencing the China-related emotions articulated in the films of the three regions, although our aim was not to establish clear and robust causality. Among these factors, the relationship between the three regions is the most significant, followed by the economic and social environments. In this sense, the image of China is not merely a cultural concept; it is also greatly influenced by politics. Economic and social factors may also determine the sentiments expressed in films. The amplification of national strengths in periods of economic optimism and the resulting relaxed social environment represent ideal conditions for the proliferation of the arts, which shift from their reliance on the West to focus on indigenous expressions with a positive mindset.
7 Conclusion

This chapter presents a panoramic view of China (in the West) through a century of films from Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan from the perspective of postcolonialism. It did so by adopting machine
13 A UNITED TALE OF THREE REGIONS: A CENTURY

learning methods (word embedding technology and LDA topic model) to explore the transformations observed in the image of China in films produced in the three regions over the last 100 years. The discrete historical contexts of the three regions have led to the construction of three distinct societies, even though all are rooted in Chinese culture. These social existences are articulated as divergent cultural characteristics in the films of the three regions, which convey different images of China to the international community. Their manifestations of China and Chinese culture have also transformed in tandem with the major historical events that the three regions have experienced over the last century.

The image of China is positive and realistic in films produced in Chinese mainland, and the number of such films is correlated with China’s economic and political circumstances. For example, explosive growth may be observed in the number of films produced in China in periods of social stability and economic prosperity such as the twenty-first century. In addition, most contexts in which the word “China” appears in mainland films are related to the country’s historical memory and future development. The sentiment scores of mainland films also correspond to the times. Greater optimism may be noted in films made during the Cultural Revolution, echoing political demands, and after the turn of the twenty-first century, as a natural expression of improved living standards and rising morale. Conversely, low moods were depicted in films made during the 1980s, a period of recovery from the traumas of the Cultural Revolution.

In Taiwan-made films, China’s image is ambiguous and changeable, and the perspective is more individual than the standpoint of the mainland. The number of films produced in Taiwan fluctuates slightly, but remains relatively low compared to the number of films produced in mainland and Hong Kong. Taiwanese films primarily focus on personal topics, stories that reveal the changing times. In particular, Japanese and war elements proliferate in Taiwan-produced films, reflecting the persistent influence of Japanese colonization on Taiwanese society. In terms of sentiment, Taiwanese films are influenced by politics. Their sentiment scores related to China touched nadirs at important historical moments, such as the island losing its membership of the United Nations in 1972 and Lee Teng-hui’s visit to the U.S. in 1995.

Hong Kong films showcase China through its traditions and international elements. Hong Kong was the first of the three regions to commercialize its films and achieve worldwide success. Consequently, the number of films produced in Hong Kong peaked between the 1970s and
Y. CHEN ET AL.

the 1990s. Subsequently, Hong Kong film production began to decline due to the boom in the mainland Chinese film industry and the rise in co-productions. Hong Kong-made films typically transcend reality, focusing on kung fu and crime, combining elements of traditional Chinese culture with Hollywood business models, and expressing the unyielding character of the Chinese people. Nevertheless, the sentiment scores of Hong Kong films are influenced by political events, revealing public confusion about the erstwhile colony’s identity and future after its return to China. Sentiment scores increased after the beginning of the current century but have dropped again because of the political turmoil of recent years.

The results of our analysis of the content, topics, and sentiments in the films of the three regions reveal that political, economic, cultural, and ideological factors combine to influence China’s image in the West. Cinema is a cultural product, and culture is both a practice and a system of symbols and meanings (Sewell 2005: 160–161). The reality is distorted by the consciousness of creators when films reflect society. In addition, truth and falsehood cannot be defined via simple binary distinctions: they are complex, multi-layered, and contextual systems influenced by national strengths and diplomacy. The vast increase in China’s national strength has made filmmakers in the three regions increasingly eager to hone their image of China and spread local awareness of change in the West through their films.

The results of the quantitative analyses also validate some of the theories outlined in Sect. 2 of this chapter, particularly postcolonialism. In the 1980s, mainland films experienced a period of emotional depression because of the historical introspection of their directors, but they also offered the West an opportunity to understand Chinese mainland. Numerous Japanese elements persist in Taiwanese films, revealing the region’s close relationship with its colonial history. Likewise, Hong Kong films demonstrate a cultural attachment to the suzerain state similar to that of Taiwanese films. To echo Bhabha’s (1994) concepts, Hong Kong and Taiwan represent regions where multiple cultures congregate, allowing intercultural communications to occur in a third space and construct a new intersubjectivity.

However, some limitations merit attention. First, it is necessary to briefly acknowledge the status quo of the three regions’ film industries. Films produced in Hong Kong and Taiwan have recently distanced themselves from those made on the mainland. For example, no Chineselanguage films, whether local or mainland productions, achieved a top
13 A UNITED TALE OF THREE REGIONS: A CENTURY

10 box office ranking in either region in 2019. Conversely, 8 of the top 10 mainland films were locally made, reflecting the boom in the mainland Chinese film industry and the decline of Hong Kong and Taiwanese films. Some mainland films have succeeded locally but have failed to replicate their success in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and overseas markets, perhaps because of political factors or a lack of openness and inclusiveness. Second, classification-related difficulties prevented us from evaluating the features of co-productions.

Nevertheless, in spite of the drawbacks, this chapter makes several contributions to the literature. First, its methodology contributes to cultural research in the social sciences. It directs cultural studies away from the analysis of micro and individual cases to large-scale cultural data. The joint use of three quantitative methods means that the results are more comprehensive, and the features of the three regions’ cultures are more objective and accurate than conclusions drawn from single cultural phenomena. Thus, this chapter better reflects social reality at the macro level. Second, the findings of this chapter increase understanding of the relationship between the three regions, a relationship that changed dramatically in the second half of the past century. Knowledge of the similarities and idiosyncrasies in the respective cultures of the three regions is not only useful for a deeper understanding of the distinctive development process of Chinese culture, but also helps to clarify the regions’ ethnic, cultural, and emotional connections, which go beyond politics. Finally, the results of this chapter show that the image of China in the West as it is portrayed in movies is a combination of its self-portrayal and selection by IMDb editors and users worldwide who all have their own tastes and ideologies.

    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)

    results.append({
        'Model': name,
        'R²': round(r2, 4),
        'MSE': round(mse, 4)
    })
results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

# Sort the DataFrame by R² in descending order
results_df = results_df.sort_values(by='R²', ascending=False)
results_df

Afterword

As Editor-in-Chief of ACM Transactions on Social Computing and former Editor-in-Chief of Journal of Social Computing, I have had the privilege of reviewing and publishing research at the intersection of machine learning and the social sciences. While **social computing** is often associated with the design of digital systems that support human interactions, its deeper purpose lies in fostering dialogue between social and computational domains—bringing social theory into conversation with computational theory, social models into dialogue with computational models, and social data into interaction with computational networks and interactions—all in service of understanding, creating, and computing social goods, flourishing, and innovation (Evans, Fu, & Luo, Journal of Social Computing, 2020). Professor Yunsong Chen’s present book aligns with this vision: it demonstrates how machine learning can **bridge domains**—connecting theory, data, and models to advance both scientific insight and social value.

This book builds on research previously published in Journal of Contemporary China, The Journal of Chinese Sociology, and Scientific Reports. While the chapters present novel applications of machine learning to cultural texts and social dynamics, their deeper significance lies not in technical novelty, but in their methodological orientation—one that responds to a growing imperative in social computing: to move beyond isolated technical innovation and toward a more integrated, reflexive, and socially responsible practice.

AFTERWORD

The work draws on the conceptual clarity of Hofman, Sharma, and Watts (Science, 2017), who first articulated the tension between prediction and explanation in social systems—a tension that remains central to the field. It also builds on Luo, Liu, Yang, and Fu (Journal of Chinese Sociology, 2019), whose triadic dialogue framework centers on the mutual shaping of theory, data, and models. This cyclical model resists data-first or model-first approaches, emphasizing theory-driven research. In this light, the book’s focus on underrepresented communities and cultural phenomena is not incidental—it is methodologically intentional.

The chapters reflect this orientation: theoretical questions guide model design; model outputs prompt reflection on meaning; empirical findings feed back into theory. Yet the field—and this book—can go further. Future work must bridge prediction and explanation, using machine learning not just to uncover patterns, but to generate testable hypotheses—validated through statistical inference, causal modeling, and qualitative engagement.

This is not a call to abandon machine learning. It is a call to **reclaim** it—not as a substitute for social science, but as a tool for deepening it. The best models are not the most complex, but the most transparent, interpretable, and grounded in real-world context.

The book reflects a broader shift in science. For too long, social computing was seen as a Western export. But the work here—and the triadic dialogue—shows innovation is global. Scholars in China and beyond are not just applying methods—they are shaping them.

It responds to Lazer et al. (Science, 2020), who called for integration and responsibility across disciplines and cultures. This book reflects that vision—in its focus on cultural meaning, institutional context, and collective behavior.

This is not a summary of trends. It is a record of sustained, high-quality work—work that has influenced research, informed policy, and inspired better questions. It signals a shift: innovation in social computing comes from many places. Global diversity strengthens the science.

For those who study human behavior through data, this book offers more than methods. It offers a model: rigorous, thoughtful, and deeply attentive to the social world. It is a reminder that the best research does not just predict the future—it helps us understand the present, and think clearly about the kind of world we wish to build.
